title: What is Programming & How Code Runs
shortDescription: Execution pipeline: compilation, bytecode (.class), JVM runtime mechanics, and the JIT compiler.
searchableTerms: Q: Why does the same .class file run on Windows x86 and macOS ARM without recompilation?

markdownContent:
## Overview
Java source code (`.java`) compiles into platform-independent bytecode (`.class`), which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) loads, verifies, and optimizes into native machine code at runtime using the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler.

---

## Architecture

```
[ Source (.java) ] ──(javac)──► [ Bytecode (.class) ] ──(JVM)──► [ Native CPU Code ]
```

### Execution Stages

1. **Compilation (`javac`):** The Java compiler parses source code, validates syntax and static types, and emits bytecode instructions (`.class` file, prefixed with magic bytes `0xCAFEBABE`).
2. **Class Loading & Verification:** The JVM ClassLoader loads bytecode into memory. The Bytecode Verifier checks structural constraints, stack bounds, and type safety before execution.
3. **Execution & JIT Optimization:** The JVM interpreter starts executing bytecode immediately. The JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler identifies frequently executed methods ("hot code") and compiles them directly into native host CPU instructions (x86, ARM) at runtime.

### Execution Model Comparison

| Model | Source to Execution | Examples | Portability | Startup Speed | Peak Performance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Purely Compiled** | Source -> Machine Binary | C, C++, Rust, Go | Platform-dependent binary | Instant | Maximum |
| **Purely Interpreted** | Source parsed & evaluated line-by-line | Python, Ruby, PHP | Portable scripts | Instant | Lower |
| **JVM Hybrid** | Source -> Bytecode (`javac`) -> JIT Native | Java, Kotlin, Scala | Write Once, Run Anywhere | Moderate | Near-native |

---

## Pitfalls

- **Filename Mismatch:** A `public` class must match its filename exactly (`public class OrderService` must reside in `OrderService.java`). Java is strictly case-sensitive.
- **Passing File Extension to Runtime:** Executing `java App.class` fails with `ClassNotFoundException`. Pass the class name only: `java App`.

---

## Example

```java
public class HardwareProbe {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int cpuCores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
        long maxMemoryMB = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024);
        String javaVersion = System.getProperty("java.specification.version");

        System.out.printf("Java %s | CPU Cores: %d | Max Heap: %d MB%n",
                javaVersion, cpuCores, maxMemoryMB);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Java 21 | CPU Cores: 16 | Max Heap: 4096 MB
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why does the same `.class` file run on Windows x86 and macOS ARM without recompilation?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** Bytecode is CPU-agnostic. The OS-specific JVM running on Windows or macOS translates those identical bytecode instructions into the host CPU's native instruction set at runtime.
</details>

shortDescription: Architectural layers: the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), Runtime Environment (JRE), and Development Kit (JDK) with environment configuration.

Execute bytecode on target host OS
cheatSheetText: Tier Full Name Primary Purpose Key Contents Target Audience JVM Java Virtual Machine Execute bytecode on target host OS ClassLoader, Execution Engine, JIT, Garbage Collector Machine runtime JRE Java Runtime Environment Run compiled Java bytecode applications JVM + Core Class Libraries (java.base, Collections, I/O) End-users / Production Servers JDK Java Development Kit Author, compile, debug, and package Java code JRE + Tools (javac, jar, jshell, jlink, jdb) Software Engineers & CI/CD
markdownContent:
## Overview
The Java platform is organized into three concentric tiers: the JVM executes bytecode, the JRE packages the JVM with core class libraries, and the JDK provides the complete development toolset including compilers, debuggers, and packaging utilities.

---

## Hierarchy

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ JDK (Development Kit)                                       │
│ javac, jar, jshell, jdb, javap, jlink                       │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ JRE (Runtime Environment)                               │ │
│ │ Standard Libraries (java.base, Collections, I/O, Net)   │ │
│ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│ │ │ JVM (Virtual Machine)                               │ │ │
│ │ │ ClassLoader, JIT Compiler, Garbage Collector, Stack │ │ │
│ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **JVM (Java Virtual Machine):** The low-level execution engine. It allocates memory, manages the thread call stack and garbage-collected heap, and translates bytecode into host CPU instructions. It cannot compile source code.
- **JRE (Java Runtime Environment):** Bundles the JVM with compiled standard class libraries (`java.lang`, `java.util`, `java.io`). Required strictly for running existing applications. Since Java 9, custom lightweight runtimes are created via `jlink` rather than standalone JRE installers.
- **JDK (Java Development Kit):** The full developer suite containing the JRE, JVM, and CLI tools: `javac` (compiler), `jar` (packager), `jshell` (REPL), `javap` (disassembler), and `jdb` (debugger).

### Component Comparison Reference

| Tier | Full Name | Primary Purpose | Key Contents | Target Audience |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **JVM** | Java Virtual Machine | Execute bytecode on target host OS | ClassLoader, Execution Engine, JIT, Garbage Collector | Machine runtime |
| **JRE** | Java Runtime Environment | Run compiled Java bytecode applications | JVM + Core Class Libraries (`java.base`, Collections, I/O) | End-users / Production Servers |
| **JDK** | Java Development Kit | Author, compile, debug, and package Java code | JRE + Tools (`javac`, `jar`, `jshell`, `jlink`, `jdb`) | Software Engineers & CI/CD |

---

## Environment

Two environment variables configure the development toolchain:

- **`JAVA_HOME`:** Points to the JDK installation root directory (e.g., `C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-21` on Windows or `/usr/lib/jvm/java-21` on Linux).
- **`PATH`:** Must append `%JAVA_HOME%\bin` (Windows) or `$JAVA_HOME/bin` (Linux/macOS) so the operating system locates `javac` and `java` globally.

---

## Pitfalls

- **`JAVA_HOME` Path Ending in `/bin`:** `JAVA_HOME` must point to the JDK root directory, not its `bin` folder. Build tools like Maven and Gradle append `/bin` internally and fail if it is duplicated.
- **Toolchain Version Mismatch:** Having multiple Java installations where `PATH` resolves a different version than `JAVA_HOME`. Verify consistency by running `javac -version` and `java -version`.

---

## Example

```java
public class RuntimeEnvironmentProbe {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Java Home    : " + System.getProperty("java.home"));
        System.out.println("Java Version : " + System.getProperty("java.version"));
        System.out.println("JVM Vendor   : " + System.getProperty("java.vm.vendor"));
        System.out.println("JVM Name     : " + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Java Home    : C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-21
Java Version : 21.0.2
JVM Vendor   : Oracle Corporation
JVM Name     : Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why do production Docker containers for Java microservices rarely include a full JDK?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** Production containers only need to execute pre-compiled `.class` or `.jar` files, not compile source code. Omitting the JDK (compiler, debuggers) minimizes image size (reducing attack surface and cold-start transfer time), often utilizing a trimmed JRE or a custom image built with `jlink`.
</details>

shortDescription: Class declaration structure, main method anatomy, bytecode execution, and basic terminal output with println.

markdownContent:
## Overview
Every standalone Java application executes starting from the `main` method entry point declared inside a class, producing basic terminal output via `System.out.println`.

---

## Program Structure

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}
```

### Keyword & Signature Reference

| Token | Scope / Type | Purpose | If Omitted |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`public`** | Access Modifier | Allows the JVM runtime launcher to access the entry point from outside | Runtime access error |
| **`class`** | Keyword | Declares the type boundary container (must match filename `.java`) | Compilation error |
| **`static`** | Memory Modifier | Binds `main` to the class directly without allocating a heap object | Fails with `Main method is not static` |
| **`void`** | Return Type | Specifies that the entry method returns no value to the runtime | Compilation error |
| **`main`** | Identifier | The exact entry point name sought by the JVM launcher | Runtime error: `Main method not found` |
| **`String[] args`** | Parameter | Receives CLI arguments passed to the program (`java App arg1 arg2`) | Method signature mismatch |

---

## Basic Console Output

Java provides `System.out` (`java.io.PrintStream`) for writing text to the standard output stream:

- **`System.out.println("text")`:** Emits text and appends a platform-specific line separator (`\r\n` on Windows, `\n` on Unix).
- **`System.out.print("text")`:** Emits text inline without terminating the current line.

---

## Pitfalls

- **Incorrect `main` Signature:** Declaring `public void main(String[] args)` (omitting `static`) compiles cleanly but crashes at runtime with `Main method is not static in class`.
- **Class and File Name Mismatch:** If the class is `public class App`, the file MUST be named `App.java`. Case mismatch will cause a compilation error.

---

## Example

```java
public class ProgramLifecycleDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.print("Initializing program... ");
        System.out.println("DONE");
        System.out.println("Hello, Java Platform!");
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Initializing program... DONE
Hello, Java Platform!
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why must the `main` method in a standard Java application be declared `static`?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** Declaring `main` as `static` allows the JVM runtime to invoke it directly on the class (`HelloWorld.main(...)`) without needing to construct an instance of the class via `new HelloWorld()` beforehand.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Java is a statically typed language with 8 built-in primitive data types stored directly on the stack for maximum execution performance, complemented by local variable type inference (`var`).

---

## Primitive Types Specification

| Type | Size | Default | Range / Format | Literal Suffix | Wrapper Class |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`byte`** | 1 byte (8 bits) | `0` | `-128` to `127` | None (explicit cast) | `Byte` |
| **`short`** | 2 bytes (16 bits) | `0` | `-32,768` to `32,767` | None | `Short` |
| **`int`** | 4 bytes (32 bits) | `0` | `-2,147,483,648` to `2,147,483,647` | None (integer default) | `Integer` |
| **`long`** | 8 bytes (64 bits) | `0L` | `~ -9.22 × 10^18` to `~ 9.22 × 10^18` | `L` or `l` (e.g. `1000L`) | `Long` |
| **`float`** | 4 bytes (32 bits) | `0.0f` | IEEE 754 32-bit (~ 7 decimal digits) | `F` or `f` (e.g. `3.14F`) | `Float` |
| **`double`** | 8 bytes (64 bits) | `0.0d` | IEEE 754 64-bit (~ 15-17 decimal digits) | `D` or `d` (decimal default) | `Double` |
| **`char`** | 2 bytes (16 bits) | `'\u0000'` | `0` to `65,535` (Unicode UTF-16) | Single quotes `'A'` | `Character` |
| **`boolean`** | 1 bit logical | `false` | `true` or `false` | None | `Boolean` |

---

## Declaration and Type Inference

```java
int count = 10;                         // Explicit primitive typing
var username = "Alice";                 // Local type inference (Java 10+)
long transactionId = 9_876_543_210L;    // Numeric readability underscores (Java 7+)
```

### Identifier Rules
1. Must begin with a letter (`a-z`, `A-Z`), underscore (`_`), or dollar sign (`$`).
2. Subsequent characters may include digits (`0-9`). Cannot use reserved keywords (`class`, `int`, etc.).
3. Standard conventions use `lowerCamelCase` for variable names.

---

## Memory Allocation: Stack vs Heap

- **Primitives:** Stored directly inside thread stack frames. Access is instantaneous with zero garbage collector overhead.
- **Reference Types:** Variables hold memory references (pointers) located on the stack that point to object data allocated on the garbage-collected heap.

---

## Pitfalls

- **Missing `L` on Large Integers:** `long n = 3000000000;` fails to compile (`integer number too large`) because literals default to 32-bit `int`. Append `L`: `3000000000L`.
- **Missing `F` on Float Literals:** `float f = 3.14;` fails to compile (`lossy conversion from double to float`) because decimals default to 64-bit `double`. Append `F`: `3.14F`.
- **Silent Integer Overflow:** Primitives wrap around silently on overflow in two's-complement arithmetic: `(byte)(127 + 1)` evaluates to `-128` without throwing an exception. Use `Math.addExact()` when bounds validation is required.

---

## Example

```java
public class PrimitivesDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int maxInt = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        long maxLong = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        double pi = 3.141592653589793;
        boolean isActive = true;

        System.out.printf("int range: [%d to %d]%n", Integer.MIN_VALUE, maxInt);
        System.out.printf("long max : %d%n", maxLong);
        System.out.printf("double   : %.5f | boolean: %b%n", pi, isActive);

        // Silent overflow demonstration
        byte counter = 127;
        counter++;
        System.out.println("byte overflow (127 + 1): " + counter);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
int range: [-2147483648 to 2147483647]
long max : 9223372036854775807
double   : 3.14159 | boolean: true
byte overflow (127 + 1): -128
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why does `float price = 19.99;` fail to compile?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** Decimal number literals default to 64-bit `double` in Java. Assigning a 64-bit `double` to a 32-bit `float` causes a compile-time "possible lossy conversion" error. The fix is to append `F` (`19.99F`) or cast: `(float) 19.99`.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Operators evaluate expressions across variables and literals, governed by operand type rules, associativity, and a 14-level precedence hierarchy.

---

## Operator Categories

| Category | Operators | Description | Example | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Arithmetic** | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` | Basic mathematical operations and remainder | `7 % 3` | `1` |
| **Unary** | `++`, `--`, `+`, `-`, `!`, `~` | Increment/decrement, sign negation, logical NOT, bitwise NOT | `!false`, `~0` | `true`, `-1` |
| **Relational** | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | Binary comparisons; returns `boolean` | `10 >= 5` | `true` |
| **Logical** | `&&`, `||`, `!` | Short-circuit boolean combinations | `true && false` | `false` |
| **Ternary** | `? :` | Compact inline conditional expression | `(x > 0) ? 1 : -1` | `1` |
| **Bitwise / Shift** | `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>` | Bit-level operations and signed/unsigned shifts | `1 << 3` | `8` |
| **Assignment** | `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=` | Evaluate and assign in-place | `x += 5` | `x = x + 5` |

---

## Precedence Hierarchy (High to Low)

| Level | Operators | Description | Associativity |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **1 (Highest)** | `()`, `[]`, `.` | Grouping parentheses, array indexing, member access | Left to Right |
| **2** | `++`, `--`, `+`, `-`, `!`, `~` | Unary pre-increment/decrement, sign, logical/bitwise NOT | Right to Left |
| **3** | `*`, `/`, `%` | Multiplication, division, modulo | Left to Right |
| **4** | `+`, `-` | Addition, subtraction, string concatenation | Left to Right |
| **5** | `<<`, `>>`, `>>>` | Signed left shift, signed right shift, unsigned right shift | Left to Right |
| **6** | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `instanceof` | Relational comparisons and type inspection | Left to Right |
| **7** | `==`, `!=` | Equality and inequality | Left to Right |
| **8** | `&` | Bitwise AND / Eager boolean AND | Left to Right |
| **9** | `^` | Bitwise XOR / Eager boolean XOR | Left to Right |
| **10** | `|` | Bitwise OR / Eager boolean OR | Left to Right |
| **11** | `&&` | Logical short-circuit AND | Left to Right |
| **12** | `||` | Logical short-circuit OR | Left to Right |
| **13** | `? :` | Ternary conditional | Right to Left |
| **14 (Lowest)** | `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=` | Assignment operators | Right to Left |

---

## Core Mechanics

### Integer Truncation vs Floating-Point Division
```java
int a = 7 / 2;       // 3   (fractional part discarded)
double b = 7.0 / 2;  // 3.5 (promoted to double)
int rem = 7 % 2;     // 1   (remainder)
```

### Prefix vs Postfix
- **Prefix (`++i`):** Increments variable first, then yields the incremented value to the enclosing expression.
- **Postfix (`i++`):** Yields the current value to the enclosing expression first, then increments variable in memory.

### Short-Circuit Evaluation
- `&&` halts evaluation immediately if the left operand is `false` (right side is never executed).
- `||` halts evaluation immediately if the left operand is `true` (right side is never executed).
- `&` and `|` always evaluate both sides unconditionally.

---

## Pitfalls

- **Accidental Integer Division:** `double pct = (score / total) * 100;` yields `0.0` if both are integers. Cast at least one operand: `((double) score / total) * 100`.
- **Eager `&` in Guard Conditions:** Writing `str != null & str.length() > 0` causes a `NullPointerException` when `str` is null because single `&` evaluates the right side. Always use `&&`.
- **Using `==` on Objects:** `==` verifies reference memory addresses. For object and string equality, use `.equals()`.

---

## Example

```java
public class OperatorsDemo {
    public static final int PERM_READ  = 1 << 0; // 0001 (1)
    public static final int PERM_WRITE = 1 << 1; // 0010 (2)

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Safe short-circuit null guard
        String token = null;
        boolean isValid = (token != null) && (token.length() > 3);
        System.out.println("Null guard passed safely: " + isValid);

        // Bitmask permission flags
        int userPerms = PERM_READ | PERM_WRITE;
        boolean canRead = (userPerms & PERM_READ) != 0;
        userPerms &= ~PERM_WRITE; // Revoke WRITE

        System.out.printf("Has READ: %b | Has WRITE: %b%n",
                canRead, (userPerms & PERM_WRITE) != 0);

        // Ternary conditional
        int score = 75;
        String status = (score >= 60) ? "PASS" : "FAIL";
        System.out.println("Result: " + status);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Null guard passed safely: false
Has READ: true | Has WRITE: false
Result: PASS
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: What is the output of the following code and why?
```java
int x = 10;
if (x > 5 || ++x > 10) {
    System.out.println("x = " + x);
}
```
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Output:** `x = 10`  
> **Explanation:** Because `(x > 5)` evaluates to `true`, the short-circuit `||` operator skips the second condition (`++x > 10`). The variable `x` is never incremented.
</details>

title: Type Casting & Numeric Conversions
shortDescription: Widening vs narrowing conversions, binary numeric promotion rules, and String parsing methods.
prerequisites: Topic 04: Variables, Identifiers & Primitive Data Types
searchableTerms: Q: Why does byte b = 10; b = b + 1; fail to compile, but b += 1; succeeds?
byte a = 10; byte b = 20; byte c = a + b;

cheatSheetText: Primitive Parsing Method Fallback on Invalid Format int Integer.parseInt(str) Throws NumberFormatException long Long.parseLong(str) Throws NumberFormatException double Double.parseDouble(str) Throws NumberFormatException boolean Boolean.parseBoolean(str) Returns false (case-insensitive "true" returns true) To String String.valueOf(val) Safe conversion for all primitives and objects
markdownContent:
## Overview
Type casting converts values across data types: widening conversions execute automatically without precision loss, whereas narrowing conversions require explicit cast operators `(type)` to acknowledge potential truncation or overflow.

---

## Conversion Types

### Widening Casting (Implicit / Automatic)
Safely promotes a smaller type to a larger type with zero data loss:
```
byte ──► short ──► int ──► long ──► float ──► double
char ──► int
```

```java
int count = 100;
double price = count; // Automatic widening: int -> double (100.0)
```

### Narrowing Casting (Explicit / Manual)
Converts a larger type into a smaller type. Fractional digits are discarded (truncated towards zero) and values exceeding target limits wrap around:

```java
double exact = 9.99;
int truncated = (int) exact; // Explicit narrowing: yields 9
```

---

## Binary Numeric Promotion Rules

When evaluating binary arithmetic expressions (`a + b`, `a * b`):

1. If either operand is `double`, the other is promoted to `double`.
2. Otherwise, if either operand is `float`, the other is promoted to `float`.
3. Otherwise, if either operand is `long`, the other is promoted to `long`.
4. **Otherwise, both operands are promoted to `int`.**

> Note: Because of rule 4, adding two `byte` values returns an `int`. `byte c = a + b;` fails to compile without `(byte)(a + b)`.

---

## String Parsing Reference

| Primitive | Parsing Method | Fallback on Invalid Format |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`int`** | `Integer.parseInt(str)` | Throws `NumberFormatException` |
| **`long`** | `Long.parseLong(str)` | Throws `NumberFormatException` |
| **`double`** | `Double.parseDouble(str)` | Throws `NumberFormatException` |
| **`boolean`** | `Boolean.parseBoolean(str)` | Returns `false` (case-insensitive "true" returns `true`) |
| **To String** | `String.valueOf(val)` | Safe conversion for all primitives and objects |

---

## Pitfalls

- **Byte and Short Arithmetic Promotion:** Writing `byte a = 10; byte b = 20; byte c = a + b;` fails compilation (`possible lossy conversion from int to byte`). Cast the evaluated expression: `byte c = (byte)(a + b);`.
- **Narrowing Overflow:** Casting integers outside a type's range wraps around in two's-complement without warning: `(byte) 130` evaluates to `-126`.
- **Truncation vs Rounding:** Explicit casting `(int) 4.9` truncates down to `4`. If mathematical rounding is desired, use `Math.round(4.9)` before casting.

---

## Example

```java
public class CastingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Automatic widening
        int rawScore = 95;
        double weightedScore = rawScore;
        System.out.println("Widened double : " + weightedScore);

        // Explicit narrowing with truncation
        double transactionAmount = 149.85;
        int dollarsOnly = (int) transactionAmount;
        System.out.println("Truncated int  : " + dollarsOnly);

        // String parsing
        String portString = "8080";
        int portNumber = Integer.parseInt(portString);
        System.out.println("Parsed port    : " + portNumber);

        // Binary promotion in bytes
        byte b1 = 50;
        byte b2 = 50;
        byte result = (byte)(b1 + b2);
        System.out.println("Byte sum       : " + result);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Widened double : 95.0
Truncated int  : 149
Parsed port    : 8080
Byte sum       : 100
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why does `byte b = 10; b = b + 1;` fail to compile, but `b += 1;` succeeds?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** In `b + 1`, the literal `1` is an `int`, causing `b` to be promoted to `int` and yielding an `int` result that cannot be assigned to `byte` without a cast. Compound assignment operators (`+=`, `-=`, etc.) automatically insert an implicit narrowing cast equivalent to `b = (byte)(b + 1);`.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Java provides `java.lang.Math` for standard mathematical operations, and `java.math.BigDecimal` for arbitrary-precision decimal arithmetic mandatory in financial systems where IEEE 754 floating-point numbers accumulate precision errors.

---

## Math Class Reference: `java.lang.Math`

Static, thread-safe utility methods in `java.lang.Math`:

| Method | Parameters | Returns | Description | Example | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`Math.abs(x)`** | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` | Same type | Absolute value $\|x\|$ | `Math.abs(-42)` | `42` |
| **`Math.max(a, b)`** | Numeric types | Same type | Returns greater value | `Math.max(10, 25)` | `25` |
| **`Math.min(a, b)`** | Numeric types | Same type | Returns lesser value | `Math.min(10, 25)` | `10` |
| **`Math.pow(a, b)`** | `double a, double b` | `double` | Power $a^b$ | `Math.pow(2.0, 8.0)` | `256.0` |
| **`Math.sqrt(x)`** | `double x` | `double` | Square root $\sqrt{x}$ | `Math.sqrt(49.0)` | `7.0` |
| **`Math.round(x)`** | `float` / `double` | `int` / `long` | Rounds to nearest whole integer | `Math.round(4.6)` | `5` |
| **`Math.floor(x)`** | `double x` | `double` | Largest integer $\le x$ | `Math.floor(4.9)` | `4.0` |
| **`Math.ceil(x)`** | `double x` | `double` | Smallest integer $\ge x$ | `Math.ceil(4.1)` | `5.0` |
| **`Math.clamp(v, min, max)`** | Numeric types | Same type | Restricts value within range (Java 21+) | `Math.clamp(120, 0, 100)` | `100` |
| **`Math.addExact(x, y)`** | `int`, `long` | Same type | Throws `ArithmeticException` on overflow | `Math.addExact(2000000000, 1000000000)` | Exception |

---

## High-Precision Financial Math: `BigDecimal`

Binary floating-point types (`float`, `double`) cannot accurately represent decimal fractions like `0.1`, leading to precision flaws (`0.1 + 0.2` becomes `0.30000000000000004`). In enterprise financial calculations, `java.math.BigDecimal` is mandatory.

### Safe Instantiation

| Constructor / Factory | Safe? | Example | Description |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **`new BigDecimal(String)`** | Yes | `new BigDecimal("0.1")` | Exact decimal string value |
| **`BigDecimal.valueOf(double)`** | Yes | `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)` | Converts double to canonical string first |
| **`new BigDecimal(double)`** | No | `new BigDecimal(0.1)` | Directly embeds IEEE 754 inaccuracy |

### Core Arithmetic Methods

`BigDecimal` instances are **immutable**. Every method returns a new instance:

- **`.add(val)`:** Sum: `a.add(b)`
- **`.subtract(val)`:** Difference: `a.subtract(b)`
- **`.multiply(val)`:** Product: `a.multiply(b)`
- **`.divide(divisor, scale, roundingMode)`:** Division with specified decimal places and rounding policy.
- **`.compareTo(val)`:** Numerical comparison. Returns `-1`, `0`, or `1`. Always use this instead of `.equals()`.

### Common Rounding Modes (`RoundingMode`)

- **`RoundingMode.HALF_UP`:** Standard commercial rounding (rounds $\ge 0.5$ away from zero). Standard for invoices.
- **`RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN`:** Banker's rounding. Rounds towards nearest even neighbor. Eliminates statistical bias in high-volume accounting.

---

## Pitfalls

- **Non-Terminating Division:** Calling `a.divide(b)` without specifying `scale` and `RoundingMode` throws `ArithmeticException: Non-terminating decimal expansion` if the quotient is a repeating decimal (e.g. $10 \div 3$).
- **Using `.equals()` on `BigDecimal`:** `.equals()` compares both value AND scale (`new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` is `false`). Use `.compareTo()` for numeric equality.
- **Discarding Method Returns:** Because `BigDecimal` is immutable, calling `amount.add(tax);` without assigning `amount = amount.add(tax);` has no effect.

---

## Example

```java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;

public class FinancialInvoiceCalculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BigDecimal unitPrice = new BigDecimal("19.99");
        BigDecimal quantity = BigDecimal.valueOf(3);
        BigDecimal discountRate = new BigDecimal("0.10"); // 10%
        BigDecimal salesTaxRate = new BigDecimal("0.0825"); // 8.25%

        // Subtotal = unitPrice * quantity
        BigDecimal subtotal = unitPrice.multiply(quantity);

        // Discount amount rounded to 2 decimal places
        BigDecimal discount = subtotal.multiply(discountRate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
        BigDecimal discountedSubtotal = subtotal.subtract(discount);

        // Tax amount
        BigDecimal tax = discountedSubtotal.multiply(salesTaxRate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
        BigDecimal total = discountedSubtotal.add(tax);

        System.out.printf("Subtotal : $%s%n", subtotal);
        System.out.printf("Discount : -$%s%n", discount);
        System.out.printf("Tax      : +$%s%n", tax);
        System.out.printf("Total    : $%s%n", total);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Subtotal : $59.97
Discount : -$6.00
Tax      : +$4.45
Total    : $58.42
```
</details>

---

## Practice

### Q: Why does `new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` return `false`, and how should equality be checked?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** `BigDecimal.equals()` compares both numerical value and scale (precision). `"2.0"` has a scale of 1, whereas `"2.00"` has a scale of 2. To compare numerical values regardless of scale, use `.compareTo()`: `new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00")) == 0` returns `true`.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Formatted console output in Java produces aligned, localized, and precision-controlled text using `System.out.printf()` or `String.format()`. It relies on the format string syntax `%[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion` to eliminate fragile string concatenation when displaying structured data.

---

## Format Specifiers Syntax

The anatomy of a format conversion token:

```
% [flags] [width] [.precision] conversion-character
│    │       │          │              │
│    │       │          │              └─ Type: s (String), d (decimal int), f (float)
│    │       │          └──────────────── Floating-point decimals or max string chars
│    │       └─────────────────────────── Minimum field width (padded if shorter)
│    └─────────────────────────────────── Formatting flags: -, +, 0, ,, (
└──────────────────────────────────────── Token start marker
```

### Common Conversion Specifiers

| Specifier | Applied Types | Output Description | Example | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `%s` | `Object`, `String` | Invokes `String.valueOf()` | `printf("%s", "Admin")` | `Admin` |
| `%d` | `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long` | Base-10 integer representation | `printf("%d", 42)` | `42` |
| `%f` | `float`, `double` | Base-10 decimal floating point | `printf("%f", 3.14159)` | `3.141590` |
| `%e` | `float`, `double` | Computerized scientific notation | `printf("%.2e", 5000.0)` | `5.00e+03` |
| `%x` / `%X` | Integer types | Hexadecimal string (lower/upper) | `printf("%04X", 255)` | `00FF` |
| `%b` | `boolean`, `Object` | `false` if `false` or `null`; else `true` | `printf("%b", isValid)` | `true` |
| `%c` | `char`, `Character` | Unicode character | `printf("%c", 'A')` | `A` |
| `%n` | Platform-independent | System newline (`\n` on Unix, `\r\n` on Windows) | `printf("Row%n")` | `Row\n` |
| `%%` | None | Escapes and prints a literal `%` character | `printf("%d%%", 95)` | `95%` |

---

## Alignment, Width, and Precision Flags

| Flag | Meaning | Typical Usage | Example | Formatted Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `-` | Left-justify inside field width | Tabular column alignment | `printf("%-10s", "CPU")` | `'CPU       '` |
| `+` | Always display sign (+ or -) | Financial and coordinate offsets | `printf("%+d", 45)` | `+45` |
| `0` | Zero-pad numbers to width | Fixed-width IDs and timers | `printf("%05d", 7)` | `00007` |
| `,` | Locale-specific grouping delimiter | Human-readable numbers | `printf("%,d", 1000000)` | `1,000,000` |
| `.` | Floating precision / String cutoff | Rounding decimals or clipping | `printf("%.2f", 19.998)` | `20.00` |

---

## Memory Mechanics: PrintStream vs String Buffering

```
                     Formatted Output Pipeline
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                      Argument Array                          │
 │         ["Transaction", 1045, 849.2599]                      │
 └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │             java.util.Formatter Parser Engine                │
 │         Template: "%-15s | ID: %06d | $%,10.2f%n"            │
 └──────────────┬────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                │                                │
                ▼                                ▼
   System.out.printf(...)              String.format(...)
   Writes bytes directly to STDOUT     Allocates a new immutable String
   No intermediate String allocation   Cached in heap for logging/REST API
```

---

## Production Tabular Logging Example

```java
public class FormattedOutputDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] services = {"AuthService", "PaymentWorker", "CacheReplica"};
        int[] portNumbers = {8080, 9092, 6379};
        double[] latencies = {12.456, 145.892, 0.412};

        // Header with column widths: 18 chars left-aligned, 8 chars right-aligned, 12 chars right-aligned
        System.out.printf("%-18s | %8s | %12s%n", "SERVICE", "PORT", "LATENCY (ms)");
        System.out.printf("%s%n", "-".repeat(44));

        for (int i = 0; i < services.length; i++) {
            System.out.printf("%-18s | %8d | %,12.2f%n", services[i], portNumbers[i], latencies[i]);
        }

        // Generating a formatted String for external systems (e.g. loggers or JSON templates)
        String logEntry = String.format("Alert: Service [%s] breached latency threshold: %.1f ms", services[1], latencies[1]);
        System.out.println(logEntry);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
SERVICE            |     PORT | LATENCY (ms)
--------------------------------------------
AuthService        |     8080 |        12.46
PaymentWorker      |     9092 |       145.89
CacheReplica       |     6379 |         0.41
Alert: Service [PaymentWorker] breached latency threshold: 145.9 ms
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Using `\n` Instead of `%n`:** Hardcoding `\n` creates platform-dependent newline bugs across Windows (`\r\n`) and Linux (`\n`). `%n` automatically queries `System.lineSeparator()`.
- **Mismatch Between Specifier and Argument Type:** Passing a floating-point number into `%d` (e.g., `printf("%d", 3.14)`) does not perform type casting; it throws `java.util.IllegalFormatConversionException` at runtime.
- **Locale-Dependent Decimal Points:** By default, `%f` uses the host operating system locale. In German or French locales, `12.5` renders as `12,5`. To enforce invariant dot-notation in serialization pipelines, use `String.format(Locale.US, "%.2f", value)`.
- **Performance in Tight Loops:** `System.out.printf()` acquires a console synchronization lock and parses regex format strings on every call. In high-throughput logging, construct buffers with `StringBuilder` or utilize structured loggers (Logback / SLF4J).

---

## Practice

### Question
Given the call `System.out.printf("[%10.3s]", "ProductionServer");`, what exact string is printed between the brackets?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. The `.3` precision applied to a string truncates the input string to its first 3 characters: `"ProductionServer"` becomes `"Pro"`.
2. The `10` width specifies a minimum field width of 10 characters.
3. Without the `-` left-align flag, the 3-character string is right-aligned and padded with 7 leading spaces: `"       Pro"`.
4. The output is `[       Pro]`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
A `String` in Java is an immutable reference type representing a sequence of characters. String literals are automatically cached in the JVM String Constant Pool on the heap to eliminate duplicate memory allocations.

---

## Memory Mechanics

```
                  JVM Heap Memory
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 String Constant Pool                   │
  │                                                        │
  │   "data" ◄────── str1 = "data"                         │
  │        ▲                                               │
  │        └───────── str2 = "data"      (Shared pointer)  │
  │                                                        │
  │   "DATA" ◄────── str3 = str1.toUpperCase()             │
  │                  (New object created, str1 unchanged)  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Immutability:** Once instantiated, a String's internal character array cannot change. Every transformation method returns a brand-new String object.
- **Literal vs `new String()`:** Writing `"Java"` reuses the interned instance from the pool. Calling `new String("Java")` explicitly allocates a redundant object on the heap outside the pool.

---

## Key Methods Reference

| Method | Return | Description | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `equals(other)` | `boolean` | Compares character content equality | `"abc".equals("abc")` -> `true` |
| `equalsIgnoreCase(s)` | `boolean` | Case-insensitive content check | `"a".equalsIgnoreCase("A")` -> `true` |
| `length()` | `int` | Returns number of UTF-16 code units | `"Java".length()` -> `4` |
| `contains(seq)` | `boolean` | Checks if substring exists | `"user_admin".contains("admin")` |
| `startsWith(prefix)` | `boolean` | Verifies prefix string | `"https://api".startsWith("https")` |
| `endsWith(suffix)` | `boolean` | Verifies suffix extension | `"report.pdf".endsWith(".pdf")` |
| `substring(start, end)` | `String` | Extracts slice `[start, end)` | `"2026-11".substring(0, 4)` -> `"2026"` |
| `strip()` | `String` | Strips leading and trailing whitespace (Java 11+) | `"  text  ".strip()` -> `"text"` |
| `isBlank()` | `boolean` | Checks if empty or whitespace-only (Java 11+) | `"   ".isBlank()` -> `true` |
| `isEmpty()` | `boolean` | Checks if length is zero | `"".isEmpty()` -> `true` |
| `split(regex)` | `String[]` | Splits string by regular expression pattern | `"a,b,c".split(",")` |
| `String.join(del, items)` | `String` | Joins elements using specified delimiter | `String.join("-", "a", "b")` -> `"a-b"` |

---

## High-Performance Construction: StringBuilder

Repeated string concatenation (`+`) inside loops creates excessive garbage objects on the heap. Use `java.lang.StringBuilder` for mutable, in-place character buffering:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    sb.append(i).append(",");
}
String result = sb.toString();
```

---

## Text Blocks (Java 15+)

Surrounded by triple quotes `"""`, text blocks represent multi-line string literals without requiring escape sequences (`\n`, `\"`):

```java
String jsonPayload = """
    {
        "status": "UP",
        "service": "%s"
    }
    """.formatted("PaymentGateway");
```
- **Incidental Indentation:** Java automatically detects and strips common leading indentation spaces.
- **`.formatted(...)`:** Injects arguments directly into template specifiers.

---

## Pitfalls

- **Comparing Content with `==`:** `str1 == str2` checks memory reference equality, NOT character content. It evaluates to `false` for strings allocated dynamically or via `new String()`. Always use `.equals()`.
- **Ignoring Return Value of String Operations:** Because strings are immutable, calling `str.trim();` or `str.toUpperCase();` does nothing to `str`. You must assign the result: `str = str.trim();`.
- **Concatenation Inside Loops:** Using `str += item;` in a loop executes in $O(N^2)$ time due to repeated memory copies. Always use `StringBuilder`.

---

## Practice

### Question
What is printed by the following code?
```java
String a = "hello";
String b = new String("hello");
String c = b.intern();
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (a == c));
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `a == b` evaluates to `false` because `b` was created via `new String()`, allocating a distinct object outside the String Pool.
2. `b.intern()` returns the canonical reference from the String Constant Pool, which is identical to `a`. Thus `a == c` evaluates to `true`.
3. Output: `false true`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Variable scope defines the boundaries within which an identifier is visible and resolvable by the compiler. Local Variable Type Inference (`var`), introduced in Java 10 (JEP 286), allows the compiler to infer static types from initializers, preserving compile-time type safety without manual repetition.

---

## Scope Levels & Memory Lifetime

```
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Class Scope (static fields)  ── Lifetime: ClassLoader unload │
 │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
 │  │ Instance Scope (fields)   ── Lifetime: Object Garbage Col│ │
 │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
 │  │  │ Method Scope (locals)  ── Lifetime: Stack Frame Pop │ │ │
 │  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │
 │  │  │  │ Block Scope ({ })   ── Lifetime: Block Exit    │ │ │ │
 │  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │
 │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
 │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Scope Level | Declaration Site | Memory Allocation | Lifetime Duration |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Static / Class** | `static` field inside class | Metaspace / Heap | Duration of application until ClassLoader is unloaded |
| **Instance / Field** | Non-static field inside class | Heap (inside enclosing object) | From `new` instantiation until GC reclamation |
| **Method Local** | Parameter or variable in method | Thread Call Stack frame | Pushed on call, destroyed on frame return |
| **Block** | Inside `{ ... }` (if, for, while) | Thread Call Stack | Created on block entry, destroyed on block exit |

---

## Type Inference with `var`

`var` is a reserved type name (not a keyword). It is resolved entirely at compile time; bytecodes generated with `var` are byte-for-byte identical to explicit type declarations.

### Where `var` Is Permitted vs Prohibited

| Context | Code Pattern | Permitted? | Compiler Rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Local variable with initializer** | `var count = 10;` | **Yes** | Inferred as `int` |
| **Enhanced `for` loop variable** | `for (var item : list)` | **Yes** | Inferred from generic element type |
| **Classic `for` loop counter** | `for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++)` | **Yes** | Inferred as `int` |
| **Try-with-resources resource** | `try (var in = openStream())` | **Yes** | Inferred from return type |
| **Uninitialized local variable** | `var count;` | **No** | Cannot infer from missing initializer |
| **Assigned to `null`** | `var data = null;` | **No** | `null` has no inferable type |
| **Class instance or static field** | `private var name = "A";` | **No** | Only permitted on local variables |
| **Method parameter or return** | `void test(var x)` | **No** | Signatures require explicit public contracts |
| **Lambda expressions directly** | `var f = () -> {};` | **No** | Target type cannot be resolved |
| **Array literal initializers** | `var arr = {1, 2, 3};` | **No** | Must write `var arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3};` |

---

## Implementation Example

```java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class ScopeAndInferenceDemo {
    // Instance variable: accessible across all instance methods
    private final String serviceName = "TelemetryPipeline";

    public void processBatches(List<String> rawLogs) {
        // Local variable with var: eliminates repetitive generic boilerplate
        var eventFrequencyMap = new HashMap<String, Integer>();

        for (var log : rawLogs) {
            // Block scope: 'normalized' exists only inside this iteration
            var normalized = log.strip().toLowerCase();
            eventFrequencyMap.merge(normalized, 1, Integer::sum);
        }

        // Display results
        System.out.printf("[%s] Event counts:%n", serviceName);
        for (var entry : eventFrequencyMap.entrySet()) {
            System.out.printf("  - %s: %d%n", entry.getKey(), entry.getValue());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var demo = new ScopeAndInferenceDemo();
        var logs = List.of("ERROR", "INFO", "WARN", "ERROR", "error ");
        demo.processBatches(logs);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
[TelemetryPipeline] Event counts:
  - warn: 1
  - error: 3
  - info: 1
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Reassigning `var` to Incompatible Types:** `var` is NOT dynamic. Once inferred as `int`, assigning `val = "text";` causes compilation error `incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int`.
- **Variable Shadowing Confusion:** Declaring a local variable with the exact same name as an instance field shadows the field. Accessing the field requires explicit `this.fieldName`.
- **Loss of Code Readability:** Writing `var result = service.execute();` hides the underlying type from reviewers when method return types are not immediately obvious. Use `var` only when the type is obvious from the right-hand side (e.g. constructors or factory methods).
- **Diamond Operator with `var`:** Writing `var list = new ArrayList<>();` infers `ArrayList<Object>`, losing compile-time generic type safety. Always specify type arguments: `var list = new ArrayList<String>();`.

---

## Practice

### Question
Which of the following variable declarations will cause a compile-time error?
```java
var a = 10;                     // Line 1
var b = new int[]{1, 2};        // Line 2
var c = {1, 2};                 // Line 3
var d = (String) null;          // Line 4
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. Line 1 infers `int`. Valid.
2. Line 2 explicitly allocates `int[]`. Valid.
3. Line 3 uses an array literal initializer without a type. Java requires an explicit target type for `{1, 2}`. Line 3 **fails compilation**.
4. Line 4 explicitly casts `null` to `String`, allowing the compiler to infer `String`. Valid.
5. Error is on **Line 3**.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
An exception represents an abnormal event interrupting sequential control flow. In Java, all faults and recoverable anomalies are represented as heap objects belonging to the `java.lang.Throwable` class hierarchy. When thrown, the runtime unwinds Call Stack frames until a matching `catch` block is discovered.

---

## The `Throwable` Hierarchy Tree

```
                           java.lang.Object
                                  │
                         java.lang.Throwable
                                  │
                 ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
                 ▼                                 ▼
         java.lang.Error                 java.lang.Exception
        (Fatal JVM Faults)             (Anticipated Conditions)
        - OutOfMemoryError                         │
        - StackOverflowError             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
        - InternalError                  ▼                   ▼
                                 Checked Exceptions   java.lang.RuntimeException
                                 - IOException        (Unchecked / Bug / Defect)
                                 - SQLException       - NullPointerException
                                                      - IllegalArgumentException
```

### Core Hierarchy Categories

| Class Branch | Recoverable? | Compiler Enforcement | Primary Root Causes |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **`java.lang.Error`** | **No** | Unchecked | Hardware failure, memory exhaustion, class loading linkage failure |
| **`java.lang.Exception`** | **Yes** | **Checked** (unless subtyped under `RuntimeException`) | Network drops, missing disk files, remote service timeout |
| **`java.lang.RuntimeException`** | **Yes** | **Unchecked** | Programming defects, null pointer dereferences, illegal arguments |

---

## `Throwable` Method Reference

| Method | Return | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `getMessage()` | `String` | Detailed description of the error condition |
| `getCause()` | `Throwable` | The underlying wrapped exception (or `null` if none) |
| `getStackTrace()` | `StackTraceElement[]` | Snapshot array of Call Stack frames at point of throw |
| `printStackTrace()` | `void` | Writes textual stack trace representation to `System.err` |

---

## Stack Unwinding Lifecycle

```
 Method C throws Exception ──► Frame C popped (no catch block found)
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               Frame B popped (no catch block found)
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               Frame A matches catch(Exception e)
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               Exception handled; normal execution resumes after try-catch
```

---

## Implementation Example

```java
public class ExceptionHierarchyDemo {
    public static void executeStepC() {
        // Throws an unchecked defect
        throw new IllegalStateException("Storage engine is offline");
    }

    public static void executeStepB() {
        executeStepC(); // Unwinds through StepB
    }

    public static void executeStepA() {
        try {
            executeStepB();
        } catch (IllegalStateException ex) {
            System.err.println("Caught exception in StepA: " + ex.getMessage());
            for (StackTraceElement element : ex.getStackTrace()) {
                System.err.printf("  at %s.%s (%s:%d)%n",
                        element.getClassName(),
                        element.getMethodName(),
                        element.getFileName(),
                        element.getLineNumber());
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        executeStepA();
        System.out.println("Application recovered safely and continues running.");
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Caught exception in StepA: Storage engine is offline
  at ExceptionHierarchyDemo.executeStepC (ExceptionHierarchyDemo.java:4)
  at ExceptionHierarchyDemo.executeStepB (ExceptionHierarchyDemo.java:8)
  at ExceptionHierarchyDemo.executeStepA (ExceptionHierarchyDemo.java:13)
Application recovered safely and continues running.
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Catching `java.lang.Throwable` or `Error`:** Catching `Throwable` accidentally captures fatal VM faults such as `OutOfMemoryError`, preventing the JVM from terminating cleanly and leaving heap state corrupted.
- **Empty Catch Blocks (Swallowing Exceptions):** Writing `catch (Exception e) {}` discards the exception silently, concealing production bugs and rendering debugging virtually impossible.
- **Losing the Cause During Re-Throwing:** Instantiating a new exception without supplying the caught instance (`throw new CustomException("Failed");`) severs the causal chain. Always pass the caught exception: `throw new CustomException("Failed", e);`.

---

## Practice

### Question
Why is the following catch block ordering rejected by the Java compiler?
```java
try {
    readFile();
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Handled Exception");
} catch (java.io.IOException e) {
    System.out.println("Handled IOException");
}
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `java.io.IOException` is a subclass of `java.lang.Exception`.
2. The first catch block `catch (Exception e)` matches all exceptions that are subclasses of `Exception`, including `IOException`.
3. Consequently, the second block `catch (IOException e)` can never be reached under any scenario.
4. Java compiler rejects unreachable catch blocks with error `exception IOException has already been caught`.
5. Fix: Specific subclasses must always precede general superclasses in catch ladders.

</details>

## Overview
The `java.util.List<E>` interface represents an ordered, zero-indexed sequence of elements that permits duplicates. The two primary implementations—`ArrayList` (backed by a dynamically resizing contiguous array) and `LinkedList` (backed by a doubly linked node chain)—exhibit fundamentally different CPU cache locality and asymptotic time complexity profiles.

---

## Memory Architecture & Big-O Comparison

```
 ArrayList Memory Layout (Contiguous Heap Array)
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ [Header] [Length: 10] [0: E] [1: E] [2: E] ... [Unused slots]  │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  * Growth policy: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)  (1.5x expansion)

 LinkedList Memory Layout (Scattered Heap Nodes)
 ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐
 │ Node 0      │◄─────►│ Node 1      │◄─────►│ Node 2      │
 │  item: E    │       │  item: E    │       │  item: E    │
 │  prev, next │       │  prev, next │       │  prev, next │
 └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘
  * 24 bytes overhead per node (64-bit JVM) + severe CPU L1/L2 cache misses
```

| Operation | `ArrayList<E>` | `LinkedList<E>` | Modern Production Guidance |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Random Access (`get(i)`)** | **$O(1)$** | $O(N)$ | Use `ArrayList` for read-heavy workloads |
| **Append to End (`add(e)`)** | **Amortized $O(1)$** | $O(1)$ | Both performant; `ArrayList` consumes far less memory |
| **Insert / Delete at Head** | $O(N)$ (shifts array) | **$O(1)$** | Use `ArrayDeque` instead of `LinkedList` |
| **Insert / Delete in Middle** | $O(N)$ (shifts elements) | $O(N)$ (traversal) | `ArrayList` typically faster due to `System.arraycopy` SIMD |
| **Memory Overhead** | Minimal (array capacity pad) | 24-32 bytes per element | `LinkedList` is almost never recommended in modern Java |

---

## Factory Methods & Immutability Matrix

| Method | Returns | Modifiable? | Structurally Resizable? | Null Tolerant? |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `new ArrayList<>()` | Standard `ArrayList` | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| `Arrays.asList(arr)` | Fixed-size array wrapper | **Yes** (in-place) | **No** (throws on `add`/`remove`) | **Yes** |
| `List.of(e1, e2)` (Java 9+) | Internal immutable list | **No** | **No** | **No** (Throws NPE) |
| `List.copyOf(coll)` (Java 10+) | Unmodifiable snapshot | **No** | **No** | **No** (Throws NPE) |

---

## `subList(from, to)` View Windowing

Calling `list.subList(fromIndex, toIndex)` returns a **live view** backed by the original list, not an independent copy. Mutating the sublist mutates the parent list. However, structurally modifying the parent list invalidates the sublist, causing subsequent sublist calls to throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.

---

## Implementation Example

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ListArchitectureDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Pre-allocating capacity to avoid resizing overhead
        List<String> eventBuffer = new ArrayList<>(16);
        eventBuffer.add("AUTH_SUCCESS");
        eventBuffer.add("ORDER_CREATED");
        eventBuffer.add("PAYMENT_PENDING");
        eventBuffer.add("SETTLED");

        // subList windowing: extracts slice [1, 3)
        List<String> pendingWindow = eventBuffer.subList(1, 3);
        System.out.println("Pending Window View: " + pendingWindow);

        // Modifying the view affects the underlying list
        pendingWindow.set(0, "ORDER_CONFIRMED");
        System.out.println("Underlying Buffer: " + eventBuffer);

        // Modern immutable list factory (Java 9+)
        List<String> immutableSnap = List.copyOf(eventBuffer);
        System.out.println("Immutable Snapshot: " + immutableSnap);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Pending Window View: [ORDER_CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING]
Underlying Buffer: [AUTH_SUCCESS, ORDER_CONFIRMED, PAYMENT_PENDING, SETTLED]
Immutable Snapshot: [AUTH_SUCCESS, ORDER_CONFIRMED, PAYMENT_PENDING, SETTLED]
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **The `remove(int)` vs `remove(Object)` Ambiguity:** In `List<Integer>`, calling `list.remove(1)` invokes the overloaded `remove(int index)` method, removing the element at index 1. To remove the integer value 1, cast explicitly: `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`.
- **Concurrent Modification via Sublist:** Modifying the parent list directly (`parent.add("X")`) while holding a reference to `subList` permanently corrupts the sublist's internal modification count, causing `ConcurrentModificationException`.
- **Using `LinkedList` Expecting Better Performance:** In theory, `LinkedList` has $O(1)$ insertions, but in practice, traversing to the insertion node requires $O(N)$ steps across non-contiguous memory, triggering severe CPU cache misses that make `ArrayList` faster even when shifting memory.

---

## Practice

### Question
Given the following operations, what is printed?
```java
List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
numbers.remove(1);
System.out.println(numbers);
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `List.of(10, 20, 30)` creates an unmodifiable list containing `[10, 20, 30]`.
2. `new ArrayList<>(...)` creates a mutable copy.
3. `numbers.remove(1)` matches the method `remove(int index)` rather than `remove(Object o)`.
4. Index 1 holds the element `20`. The element `20` is removed.
5. Remaining elements: `[10, 30]`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
The `java.util.Queue<E>` and `java.util.Deque<E>` (Double-Ended Queue) interfaces model ordered collection processing pipelines. `Queue` enforces FIFO (First-In, First-Out) dispatch, `Deque` supports both FIFO queues and LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) stacks in $O(1)$ constant time, and `PriorityQueue` implements a binary min-heap for priority-ordered extraction.

---

## The Queue Method Matrix

The `Queue` interface defines two distinct error-handling conventions for operations:

| Operation | Throws Exception (on full/empty) | Returns Special Sentinel (`false` or `null`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Insert** | `add(e)` | `offer(e)` |
| **Remove** | `remove()` | `poll()` |
| **Examine** | `element()` | `peek()` |

---

## Implementation Comparison & Memory Architecture

```
 ArrayDeque (Circular Buffer Array)               PriorityQueue (Binary Min-Heap)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────┐
 │ [Tail] ──► [E3] [E4] ... [E1] [E2]   │        │           [Root: 10]          │
 │              ▲            │          │        │          /          \         │
 │              └─ head ─────┘          │        │     [Node: 25]   [Node: 30]   │
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────────┘
  * Head & tail wrap via bitwise masking:         * Array-backed binary min-heap:
    head = (head - 1) & (elements.length - 1)      parent(i) = (i - 1) / 2
```

| Dimension | `ArrayDeque<E>` | `PriorityQueue<E>` | `LinkedList<E>` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ordering Model** | FIFO Queue or LIFO Stack | Natural / Custom Priority | FIFO Queue or LIFO Stack |
| **Insert Complexity** | **Amortized $O(1)$** | **$O(\log N)$** | $O(1)$ |
| **Extract Complexity** | **$O(1)$** | **$O(\log N)$** | $O(1)$ |
| **Internal Structure** | Circular dynamic array | Array-backed binary heap | Doubly linked node pointers |
| **Null Elements** | **Forbidden** | **Forbidden** | Allowed (discouraged) |
| **Modern Stack Usage**| **Recommended** (`push`/`pop`) | N/A | Discouraged |

> [!NOTE]
> The legacy class `java.util.Stack` extends `Vector` and synchronizes every operation. In modern Java, always use `ArrayDeque` for stack (LIFO) implementations:
> `Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); stack.push("A"); stack.pop();`

---

## Implementation Example

```java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.Queue;

public class QueueArchitectureDemo {
    public record WorkTask(String taskId, int priorityRank) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. High-Performance FIFO Queue via ArrayDeque
        Queue<String> eventPipeline = new ArrayDeque<>();
        eventPipeline.offer("EVENT-01");
        eventPipeline.offer("EVENT-02");
        eventPipeline.offer("EVENT-03");

        System.out.println("Processing FIFO Event: " + eventPipeline.poll()); // EVENT-01
        System.out.println("Next up without removing: " + eventPipeline.peek()); // EVENT-02

        // 2. Binary Min-Heap PriorityQueue (lowest rank number = highest priority)
        Queue<WorkTask> scheduler = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(WorkTask::priorityRank));
        scheduler.offer(new WorkTask("Batch-Report", 5));
        scheduler.offer(new WorkTask("Security-Alert", 1));
        scheduler.offer(new WorkTask("User-Signup", 3));

        System.out.println("--- Draining Priority Scheduler ---");
        while (!scheduler.isEmpty()) {
            WorkTask task = scheduler.poll();
            System.out.printf("Dispatched [%s] with priority %d%n", task.taskId(), task.priorityRank());
        }
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Processing FIFO Event: EVENT-01
Next up without removing: EVENT-02
--- Draining Priority Scheduler ---
Dispatched [Security-Alert] with priority 1
Dispatched [User-Signup] with priority 3
Dispatched [Batch-Report] with priority 5
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Iterating over `PriorityQueue` Expecting Sorted Order:** The `iterator()` of `PriorityQueue` traverses the internal array representation directly, which is a binary heap, NOT a sorted list. To extract elements in priority order, you must repeatedly invoke `poll()`.
- **Inserting `null` into `ArrayDeque` or `PriorityQueue`:** Both collections prohibit `null` elements because methods like `poll()` and `peek()` return `null` as a sentinel to indicate that the queue is empty.
- **Using `java.util.Stack`:** `Stack` inherits synchronization locks on every method from `Vector`, causing unnecessary thread lock contention. Always use `ArrayDeque` for LIFO operations.

---

## Practice

### Question
What happens when you execute `new PriorityQueue<>().offer(new Object());`?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `new PriorityQueue<>()` utilizes the natural ordering of elements by default.
2. In natural ordering, elements must implement `java.lang.Comparable`.
3. `Object` does not implement `Comparable`.
4. When `offer()` attempts to cast the object to `Comparable` during heap sift-up, it throws `java.lang.ClassCastException`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
The Java Stream API (`java.util.stream.Stream<T>`, introduced in Java 8) enables declarative, functional transformations over sequences of elements. Streams do not store data; they convey elements from a source through a pipeline of lazy intermediate operations, executing only when a terminal operation triggers processing.

---

## Stream Pipeline Architecture & Lazy Evaluation

```
               Three-Phase Stream Execution Lifecycle
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1. Source:              collection.stream(), Stream.of(...)      │
 │                                │                                 │
 │                                ▼                                 │
 │ 2. Intermediate (Lazy): filter(...) ──► map(...) ──► limit(5)    │
 │    - Operations return Stream<T>; execute ZERO code on declaration
 │                                │                                 │
 │                                ▼                                 │
 │ 3. Terminal (Eager):    collect(...), findFirst(), forEach(...)  │
 │    - Triggers pipeline execution; consumes and closes the stream │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Loop Fusion:** The JVM fuses multiple operations (`filter` + `map`) into a single pass over the elements rather than creating intermediate collection buffers.
- **Short-Circuiting:** Operations like `limit(n)` or `findFirst()` terminate traversal as soon as conditions are met, avoiding processing the remainder of the dataset.

---

## Intermediate Operations Reference

| Operation | Parameter | Output | Statefulness | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `filter(p)` | `Predicate<T>` | `Stream<T>` | Stateless | Retains elements evaluating to `true` |
| `map(f)` | `Function<T, R>` | `Stream<R>` | Stateless | 1-to-1 transformation of elements |
| `flatMap(f)` | `Function<T, Stream<R>>`| `Stream<R>` | Stateless | 1-to-N transformation; flattens nested streams |
| `distinct()` | None | `Stream<T>` | **Stateful** | Eliminates duplicates using `equals()` |
| `sorted()` | `Comparator<T>` | `Stream<T>` | **Stateful** | Buffers all elements to sort |
| `limit(max)` | `long` | `Stream<T>` | Short-circuit | Truncates stream to at most `max` elements |
| `skip(n)` | `long` | `Stream<T>` | Stateless | Discards the first `n` elements |
| `peek(c)` | `Consumer<T>` | `Stream<T>` | Stateless | Debug side-effect tap (does not alter elements) |

---

## Specialized Primitive Streams

Using `Stream<Integer>` introduces autoboxing overhead for numerical data. Use primitive specializations:
- `IntStream`, `LongStream`, `DoubleStream`
- Methods: `.mapToInt()`, `.summaryStatistics()`, `.range(start, end)`, `.average()`, `.sum()`

---

## Implementation Example

```java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class StreamPipelineDemo {
    public record Developer(String name, String department, List<String> skills) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Developer> team = List.of(
            new Developer("Alex", "Platform", List.of("Java", "Go", "Docker")),
            new Developer("Beth", "Data", List.of("Python", "SQL", "Java")),
            new Developer("Carl", "Platform", List.of("Rust", "Kubernetes")),
            new Developer("Dana", "Platform", List.of("Java", "TypeScript"))
        );

        // Extract distinct skills from Platform department sorted alphabetically
        List<String> platformSkills = team.stream()
            .filter(dev -> "Platform".equals(dev.department())) // Filter
            .flatMap(dev -> dev.skills().stream())              // Flatten List<String> to Stream<String>
            .distinct()                                         // Deduplicate
            .sorted()                                           // Sort natural
            .toList();                                          // Terminal (Java 16+)

        System.out.println("Distinct Platform Skills: " + platformSkills);

        // Primitive stream aggregation without boxing overhead
        int totalSkillCount = team.stream()
            .mapToInt(dev -> dev.skills().size())
            .sum();

        System.out.println("Total combined skill assignments: " + totalSkillCount);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Distinct Platform Skills: [Docker, Go, Java, Kubernetes, Rust, TypeScript]
Total combined skill assignments: 11
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Streams are Single-Use Only:** Invoking a second terminal operation on an already consumed stream throws `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. You must create a new stream from the source.
- **Side-Effects in `peek()` / `map()`:** Stream pipelines assume pure functions. Performing mutations or modifying external state within intermediate operations causes nondeterministic bugs when run in parallel.
- **Unbounded Memory in `sorted()` or `distinct()`:** Applying `sorted()` on an infinite stream (`Stream.generate()`) causes an immediate `OutOfMemoryError` because stateful operations must buffer all elements before yielding.

---

## Practice

### Question
Given the code below, how many times is `"Filtering: "` printed?
```java
List<String> items = List.of("one", "two", "three");
Stream<String> stream = items.stream().filter(s -> {
    System.out.println("Filtering: " + s);
    return s.length() > 3;
});
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `filter()` is an **intermediate operation**.
2. Stream intermediate operations are **lazy**: they execute zero code until a terminal operation is invoked.
3. Because no terminal operation (such as `toList()`, `findFirst()`, or `count()`) is attached to `stream`, the pipeline is never executed.
4. Output: `"Filtering: "` is printed **zero times**.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Terminal operations are eager operations that trigger execution of a stream pipeline, consume its elements, and produce a materialized result or side effect. The `java.util.stream.Collectors` utility provides implementations of the `Collector` interface to perform complex multi-level aggregations, grouping, partitioning, and statistical summaries.

---

## Terminal Operations Reference

| Operation Category | Method Signature | Return Type | Characteristics |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Materialization** | `.toList()` (Java 16+) | `List<T>` | Returns an unmodifiable list (null-hostile) |
| **Collection** | `.collect(Collector)` | `R` | Custom accumulation into containers |
| **Fold Reduction** | `.reduce(identity, accumulator)`| `T` | Associative folding aggregation |
| **Search (Short-circuit)**| `.findFirst()` / `.findAny()` | `Optional<T>` | Returns first matching element encountered |
| **Matching (Short-circuit)**| `.anyMatch(p)` / `.allMatch(p)` | `boolean` | Short-circuits as soon as outcome is determined |
| **Aggregation** | `.count()` / `.min(comp)` / `.max(comp)`| `long` / `Optional<T>`| Computes counts and boundary extrema |
| **Iteration** | `.forEach(consumer)` | `void` | Executes side effect for each element |

---

## The `java.util.stream.Collectors` Catalog

```
              Multi-Level Collector Architecture
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Collectors.groupingBy(                                      │
 │     Order::region,                                          │
 │     Collectors.groupingBy(                                  │
 │         Order::status,                                      │
 │         Collectors.summingDouble(Order::amount)             │
 │     )                                                       │
 │ )                                                           │
 └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                ▼
         Map<String, Map<String, Double>> Nested Result
```

| Collector | Return Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `toList()` / `toSet()` | `List<T>` / `Set<T>` | Collects elements into standard collections |
| `toUnmodifiableList()` | `List<T>` | Collects into an immutable list (Java 10+) |
| `joining(delimiter)` | `String` | Concatenates CharSequence elements with delimiter |
| `groupingBy(classifier)` | `Map<K, List<T>>` | Groups elements by key |
| `groupingBy(k, downstream)`| `Map<K, D>` | Groups elements and applies downstream reduction |
| `partitioningBy(predicate)`| `Map<Boolean, List<T>>`| Splits elements into `true` and `false` groups |
| `toMap(keyMapper, valMapper)`| `Map<K, V>` | Collects elements into map; throws on duplicate key |

---

## Implementation Example

```java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class CollectorsArchitectureDemo {
    public enum Priority { HIGH, NORMAL, LOW }
    public record Incident(String ticketId, Priority priority, double cost) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Incident> incidents = List.of(
            new Incident("INC-101", Priority.HIGH, 450.0),
            new Incident("INC-102", Priority.NORMAL, 120.0),
            new Incident("INC-103", Priority.HIGH, 850.0),
            new Incident("INC-104", Priority.LOW, 50.0),
            new Incident("INC-105", Priority.NORMAL, 200.0)
        );

        // 1. Grouping by Priority with downstream total cost aggregation
        Map<Priority, Double> costByPriority = incidents.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Incident::priority,
                Collectors.summingDouble(Incident::cost)
            ));

        System.out.println("Cost breakdown by priority: " + costByPriority);

        // 2. Partitioning into High-Cost (> 300) vs Normal
        Map<Boolean, List<String>> costTiers = incidents.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
                inc -> inc.cost() > 300.0,
                Collectors.mapping(Incident::ticketId, Collectors.toList())
            ));

        System.out.println("Major incidents (> $300): " + costTiers.get(true));
        System.out.println("Minor incidents (<= $300): " + costTiers.get(false));
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Cost breakdown by priority: {LOW=50.0, NORMAL=320.0, HIGH=1300.0}
Major incidents (> $300): [INC-101, INC-103]
Minor incidents (<= $300): [INC-102, INC-104, INC-105]
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Duplicate Keys in `Collectors.toMap()`:** Calling `toMap(k, v)` without providing a merge binary operator throws runtime `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key` when duplicate keys are encountered. Always supply a conflict resolver: `toMap(k, v, (v1, v2) -> v1)`.
- **Side-Effects in `forEach()` vs `collect()`:** Mutating a shared external collection from within `.forEach(item -> externalList.add(item))` is an anti-pattern that violates functional isolation and causes race conditions in parallel streams. Always use `.collect(Collectors.toList())`.
- **Non-Associative Accumulators in `reduce()`:** When using `reduce()`, the accumulator function must be strictly associative: $(a \circ b) \circ c = a \circ (b \circ c)$. Non-associative functions (such as subtraction `(a, b) -> a - b`) produce unpredictable results when executed on parallel streams.

---

## Practice

### Question
Given the code below, why does `main` throw an exception at runtime?
```java
List<String> items = List.of("alpha", "beta", "apple");
Map<Integer, String> map = items.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(String::length, s -> s));
```

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `String::length` extracts the string length as the map key.
2. Both `"alpha"` and `"apple"` have a length of 5.
3. The overloaded `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)` requires unique keys by default.
4. When encountering duplicate key `5`, it throws `java.lang.IllegalStateException: Duplicate key 5 (attempted merging values alpha and apple)`.
5. Fix: Provide a merge function: `Collectors.toMap(String::length, s -> s, (s1, s2) -> s1)`.

</details>

title: Executor Framework & Thread Pools
