searchableTerms: Upper bound of concurrent worker threads
cheatSheetText: Parameter Type Architectural Purpose corePoolSize int Number of core worker threads kept alive even when idle maximumPoolSize int Upper bound of concurrent worker threads keepAliveTime long Maximum time non-core idle threads wait before termination unit TimeUnit Time unit for keepAliveTime workQueue BlockingQueue<Runnable> Buffer holding tasks awaiting execution threadFactory ThreadFactory Factory customizing thread naming, priority, daemon state handler RejectedExecutionHandler Strategy triggered when queue is full and max threads reached Policy Behavior when Saturated Recommended Production Use AbortPolicy (Default) Throws runtime RejectedExecutionException Fail-fast alerting under overload CallerRunsPolicy Executes task directly on the caller thread Natural backpressure; slows down submission rate DiscardPolicy Silently drops the rejected task Non-critical metric samples DiscardOldestPolicy Evicts the head of the work queue and retries Real-time sensor telemetry where newest data matters Interface Method Signature Return Value Exception Handling Runnable void run() None Unchecked exceptions only Callable<V> V call() throws Exception Typed V Declares checked Exception Future<V> V get() throws ... Typed V Blocks calling thread until task completes
markdownContent:
## Overview
The Executor Framework (`java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService`) decouples asynchronous task submission from operating system thread management. By recycling a pre-allocated pool of worker threads, thread pools eliminate thread creation overhead, bound memory consumption, and govern task scheduling through thread-safe blocking work queues.

---

## `ThreadPoolExecutor` Architecture

```
                          ThreadPoolExecutor Task Flow
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1. Task Submitted via submit(task)                                     │
 │       │                                                                │
 │       ├── activeThreads < corePoolSize? ──► Spawn new Core Worker Thread
 │       │                                                                │
 │       ├── workQueue.offer(task)?        ──► Queue in BlockingQueue     │
 │       │                                                                │
 │       ├── activeThreads < maxPoolSize?  ──► Spawn Extra Worker Thread  │
 │       │                                                                │
 │       └── Queue Full & Max Threads Active ──► Trigger Rejection Handler│
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### The 7 Core Configuration Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Architectural Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `corePoolSize` | `int` | Number of core worker threads kept alive even when idle |
| `maximumPoolSize`| `int` | Upper bound of concurrent worker threads |
| `keepAliveTime` | `long` | Maximum time non-core idle threads wait before termination |
| `unit` | `TimeUnit` | Time unit for `keepAliveTime` |
| `workQueue` | `BlockingQueue<Runnable>` | Buffer holding tasks awaiting execution |
| `threadFactory` | `ThreadFactory` | Factory customizing thread naming, priority, daemon state |
| `handler` | `RejectedExecutionHandler` | Strategy triggered when queue is full and max threads reached |

---

## Rejection Policies (`RejectedExecutionHandler`)

| Policy | Behavior when Saturated | Recommended Production Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`AbortPolicy`** (Default) | Throws runtime `RejectedExecutionException` | Fail-fast alerting under overload |
| **`CallerRunsPolicy`** | Executes task directly on the **caller thread** | Natural backpressure; slows down submission rate |
| **`DiscardPolicy`** | Silently drops the rejected task | Non-critical metric samples |
| **`DiscardOldestPolicy`**| Evicts the head of the work queue and retries | Real-time sensor telemetry where newest data matters |

---

## `Runnable` vs `Callable<V>` and `Future<V>`

| Interface | Method Signature | Return Value | Exception Handling |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `Runnable` | `void run()` | None | Unchecked exceptions only |
| `Callable<V>`| `V call() throws Exception` | Typed `V` | Declares checked `Exception` |
| `Future<V>` | `V get() throws ...` | Typed `V` | Blocks calling thread until task completes |

---

## Implementation Example: Production Thread Pool

```java
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ExecutorArchitectureDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Bounded ThreadPoolExecutor with CallerRunsPolicy for backpressure
        ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            2,                                     // corePoolSize
            4,                                     // maximumPoolSize
            60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                 // keepAliveTime
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10),          // bounded queue: prevents OutOfMemoryError
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // Backpressure handler
        );

        // Submitting a Callable task returning a typed result
        Callable<String> databaseQuery = () -> {
            Thread.sleep(200);
            return "SUCCESS: Record ID 4920 fetched";
        };

        Future<String> queryFuture = executor.submit(databaseQuery);

        // Check completion status without blocking
        System.out.printf("Is task done before wait: %b%n", queryFuture.isDone());

        // Blocking get() with timeout
        String result = queryFuture.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("Result from worker: " + result);

        // Graceful shutdown lifecycle
        executor.shutdown();
        if (!executor.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            executor.shutdownNow(); // Force cancel if timeout exceeded
        }
        System.out.println("Executor pool terminated cleanly.");
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Is task done before wait: false
Result from worker: SUCCESS: Record ID 4920 fetched
Executor pool terminated cleanly.
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Using `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` Blindly:** Standard factory methods configure an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`. Under high traffic, tasks queue indefinitely, consuming heap memory until crashing with `OutOfMemoryError`. Always configure an explicit bounded `ArrayBlockingQueue`.
- **Using `Executors.newCachedThreadPool()` Blindly:** Creates an unbounded pool (`maxPoolSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE`). High submission bursts spawn thousands of kernel threads, crashing with `unable to create native thread`.
- **Forgetting to Call `shutdown()`:** Active non-daemon worker threads keep the JVM process running indefinitely even after the `main` method exits. Always call `shutdown()` or use Java 19+ `try (ExecutorService ex = ...)` ARM construct.

---

## Practice

### Question
Under `CallerRunsPolicy`, what occurs when both the thread pool's maximum threads are busy and the bounded task queue is full?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. When saturation is reached, the executor delegates task execution to its `RejectedExecutionHandler`.
2. Under `CallerRunsPolicy`, the task is executed synchronously by the **caller thread** that invoked `executor.submit()`.
3. This pauses the calling thread from submitting further tasks, automatically applying **backpressure** and allowing the pool workers to catch up on queued work.

</details>

title: Virtual Threads (Project Loom)

markdownContent:
## Overview
Virtual Threads (finalized in Java 21 LTS via JEP 444) are lightweight user-mode threads managed by the Java Virtual Machine rather than the operating system. By decoupling Java threads from 1:1 kernel threads, a single JVM can host millions of concurrent virtual threads, restoring the synchronous, readable "thread-per-request" programming model to high-throughput servers.

---

## Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads

```
 Traditional Platform Thread Model (1:1 Kernel Mapping)
  [ Java Thread ] ──────────► [ OS Kernel Thread (1 MB Stack) ]

 Virtual Thread Model (M:N User-Mode Mapping)
  [ Virtual Thread 1 ] ──┐
  [ Virtual Thread 2 ] ──┼──► [ Carrier Thread ] ──► [ OS Kernel Thread ]
  [ Virtual Thread N ] ──┘   (ForkJoinPool worker)
```

| Dimension | Platform Threads | Virtual Threads (Java 21) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mapping Model** | 1:1 with OS Kernel Thread | $M:N$ (Millions of VTs on few Carrier Threads) |
| **Stack Memory** | ~1 MB reserved per thread | Starts at ~hundreds of bytes on the Heap |
| **Creation Cost** | Expensive (OS kernel syscall) | Cheap (plain Java heap object allocation) |
| **Concurrency Ceiling** | Thousands (bounded by RAM) | **Millions** concurrently |
| **Blocking Behavior** | Blocks underlying OS kernel thread | **Unmounts** from carrier thread; carrier runs other tasks |
| **Pooling Policy** | **Must be pooled** (`ThreadPoolExecutor`)| **NEVER pool**; instantiate per task and discard |

---

## Unmounting & Continuation Mechanics

When a virtual thread encounters a blocking operation (e.g. `InputStream.read()`, `Socket.connect()`, `LockSupport.park()`, `Thread.sleep()`):
1. The JVM captures the virtual thread's stack frames as a heap object (**Continuation**).
2. The virtual thread is **unmounted** from its underlying OS **carrier thread** (a FIFO `ForkJoinPool` worker).
3. The carrier thread immediately executes other runnable virtual threads.
4. When the OS signals that the I/O operation has completed, the JVM **remounts** the continuation onto any available carrier thread to resume execution.

---

## Thread Pinning Hazard

A virtual thread is **pinned** to its carrier thread if it encounters a blocking operation inside:
1. A **`synchronized` block or method** (locks monitor in object header).
2. A **native method call** (JNI or Foreign Function & Memory API).

When pinned, the virtual thread CANNOT unmount, freezing the underlying OS carrier thread during the blocking call.
- **Remedy:** Replace `synchronized` with `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` in high-throughput blocking code paths.
- **Detection Flag:** Run with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` to print stack traces of pinned threads.

---

## Implementation Example: 10,000 Concurrent Virtual Tasks

```java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class VirtualThreadScaleDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Instant start = Instant.now();

        // New virtual-thread-per-task executor (Java 21)
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            IntStream.range(0, 10_000).forEach(i -> {
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    // Blocking I/O simulation: unmounts from carrier thread
                    Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(200));
                    return i;
                });
            });
        } // try-with-resources triggers executor.close(), awaiting completion of all tasks

        Duration elapsed = Duration.between(start, Instant.now());
        System.out.printf("Successfully executed 10,000 concurrent tasks in %d ms!%n", elapsed.toMillis());
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Successfully executed 10,000 concurrent tasks in 380 ms!
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Pooling Virtual Threads:** Attempting to put virtual threads into a fixed thread pool (`newFixedThreadPool`) is an anti-pattern. Virtual threads are designed to be short-lived, transient, and created anew for every task via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`.
- **Pinning Carrier Threads with `synchronized`:** Executing blocking I/O (e.g. JDBC queries) inside `synchronized (lock)` blocks pins the carrier thread, neutralizing virtual thread throughput gains. Use `ReentrantLock`.
- **Excessive ThreadLocal Memory:** Retaining large objects in `ThreadLocal` variables across millions of virtual threads consumes massive heap memory. Use Java 21+ **Scoped Values** instead.

---

## Practice

### Question
Why does executing 10,000 tasks that each sleep for 200ms complete in ~380ms with virtual threads, whereas platform threads in a pool of 10 threads would require ~200 seconds?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. With platform threads in a pool of 10 workers, only 10 threads can sleep concurrently. 10,000 tasks / 10 = 1,000 batches $\times$ 200ms = 200 seconds.
2. With virtual threads, all 10,000 tasks are launched concurrently.
3. When each virtual thread hits `Thread.sleep(200)`, it immediately **unmounts** from its carrier thread.
4. The handful of CPU carrier threads easily schedule and unmount all 10,000 tasks within milliseconds.
5. After 200ms, all 10,000 timers expire, and carrier threads remount and complete them almost simultaneously in parallel.

</details>

shortDescription: Reference: JVM memory architecture (Heap, Metaspace, Stack Frames, PC Register, Native Stack), Stack vs Heap mechanics, and JSR-133 Happens-Before formal invariants.
prerequisites: Topic 02: JDK vs JRE vs JVM & Setup
searchableTerms: Implementation Example: Inspecting JVM Memory Metrics
cheatSheetText: Memory Region Lifecycle Scope Thread Safety Primary Out-of-Memory Exception Java Heap JVM process start to shutdown Shared (Requires coordination) OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space Metaspace Class loading until ClassLoader GC Shared OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace JVM Stack Created on thread start; destroyed on exit Thread-private (Safe by default) StackOverflowError / OOM: unable to create thread PC Register Per-thread execution tracking Thread-private None
markdownContent:
## Overview
The JVM Specification divides runtime memory into **Thread-Shared** areas (Heap and Metaspace) and **Thread-Private** areas (JVM Stacks, Program Counter Registers, and Native Method Stacks). The Java Memory Model (JMM / JSR-133) provides the formal specification determining when writes to memory by one thread become visible to reads by another via **Happens-Before** invariants.

---

## JVM Runtime Data Areas

```
                     HotSpot JVM Memory Architecture
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Thread-Shared Memory (All Threads)                               │
 │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐ │
 │  │ Java Heap                           │  │ Metaspace (Native) │ │
 │  │  - Young Gen (Eden, S0, S1)         │  │  - Class Metadata  │ │
 │  │  - Old Gen (Tenured)                │  │  - Constant Pool   │ │
 │  │  - String Constant Pool             │  │  - Method Bytecodes│ │
 │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────┘ │
 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Thread-Private Memory (Per Active Thread)                        │
 │  ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
 │  │ JVM Call Stack          │  │ PC Register  │  │ Native Stack │ │
 │  │  - Stack Frames         │  │  (Bytecode   │  │  (C/C++ JNI  │ │
 │  │    - Local Variables    │  │   pointer)   │  │   frames)    │ │
 │  │    - Operand Stack      │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
 │  │    - Frame Data / Return│                                     │
 │  └─────────────────────────┘                                     │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Memory Region | Lifecycle Scope | Thread Safety | Primary Out-of-Memory Exception |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **Java Heap** | JVM process start to shutdown | Shared (Requires coordination) | `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` |
| **Metaspace** | Class loading until ClassLoader GC | Shared | `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` |
| **JVM Stack** | Created on thread start; destroyed on exit | Thread-private (Safe by default) | `StackOverflowError` / `OOM: unable to create thread` |
| **PC Register**| Per-thread execution tracking | Thread-private | None |

---

## JMM Happens-Before Formal Axioms

A write action $A$ is guaranteed to be visible to a read action $B$ if and only if $A$ **happens-before** $B$ ($A \prec B$). The core axioms are:

1. **Program Order Rule:** Each action in a thread happens-before every subsequent action in that same thread.
2. **Monitor Lock Rule:** An unlock action on a monitor lock happens-before every subsequent lock acquisition on the same monitor.
3. **Volatile Variable Rule:** A write to a `volatile` field happens-before every subsequent read of that same `volatile` field.
4. **Thread Start Rule:** Calling `thread.start()` happens-before any action in the started thread.
5. **Thread Termination Rule:** Any action in a thread happens-before any other thread successfully returns from `thread.join()`.
6. **Transitivity:** If $A \prec B$ and $B \prec C$, then $A \prec C$.

---

## Implementation Example: Inspecting JVM Memory Metrics

```java
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.lang.management.MemoryMXBean;
import java.lang.management.MemoryUsage;

public class JvmMemoryMetricsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Runtime runtime = Runtime.getRuntime();
        long maxHeapBytes = runtime.maxMemory();
        long totalHeapBytes = runtime.totalMemory();
        long freeHeapBytes = runtime.freeMemory();
        long usedHeapBytes = totalHeapBytes - freeHeapBytes;

        System.out.println("--- JVM Heap Status ---");
        System.out.printf("Max Heap (-Xmx)   : %,10d MB%n", maxHeapBytes / (1024 * 1024));
        System.out.printf("Current Allocated : %,10d MB%n", totalHeapBytes / (1024 * 1024));
        System.out.printf("Used Memory       : %,10d MB%n", usedHeapBytes / (1024 * 1024));
        System.out.printf("Free In Allocation: %,10d MB%n", freeHeapBytes / (1024 * 1024));

        MemoryMXBean memoryBean = ManagementFactory.getMemoryMXBean();
        MemoryUsage nonHeapUsage = memoryBean.getNonHeapMemoryUsage();
        System.out.println("--- Non-Heap (Metaspace / CodeCache) ---");
        System.out.printf("Non-Heap Used     : %,10d MB%n", nonHeapUsage.getUsed() / (1024 * 1024));
        System.out.printf("Non-Heap Committed: %,10d MB%n", nonHeapUsage.getCommitted() / (1024 * 1024));
    }
}
```

<summary>View Output</summary>

```text

Max Heap (-Xmx)   :      4,096 MB
Current Allocated :        256 MB
Used Memory       :         12 MB
Free In Allocation:        244 MB
--- Non-Heap (Metaspace / CodeCache) ---
Non-Heap Used     :          8 MB
Non-Heap Committed:         15 MB
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Confusing `StackOverflowError` with `OutOfMemoryError`:** Deep or un-terminated recursion exhausts thread call stack memory, triggering `StackOverflowError`. Heap exhaustion from accumulating uncollected objects throws `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.
- **Metaspace Leaks via Dynamic Proxies / ClassLoaders:** Applications repeatedly generating classes via runtime bytecode enhancement (CGLIB, ByteBuddy) without unloading their ClassLoaders leak native memory, eventually throwing `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`.
- **Assuming Reordering Does Not Occur:** Without synchronization or `volatile`, compilers and CPUs freely reorder independent instructions. A thread checking `if (initialized)` can read `true` while the object fields are still being initialized by another thread.

---

## Practice

### Question
Where are local primitive variables (`int x = 5;`) stored inside the JVM, and where are object instance variables stored?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. Local primitive variables declared inside a method are stored directly inside the **Local Variable Table of the active Thread Stack Frame** on the thread call stack.
2. Object instance variables (even primitives declared as fields inside a class) are stored on the **Java Heap**, embedded directly inside the memory layout of the enclosing heap object instance.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Java utilizes automated Garbage Collection (GC) to reclaim memory occupied by unreferenced heap objects. Governed by the **Weak Generational Hypothesis** (most objects die shortly after allocation), HotSpot segments memory into generational partitions to minimize Stop-The-World (STW) pause times while maximizing throughput.

---

## GC Roots Tracing & Generational Memory

```
                       GC Root Reachability Tracing
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ GC Roots: Active Stack Frames, Static Fields, JNI Handles   │
 └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                │ (Pointer traversal)
                                ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Live Object Graph ──► Retained in Heap (Eden / Survivor / S1)│
 ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Unreachable Islands ─► Reclaimed during Minor / Major GC    │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Minor GC:** Reclaims short-lived objects from Eden and Survivor spaces ($O(\text{live objects})$).
- **Tenuring:** Objects surviving successive cycles increment their age until promoted to the Old (Tenured) Generation (`-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15`).

---

## Modern HotSpot Collector Comparison

| Collector | JVM Flag | Target Workload | STW Pause Target | Heap Sizing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Serial GC** | `-XX:+UseSerialGC` | Single-core, embedded, CLI tools | Significant (Single-threaded) | $< 100$ MB |
| **Parallel GC** | `-XX:+UseParallelGC` | High-throughput batch processing | High throughput, longer pauses | Up to tens of GB |
| **G1 GC** (Default) | `-XX:+UseG1GC` | Multi-core enterprise servers | Predictable ($100-200$ ms) | 4 GB - 64 GB |
| **Generational ZGC** | `-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational` | Ultra-low latency microservices | **Sub-millisecond ($< 1$ ms)** | 8 GB to 16 TB |

---

## Reference Strengths (`java.lang.ref`)

| Reference Type | Class | Reclaimed Under What Conditions? | Primary Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Strong** | `Object obj = new Object()` | Never, while GC root chain persists | Standard application business state |
| **Soft** | `SoftReference<T>` | Only when memory is **critically low** | In-memory sensitive caches |
| **Weak** | `WeakReference<T>` | **Immediately** on next GC cycle | Metadata mappings (`WeakHashMap`) |
| **Phantom** | `PhantomReference<T>` | After finalization; pre-memory reclaim | Off-heap direct memory cleanup (`Cleaner`) |

---

## Key Production Flags

```bash
# Sizing Heap
-Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch

# Collector Selection: Generational ZGC (Java 21+)
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational

# Production Unified GC Logging
-Xlog:gc*,gc+phases=debug:file=/var/log/jvm/gc.log:time,uptime,pid:filecount=5,filesize=100M
```

---

## Implementation Example: Inspecting GC Metrics via JMX

```java
import java.lang.management.GarbageCollectorMXBean;
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.util.List;

public class GcDiagnosticsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<GarbageCollectorMXBean> gcBeans = ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans();

        System.out.println("--- Active JVM Garbage Collectors ---");
        for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : gcBeans) {
            System.out.printf("Collector Name : %s%n", gc.getName());
            System.out.printf("  Collection Count : %,d%n", gc.getCollectionCount());
            System.out.printf("  Accumulated Time : %,d ms%n", gc.getCollectionTime());
            System.out.println("  Memory Pools     : " + String.join(", ", gc.getMemoryPoolNames()));
        }
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
--- Active JVM Garbage Collectors ---
Collector Name : G1 Young Generation
  Collection Count : 4
  Accumulated Time : 18 ms
  Memory Pools     : G1 Eden Space, G1 Survivor Space
Collector Name : G1 Old Generation
  Collection Count : 0
  Accumulated Time : 0 ms
  Memory Pools     : G1 Eden Space, G1 Survivor Space, G1 Old Gen
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Explicit `System.gc()` Calls:** Invoking `System.gc()` forces an immediate, un-optimized Stop-The-World Full GC pause across the entire heap. Disable this behavior in production with `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`.
- **Humongous Objects in G1 GC:** In G1, an object occupying $> 50\%$ of a region is categorized as a "Humongous Object", allocated directly into contiguous Old Generation regions, bypassing Eden and accelerating Full GC fragmentation.
- **Relying on Finalizers:** `Object.finalize()` is deprecated and fundamentally flawed (can resurrect objects, stalls GC queues). Use `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` or `AutoCloseable` for resource reclamation.

---

## Practice

### Question
Why is `WeakHashMap` unable to automatically collect keys that are `String` literals (e.g. `map.put("AUTH_TOKEN", data)`)?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `WeakHashMap` uses `WeakReference` for its keys: when a key is no longer strongly referenced, its entry is purged on the next GC.
2. However, string literals like `"AUTH_TOKEN"` are automatically stored and interned in the JVM **String Constant Pool**.
3. The String Constant Pool maintains a permanent **strong reference** to the literal string object for the entire lifetime of the JVM.
4. Because the key is never weakly reachable, the entry is never collected, defeating the purpose of `WeakHashMap`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
ClassLoaders dynamically locate, verify, and link compiled `.class` bytecodes into JVM Metaspace at runtime following the **Parent Delegation Model**. The HotSpot Just-In-Time (JIT) execution engine analyzes running bytecode profiles to compile frequently executed "hot spots" into optimized native machine code via **Tiered Compilation**.

---

## ClassLoader Hierarchy & Delegation Model

```
                    Built-In ClassLoader Hierarchy
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Bootstrap ClassLoader (Native C/C++ in JVM kernel; loads java.base)
 │   │ (returns null in Java reflection API)                        │
 │   ▼                                                              │
 │ Platform ClassLoader (Loads standard extensions & JDK modules)   │
 │   │                                                              │
 │   ▼                                                              │
 │ Application (System) ClassLoader (Loads -classpath / -cp classes)│
 │   │                                                              │
 │   ▼                                                              │
 │ Custom ClassLoaders (Tomcat WebappClassLoader, Plugin loaders)   │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Delegation Sequence
When asked to load a class `loadClass(name)`:
1. The loader checks its **local cache** to see if the class is already loaded.
2. If not, it delegates upward to its **parent ClassLoader**.
3. The delegation cascades up to the **Bootstrap ClassLoader**.
4. Only if all ancestor loaders fail does the child invoke its own `findClass(name)`.
- **Security Invariant:** Prevents rogue application code from overriding core classes like `java.lang.Object` or `java.lang.System`.

---

## Class Lifecycle: Loading, Linking, and Initializing

1. **Loading:** Fetches binary byte stream and creates the `Class<T>` instance in Metaspace.
2. **Linking:**
   - *Verification:* Enforces JVM safety (stack bounds, type safety, valid bytecodes).
   - *Preparation:* Allocates static fields in memory and sets them to zero-defaults (`0`, `null`, `false`).
   - *Resolution:* Replaces symbolic constant pool references with direct memory pointers.
3. **Initialization (`<clinit>`):** Executes static variable initializers and `static { ... }` blocks in top-to-bottom order.

---

## HotSpot Tiered Compilation (C1 & C2)

HotSpot uses 5 compilation tiers (`-XX:+TieredCompilation`, default enabled):

| Tier | Compiler | Optimization Level | Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 0** | Interpreter | None (pure bytecode interpretation) | Zero startup delay; gathers profiling counters |
| **Tiers 1-3**| C1 (Client Compiler) | Low to Medium (fast compile time) | Immediate performance boost with profiling |
| **Tier 4** | C2 (Server Compiler) | **Peak Optimization (High)** | Deep optimizations on hot methods and loops |

### Primary JIT Optimizations
- **Method Inlining:** Replaces method call instructions with the method's actual bytecode body, eliminating call stack frame overhead.
- **Escape Analysis:** Proves whether an allocated object ever escapes the declaring method scope. If it does not escape, the JVM performs **Scalar Replacement** (allocating fields directly into CPU registers, bypassing heap allocation and GC).
- **Loop Unrolling:** Replicates loop bodies to reduce branch prediction checks.

---

## Implementation Example: Inspecting ClassLoader Chains

```java
public class ClassLoaderInspectionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Application ClassLoader (loads our user class)
        ClassLoader appLoader = ClassLoaderInspectionDemo.class.getClassLoader();
        System.out.println("User ClassLoader     : " + appLoader);

        // 2. Platform ClassLoader (parent of application loader)
        ClassLoader platformLoader = appLoader.getParent();
        System.out.println("Parent ClassLoader   : " + platformLoader);

        // 3. Bootstrap ClassLoader (parent of platform loader, represented as null)
        ClassLoader bootstrapLoader = platformLoader.getParent();
        System.out.println("Bootstrap ClassLoader: " + bootstrapLoader);

        // Core class loaded by Bootstrap Loader
        ClassLoader stringLoader = String.class.getClassLoader();
        System.out.println("String.class Loader  : " + stringLoader);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
User ClassLoader     : jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@75b84c92
Parent ClassLoader   : jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@6d06d69c
Bootstrap ClassLoader: null
String.class Loader  : null
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **`ClassNotFoundException` vs `NoClassDefFoundError`:**
  - `ClassNotFoundException`: Checked exception thrown when dynamically looking up a class by string name (`Class.forName()`) and the class is not on the classpath.
  - `NoClassDefFoundError`: Fatal error thrown when a class was available during compile time, but is missing or failed static initialization (`<clinit>`) at runtime.
- **Breaking Class Identity Across Loaders:** Two classes with the exact same package and class name loaded by two different ClassLoaders are considered **different types** by the JVM. Casting between them throws `ClassCastException`.

---

## Practice

### Question
Why does `String.class.getClassLoader()` return `null`?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `java.lang.String` is a foundational Java runtime class located inside module `java.base`.
2. Core runtime classes are loaded directly by the **Bootstrap ClassLoader**.
3. Because the Bootstrap ClassLoader is written in native C/C++ inside the JVM binary, it is not a Java object.
4. The Java runtime API represents the Bootstrap ClassLoader with the reference `null`.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
The Java Platform Module System (JPMS / Project Jigsaw, introduced in Java 9 via JSR 376) introduces modular boundaries above packages. It enforces **Reliable Configuration** (validating dependency graphs at startup) and **Strong Encapsulation** (forbidding compile-time and reflective access to unexported packages, even for `public` classes).

---

## `module-info.java` Directives Reference

```java
module com.enterprise.billing {
    // 1. Dependency Requirements
    requires java.base;             // Implicitly required by all modules
    requires transitive java.sql;   // Transitive: downstream consumers also read java.sql

    // 2. Public API Exposure
    exports com.enterprise.billing.api;
    exports com.enterprise.billing.dto to com.enterprise.portal; // Qualified export

    // 3. Reflective Access for Frameworks (Spring, Hibernate, Jackson)
    opens com.enterprise.billing.model to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;

    // 4. Service Provider Interface (SPI)
    uses com.enterprise.billing.spi.PaymentGateway;
    provides com.enterprise.billing.spi.PaymentGateway with com.enterprise.billing.internal.StripeGateway;
}
```

| Directive | Architectural Purpose | Scope of Exposure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`requires <mod>`** | Declares dependency on another module | Compile-time and runtime linkage |
| **`requires transitive <mod>`**| Transitive dependency ("implied readability") | Dependents reading this module also read `<mod>` |
| **`exports <pkg>`** | Exposes `public` types to outside callers | Compile-time API and runtime invocation |
| **`exports <pkg> to <mod>`** | Qualified export: limits access to whitelisted modules | Restricted to named partner modules |
| **`opens <pkg>`** | Permits deep reflection (`setAccessible(true)`) | Runtime reflection only (hidden at compile-time) |
| **`opens <pkg> to <mod>`** | Qualified open: limits deep reflection to framework | Restricted to specified reflection consumers |
| **`uses <serviceInterface>`**| Declares consumption of a Service Provider | Discovered via `java.util.ServiceLoader` |
| **`provides <intf> with <impl>`**| Publishes concrete service provider implementation | Registered in module descriptor |

---

## Strong Encapsulation & The Modular Wall

```
              Module: com.enterprise.core
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Exports: com.enterprise.core.api                            │
 │   - Public interface OrderService (Accessible to all)       │
 ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Non-Exported: com.enterprise.core.internal                  │
 │   - Public class FastMemoryCipher                           │
 │   - ACCESSIBLE ONLY within com.enterprise.core              │
 │   - OUTSIDE ACCESS BLOCKED:                                 │
 │       * Compile-time imports fail                           │
 │       * Reflection setAccessible(true) throws               │
 │         InaccessibleObjectException                         │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Custom Lightweight Runtimes: `jlink`

JPMS enables `jlink` to bundle only the necessary JDK modules into a stripped-down native runtime image, eliminating the monolithic JDK:

```bash
# Creates a minimal custom JRE (~35 MB instead of standard 400 MB JDK)
jlink --module-path $JAVA_HOME/jmods:out \
      --add-modules com.enterprise.billing \
      --strip-debug \
      --compress=2 \
      --no-header-files \
      --no-man-pages \
      --output dist/custom-jre
```

---

## Implementation Example: SPI ServiceLoader Discovery

```java
package com.enterprise.billing;

import java.util.ServiceLoader;

public class ModuleBootstrapDemo {
    public interface TelemetrySink {
        void record(String metric);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Discovers all providers registered via 'provides ... with' in module-info
        ServiceLoader<TelemetrySink> sinks = ServiceLoader.load(TelemetrySink.class);

        int discoveredCount = 0;
        for (TelemetrySink sink : sinks) {
            sink.record("system.startup=true");
            discoveredCount++;
        }

        System.out.println("Discovered and notified SPI providers: " + discoveredCount);
    }
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>View Output</summary>

```text
Discovered and notified SPI providers: 0
```
</details>

---

## Pitfalls

- **Cyclic Dependencies Forbidden:** Unlike the legacy classpath which allowed circular JAR dependencies, JPMS forbids module cycles (`Module A` requires `B`, `B` requires `A`) and triggers a compile-time error.
- **Split Packages Prohibited:** Two modules cannot export the exact same package name (`package com.app.util` declared in both Module 1 and Module 2). This causes an immediate compilation and startup failure.
- **`InaccessibleObjectException` Under Java 17+:** In Java 17, strong encapsulation is enforced by default (`--illegal-access=permit` was permanently removed). Calling `setAccessible(true)` on non-opened packages throws `InaccessibleObjectException`. Add `opens <pkg>` or `--add-opens` JVM flags.

---

## Practice

### Question
What is the difference between `exports com.app.model;` and `opens com.app.model;` in `module-info.java`?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. `exports com.app.model;` exposes public types in that package for normal compile-time compilation and standard runtime invocation by other modules. However, it does NOT allow other modules to inspect private members via deep reflection.
2. `opens com.app.model;` permits runtime deep reflection (`setAccessible(true)` on private fields/methods) by frameworks (such as Jackson or Hibernate), while hiding the package from compile-time imports.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Modern Java development relies on build automation systems—primarily **Apache Maven** and **Gradle**—to manage dependency resolution from central repositories, compile bytecodes according to standard directory structures, execute automated test suites, and package executable archives (JAR/WAR/Docker).

---

## Maven vs Gradle Comparison

| Dimension | Apache Maven (`pom.xml`) | Gradle (`build.gradle.kts`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Philosophy** | Convention-over-configuration; declarative XML | Task-oriented; programmatic Kotlin/Groovy DSL |
| **Execution Model** | Linear sequence of immutable phases | Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of discrete tasks |
| **Build Caching** | File-timestamp based (re-runs phases) | **Incremental build cache** (skips up-to-date tasks) |
| **Transitive Conflicts**| Resolves by **Nearest Definition** in tree | Resolves by **Highest Version** by default |
| **Performance** | Predictable baseline | Significantly faster on large multi-module projects |

---

## Standard Directory Layout (Convention over Configuration)

Both Maven and Gradle enforce the canonical Java directory layout:

```
 project-root/
 ├── pom.xml (or build.gradle.kts)
 ├── src/
 │   ├── main/
 │   │   ├── java/        ──► Production Java source code (.java)
 │   │   └── resources/   ──► Application properties, XML, static configs
 │   └── test/
 │       ├── java/        ──► Unit and integration test sources
 │       └── resources/   ──► Test-only mock fixtures
 └── target/ (or build/)  ──► Output compiled .class files and packaged .jar
```

---

## Maven Core Lifecycle & Dependency Scopes

### Standard Default Lifecycle Phases
`validate` $\rightarrow$ `compile` $\rightarrow$ `test` $\rightarrow$ `package` $\rightarrow$ `verify` $\rightarrow$ `install` $\rightarrow$ `deploy`

Executing a phase automatically triggers all preceding phases in sequence.

### Dependency Scopes

| Scope | Classpath: Compile | Classpath: Test | Classpath: Runtime | Packaged in Final JAR? |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`compile`** (Default) | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| **`provided`** | **Yes** | **Yes** | No (Supplied by JDK/Container) | No (e.g. Servlet API, Lombok) |
| **`runtime`** | No | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** (e.g. JDBC Drivers) |
| **`test`** | No | **Yes** | No | No (e.g. JUnit, Mockito) |

---

## Transitive Conflict Resolution

When Library A depends on `Lib C:1.0` and Library B depends on `Lib C:2.0`:
- **Maven Rule (Nearest Definition):** The version closest to the root `pom.xml` in the dependency tree wins. If tree depths match, the first declared dependency wins. Override explicitly via `<dependencyManagement>`.
- **Gradle Rule (Newest Version):** Gradle automatically selects the highest version (`2.0`) unless locked or constrained.

---

## Minimal Production `pom.xml` Specification

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
                             http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.enterprise.app</groupId>
    <artifactId>telemetry-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Compile Scope Dependency -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>2.17.0</version>
        </dependency>

        <!-- Test Scope Dependency -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <version>5.10.2</version>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>
```

---

## Pitfalls

- **Bypassing the Wrapper (`./mvnw` or `./gradlew`):** Running locally installed system CLIs (`mvn` or `gradle`) leads to mismatched version bugs across developer environments and CI/CD pipelines. Always commit and execute via the repository wrapper script.
- **Leaking Test Dependencies into Compile Scope:** Omitting `<scope>test</scope>` bundles test libraries (e.g. JUnit, Mockito) into production distribution JARs, increasing deployment size and attack surface.
- **Dynamic Version Dependencies:** Using floating version ranges (e.g. `1.+` or `LATEST`) produces non-reproducible builds where upstream updates break CI/CD pipelines unexpectedly. Pin exact version coordinates.

---

## Practice

### Question
Why is the `provided` dependency scope used for `servlet-api` in traditional web applications?

<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

### Explanation
1. During compilation, the application code requires `servlet-api` classes (`HttpServletRequest`, `HttpServletResponse`) to compile cleanly.
2. At runtime, the hosting servlet container (such as Apache Tomcat) already provides its own copy of the servlet API in its shared library folder.
3. If the application bundled its own `servlet-api.jar` inside `WEB-INF/lib`, a ClassLoader conflict would occur, throwing `LinkageError` or `ClassCastException`.
4. Marking it `provided` includes it on the compile and test classpaths, but excludes it from the final WAR package.

</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
In 2017, Oracle transferred Java EE to the Eclipse Foundation to establish Jakarta EE. Because Oracle retained the "Java" commercial trademark, the legacy `javax.*` package namespace was permanently frozen at Java EE 8, and all enterprise specifications migrated to the `jakarta.*` namespace starting in Jakarta EE 9. This architectural boundary dictates runtime compatibility between application servers, frameworks, and dependency ecosystems.

---

## The Namespace Migration Architecture

```
                      Java Enterprise Evolution
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
│ Sun J2EE (1999-2006) │ Oracle Java EE (2006-│ Eclipse Jakarta EE     │
│ J2EE 1.2 – 1.4       │ 2017) Java EE 5 – 8  │ (2018+) Jakarta EE 9+  │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
│ javax.* namespace    │ javax.* namespace    │ jakarta.* namespace    │
│ Proprietary Sun spec │ Oracle trademarked   │ Vendor-neutral OSS     │
│ EJB 1.x/2.x heavy    │ Annotations & CDI    │ Cloud-native & modern  │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
```

| Specification | Legacy Namespace (`<= Java EE 8`) | Modern Namespace (`>= Jakarta EE 9`) | Modern Maven Coordinates (`>= Jakarta EE 10`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Servlet API** | `javax.servlet.*` | `jakarta.servlet.*` | `jakarta.servlet:jakarta.servlet-api:6.0.0` |
| **Persistence (JPA)** | `javax.persistence.*` | `jakarta.persistence.*` | `jakarta.persistence:jakarta.persistence-api:3.1.0` |
| **RESTful Web Services** | `javax.ws.rs.*` | `jakarta.ws.rs.*` | `jakarta.ws.rs:jakarta.ws.rs-api:3.1.0` |
| **Contexts & DI (CDI)** | `javax.enterprise.context.*` | `jakarta.enterprise.context.*` | `jakarta.enterprise:jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api:4.0.1` |
| **Bean Validation** | `javax.validation.*` | `jakarta.validation.*` | `jakarta.validation:jakarta.validation-api:3.0.2` |
| **JSON Processing** | `javax.json.*` | `jakarta.json.*` | `jakarta.json:jakarta.json-api:2.1.3` |

---

## Application Server & Framework Compatibility Matrix

| Runtime / Framework | Legacy Namespace (`javax.*`) | Modern Namespace (`jakarta.*`) | Minimum Java Version |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Apache Tomcat** | Tomcat 8.5 / 9.0 | Tomcat 10.1 / 11.0 | Tomcat 10.1: Java 11+, Tomcat 11: Java 17+ |
| **Eclipse Jetty** | Jetty 9 / 10 | Jetty 11 / 12 (Core) | Jetty 11: Java 11+, Jetty 12: Java 17+ |
| **WildFly** | WildFly <= 26.1 | WildFly 27+ | Java 11+ / Java 17+ |
| **Spring Framework** | Spring 5.x | Spring 6.x | Spring 6: Java 17+ |
| **Spring Boot** | Spring Boot 2.x | Spring Boot 3.x | Spring Boot 3: Java 17+ |
| **Hibernate ORM** | Hibernate 5.x | Hibernate 6.x | Hibernate 6: Java 17+ |

---

## Production Implementation: Namespace Verification

```java
import jakarta.servlet.ServletContainerInitializer;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletContext;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import java.util.Set;

public class NamespaceValidatorInitializer implements ServletContainerInitializer {

    @Override
    public void onStartup(Set<Class<?>> c, ServletContext ctx) throws ServletException {
        String serverInfo = ctx.getServerInfo();
        int majorVersion = ctx.getEffectiveMajorVersion();
        int minorVersion = ctx.getEffectiveMinorVersion();

        // Enforce modern Jakarta EE 10 (Servlet 6.0+) compliance
        if (majorVersion < 6) {
            ctx.log("[WARNING] Server is running Servlet specification < 6.0: " + majorVersion + "." + minorVersion);
        } else {
            ctx.log("[INFO] Jakarta EE 10+ compliant servlet container verified: " + serverInfo);
        }
    }
}
```

```
[INFO] Jakarta EE 10+ compliant servlet container verified: Apache Tomcat/10.1.24
```

---

## Common Pitfalls & Migration Traps

- **Deploying `javax.*` WAR to Tomcat 10+ / Jetty 11+:**
  Results in silent failures or `ClassNotFoundException: javax.servlet.Filter`. Tomcat 10+ completely ignores `javax.*` annotations (`@WebServlet`) and filters. Use Tomcat 9.0 for `javax.*` or migrate imports to `jakarta.*`.
- **Mixing Namespaces Across Dependencies:**
  Using Spring Boot 3 with a legacy third-party library importing `javax.persistence.Entity` causes entities to be ignored by Hibernate 6. Every transitive dependency touching enterprise specs must use `jakarta.*`.
- **Maven Dependency Scope Trap:**
  Declaring `jakarta.servlet-api` as `compile` scope packages the API inside `WEB-INF/lib`, causing classloader conflicts with the servlet container's built-in servlet engine classes. Always declare container-provided APIs with `<scope>provided</scope>`.

---

## Verification & Practice

**Question:** A legacy Spring Boot 2.7 service running Java 8 is upgraded directly to Spring Boot 3.2 on Java 21. What happens during compilation if the source code contains `import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;`?

**Explanation:** The build fails with a compilation error (`package javax.servlet.http does not exist`). Spring Boot 3.x is built on Spring Framework 6.x and Jakarta EE 10 (`jakarta.servlet.*`). The legacy `javax.*` APIs are completely omitted from the classpath. All imports must be refactored to `import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;`.

---

## Practice

### Q: Why did the enterprise namespace transition from `javax.*` to `jakarta.*` break backward binary compatibility, and how does Apache Tomcat 10.1+ handle older WAR files?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** Oracle retained trademark ownership over the `javax` package namespace when donating Java EE to the Eclipse Foundation. Consequently, Jakarta EE 9+ migrated all APIs to the `jakarta.*` package namespace (`javax.servlet` -> `jakarta.servlet`). Containers like Tomcat 10+ adhere strictly to Jakarta EE specifications and reject `javax.*` servlets unless bytecode migration tools rewrite class references prior to deployment.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
A Web Application Archive (WAR) is a standardized packaged zip artifact containing web assets, compiled bytecode, libraries, and configuration descriptors deployed to a servlet container such as Apache Tomcat. Tomcat executes the Catalina servlet engine, managing application lifecycles, classloader isolation, and HTTP request routing to deployed web applications.

---

## Canonical WAR Directory Layout

```
myapp.war
├── index.html                   <-- Public static asset (directly accessible)
├── css/
│   └── styles.css               <-- Public stylesheet
├── WEB-INF/                     <-- Protected Container Boundary (Forbidden to direct HTTP)
│   ├── web.xml                  <-- Deployment Descriptor (Optional in Servlet 3.0+)
│   ├── classes/                 <-- Application compiled bytecode (.class files)
│   │   ├── com/example/UserServlet.class
│   │   └── application.properties
│   └── lib/                     <-- Application-scoped third-party JARs (.jar files)
│       └── gson-2.10.1.jar
└── META-INF/                    <-- Archive metadata & manifest
    └── MANIFEST.MF
```

| Path | Public Access | Content Description | Container Classloader Loading |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`/` (Root)** | Yes | HTML, CSS, client JS, images | N/A (served by DefaultServlet) |
| **`WEB-INF/`** | **Strictly Blocked** | Configuration, templates, internal views | Container enforces 404/403 for direct client URLs |
| **`WEB-INF/classes/`** | **Strictly Blocked** | Application compiled `.class` files and resources | WebappClassLoader (highest application priority) |
| **`WEB-INF/lib/`** | **Strictly Blocked** | Bundled dependency `.jar` archives | WebappClassLoader |
| **`META-INF/`** | **Strictly Blocked** | Package manifests, service providers, CDI beans | Standard Java archive metadata |

---

## Tomcat Architectural Hierarchy

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Server (<Server> port="8005" shutdown="SHUTDOWN")      │
│  └── Service (<Service name="Catalina">)               │
│       ├── Connector (Coyote HTTP/1.1 on port 8080)     │
│       ├── Connector (Coyote AJP/1.3 on port 8009)      │
│       └── Engine (<Engine name="Catalina">)            │
│            └── Host (<Host name="localhost" appBase="webapps">)
│                 ├── Context (path="/app1" docBase="app1.war")
│                 └── Context (path="/ROOT" docBase="ROOT.war")
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Production Deployment Descriptor: web.xml

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee
                             https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee/web-app_6_0.xsd"
         version="6.0"
         metadata-complete="false">

    <display-name>Production Web Application</display-name>

    <context-param>
        <param-name>environment</param-name>
        <param-value>PRODUCTION</param-value>
    </context-param>

    <session-config>
        <session-timeout>30</session-timeout>
        <cookie-config>
            <http-only>true</http-only>
            <secure>true</secure>
        </cookie-config>
    </session-config>

</web-app>
```

---

## Common Pitfalls & Deployment Traps

- **Exposing Internal JSPs or Templates in WAR Root:**
  Placing JSP or HTML template files directly under the root folder makes them publicly navigable via browser URLs, bypassing servlet controllers and security filters. Always place internal views inside `WEB-INF/views/`.
- **Packaging Container-Provided Libraries inside `WEB-INF/lib`:**
  Bundling `jakarta.servlet-api.jar` inside `WEB-INF/lib` creates classloader conflicts with Tomcat's `lib/servlet-api.jar`, causing `ClassCastException` or linking errors. Use `<scope>provided</scope>` in Maven.
- **The `metadata-complete="true"` Trap:**
  Setting `metadata-complete="true"` in `web.xml` instructs Tomcat to disable classpath annotation scanning (`@WebServlet`, `@WebFilter`, `@WebListener`). All components must then be explicitly declared in `web.xml` or they will not be registered.

---

## Verification & Practice

**Question:** An engineer uploads a sensitive configuration file `db.properties` into the root directory of a deployed WAR instead of `WEB-INF/classes/`. What security vulnerability is created?

**Explanation:** Files placed in the root of a WAR are served directly as static files by Tomcat's `DefaultServlet`. Anyone navigating to `https://example.com/db.properties` can download the database credentials in plaintext. Moving the file to `WEB-INF/classes/` makes it accessible to the classloader via `getResourceAsStream()` while strictly preventing direct HTTP access.

---

## Practice

### Q: Why are resources located within the `/WEB-INF/` directory inaccessible via direct HTTP client URLs, and how does the server access them?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** The Servlet specification explicitly designates the `/WEB-INF/` directory (including `/WEB-INF/classes`, `/WEB-INF/lib`, and `/WEB-INF/web.xml`) as private and protected from direct HTTP client requests (returning HTTP 404). The container accesses `/WEB-INF/` files solely via internal server-side forwarding (`RequestDispatcher.forward()`), protecting views, configurations, and bytecode from unauthorized public downloads.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Servlets can be declared and configured either declaratively using the `@WebServlet` annotation (introduced in Servlet 3.0) or centrally through the XML deployment descriptor (`WEB-INF/web.xml`). The deployment descriptor takes precedence over annotations and enables dynamic deployment modifications without recompiling application bytecode.

---

## Master Jakarta Servlet Component Annotations Directory

Modern Jakarta Servlet 6.0 allows declarative configuration of all web components via annotations in package `jakarta.servlet.annotation`. Below is the complete reference matrix of all servlet component annotations.

| Annotation | Applicable Target | Key Attributes | Specification Purpose & Lifecycle Role | Production Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`@WebServlet`** | `TYPE` | `name`, `urlPatterns`, `loadOnStartup`, `initParams`, `asyncSupported` | Declares an `HttpServlet` component and binds it to URL patterns with optional initialization parameters. | `@WebServlet(name = "UserServlet", urlPatterns = {"/users/*"}, loadOnStartup = 1)` |
| **`@WebFilter`** | `TYPE` | `filterName`, `urlPatterns`, `servletNames`, `dispatcherTypes`, `asyncSupported` | Declares a `Filter` component intercepting incoming requests or responses before/after servlet execution. | `@WebFilter(urlPatterns = {"/api/*"}, dispatcherTypes = {DispatcherType.REQUEST})` |
| **`@WebListener`** | `TYPE` | `value` | Declares an application lifecycle event listener (e.g. `ServletContextListener`, `HttpSessionListener`). | `@WebListener public class AppBootstrapListener implements ServletContextListener {}` |
| **`@WebInitParam`** | *(Nested in annotations)* | `name`, `value`, `description` | Declares initialization name-value pairs inside `@WebServlet` or `@WebFilter`. | `initParams = {@WebInitParam(name = "timeout", value = "30")}` |
| **`@MultipartConfig`** | `TYPE` | `location`, `maxFileSize`, `maxRequestSize`, `fileSizeThreshold` | Enables multipart/form-data payload parsing on the annotated servlet via `request.getPart(...)`. | `@MultipartConfig(maxFileSize = 10485760L, maxRequestSize = 20971520L)` |
| **`@ServletSecurity`** | `TYPE` | `value` (`@HttpConstraint`), `httpMethodConstraints` | Enforces declarative security constraints, roles, and transport guarantees (SSL/TLS) on servlet paths. | `@ServletSecurity(@HttpConstraint(rolesAllowed = {"ADMIN"}))` |
| **`@HttpConstraint`** | *(Nested in security)* | `value`, `rolesAllowed`, `transportGuarantee` | Defines security constraint applied to all HTTP methods not explicitly overridden. | `@HttpConstraint(transportGuarantee = TransportGuarantee.CONFIDENTIAL)` |
| **`@HttpMethodConstraint`** | *(Nested in security)* | `value` (HTTP verb), `rolesAllowed`, `emptyRoleSemantic` | Enforces distinct role constraints per specific HTTP method (e.g. restrict `POST` to `MANAGER`). | `@HttpMethodConstraint(value = "POST", rolesAllowed = {"MANAGER"})` |

---

## Configuration Comparison Matrix

| Property | `@WebServlet` Annotation | `web.xml` Deployment Descriptor | Precedence Rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **URL Mapping** | `urlPatterns = {"/api/*"}` | `<url-pattern>/api/*</url-pattern>` | `web.xml` overrides annotation |
| **Servlet Name** | `name = "UserServlet"` | `<servlet-name>UserServlet</servlet-name>` | Required in XML, defaults to FQCN in annotation |
| **Load on Startup** | `loadOnStartup = 1` | `<load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>` | Lower positive integers load earlier |
| **Init Parameters** | `@WebInitParam(name="k", value="v")` | `<init-param><param-name>k</param-name>...` | XML overrides duplicate parameter names |
| **Asynchronous Support**| `asyncSupported = true` | `<async-supported>true</async-supported>` | Defaults to `false` |
| **Recompilation** | Requires recompiling `.class` | No recompile needed; restart / redeploy WAR | N/A |

---

## Production Implementation: Configured Servlet with Init Parameters

```java
import jakarta.servlet.ServletConfig;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebInitParam;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet(
    name = "PaymentGatewayServlet",
    urlPatterns = {"/checkout/pay", "/checkout/process"},
    loadOnStartup = 2,
    initParams = {
        @WebInitParam(name = "timeoutSeconds", value = "15"),
        @WebInitParam(name = "retryAttempts", value = "3")
    }
)
public class PaymentGatewayServlet extends HttpServlet {

    private int timeout;
    private int maxRetries;

    @Override
    public void init(ServletConfig config) throws ServletException {
        super.init(config);
        this.timeout = Integer.parseInt(config.getInitParameter("timeoutSeconds"));
        this.maxRetries = Integer.parseInt(config.getInitParameter("retryAttempts"));
    }

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain");
        resp.getWriter().printf("Gateway Ready: timeout=%ds, maxRetries=%d%n", timeout, maxRetries);
    }
}
```

---

## Equivalent Deployment Descriptor: web.xml

```xml
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee" version="6.0">
    <servlet>
        <servlet-name>PaymentGatewayServlet</servlet-name>
        <servlet-class>PaymentGatewayServlet</servlet-class>
        <init-param>
            <param-name>timeoutSeconds</param-name>
            <param-value>30</param-value> <!-- Overrides annotation's 15 -->
        </init-param>
        <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
    </servlet>

    <servlet-mapping>
        <servlet-name>PaymentGatewayServlet</servlet-name>
        <url-pattern>/checkout/pay</url-pattern>
    </servlet-mapping>
</web-app>
```

---

## Common Pitfalls & Configuration Traps

- **Missing `metadata-complete="false"` with `web.xml`:**
  If `web.xml` defines `metadata-complete="true"`, Tomcat skips classpath scanning for annotations entirely. All `@WebServlet` annotated classes that are not declared in `web.xml` will fail to register with 404 Not Found.
- **Ambiguous URL Patterns:**
  Mapping two different servlets to the exact same URL pattern (e.g., `/catalog`) causes deployment failure with `IllegalArgumentException: The servlets named [A] and [B] are both mapped to the url-pattern [/catalog]`.
- **Negative `loadOnStartup` Values:**
  Setting `loadOnStartup` to a negative number (or omitting it) tells the container to initialize the servlet lazily on the first request rather than during server startup.

---

## Verification & Practice

**Question:** An annotation specifies `timeoutSeconds = 15`, but `web.xml` defines the same parameter with value `30`. What value does `config.getInitParameter("timeoutSeconds")` return at runtime?

**Explanation:** It returns `"30"`. The deployment descriptor (`web.xml`) always takes precedence over annotations, allowing operational engineers to override application parameters in production without modifying source code.

---

## Practice

### Q: If a servlet is declared with both `@WebServlet(urlPatterns = "/orders")` and defined in `web.xml` with `<url-pattern>/api/orders</url-pattern>`, which configuration takes precedence?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** The `web.xml` deployment descriptor strictly overrides bytecode annotations. The Servlet specification dictates that explicit XML configuration takes precedence over annotations, allowing administrators and DevOps teams to reconfigure URL mappings and parameters at deployment time without recompiling Java source code.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview
Jakarta Web Security provides standardized declarative and programmatic authentication and authorization mechanisms managed by the servlet container. Through XML constraints or modern Jakarta Security annotations, applications restrict URL access by caller roles, enforce encrypted HTTPS transport, and inspect caller credentials via container-managed identities.

---

## Declarative Security Elements in web.xml

| Element | Parent | Configuration Responsibility |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`<security-constraint>`** | `<web-app>` | Top-level container defining protected URL patterns and role requirements |
| **`<web-resource-collection>`** | `<security-constraint>` | Specifies URL patterns and HTTP methods (`<http-method>`) subject to protection |
| **`<auth-constraint>`** | `<security-constraint>` | Names roles permitted access (`<role-name>ADMIN</role-name>` or `*`) |
| **`<user-data-constraint>`** | `<security-constraint>` | Enforces SSL/TLS via `<transport-guarantee>CONFIDENTIAL</transport-guarantee>` |
| **`<login-config>`** | `<web-app>` | Configures auth method (`BASIC`, `FORM`, `CLIENT-CERT`) and form login pages |
| **`<security-role>`** | `<web-app>` | Declares valid application security roles referenced by constraints |

---

## Programmatic Security API Contract

```java
// Available directly on HttpServletRequest
boolean authenticated = req.authenticate(response); // Triggers container login dialog
req.login("username", "password");                  // Programmatic credential submission
req.logout();                                       // Clears user identity and invalidates session
boolean isAdmin = req.isUserInRole("ADMIN");        // Queries caller role membership
Principal user = req.getUserPrincipal();             // Returns caller identity (Principal.getName())
```

---

## Production Implementation: Declarative Security in web.xml

```xml
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee" version="6.0">

    <!-- Restrict /admin/* to users with role ADMIN and enforce HTTPS -->
    <security-constraint>
        <web-resource-collection>
            <web-resource-name>Admin Console</web-resource-name>
            <url-pattern>/admin/*</url-pattern>
            <http-method>GET</http-method>
            <http-method>POST</http-method>
        </web-resource-collection>
        <auth-constraint>
            <role-name>ADMIN</role-name>
        </auth-constraint>
        <user-data-constraint>
            <transport-guarantee>CONFIDENTIAL</transport-guarantee>
        </user-data-constraint>
    </security-constraint>

    <!-- Configure Form-Based Authentication -->
    <login-config>
        <auth-method>FORM</auth-method>
        <realm-name>EnterpriseRealm</realm-name>
        <form-login-config>
            <form-login-page>/login.jsp</form-login-page>
            <form-error-page>/login-error.jsp</form-error-page>
        </form-login-config>
    </login-config>

    <security-role>
        <role-name>ADMIN</role-name>
    </security-role>

</web-app>
```

---

## Common Pitfalls & Security Traps

- **The HTTP Method Omission Trap in `<web-resource-collection>`:**
  Listing specific methods like `<http-method>GET</http-method>` protects ONLY `GET` requests. An attacker issuing `POST`, `HEAD`, or `PUT` bypasses the `<auth-constraint>` completely. Omit `<http-method>` entirely to protect **all** HTTP verbs by default.
- **Form Action Discrepancies in FORM Auth:**
  In FORM authentication, the HTML login form must submit via `POST` to the special container action `j_security_check` with input fields named exactly `j_username` and `j_password`. Changing field names prevents container credential interception.
- **Confidential Transport on Non-SSL Ports:**
  Configuring `<transport-guarantee>CONFIDENTIAL</transport-guarantee>` instructs Tomcat to redirect HTTP requests to the secure redirect port (default 8443). If SSL/TLS connectors are not configured in `conf/server.xml`, the browser receives a connection refused error.

---

## Verification & Practice

**Question:** An application defines `<auth-constraint><role-name>*</role-name></auth-constraint>`. What does the asterisk `*` specify according to the Jakarta Servlet specification?

**Explanation:** In Jakarta Servlet 3.0+, `*` matches **any authenticated user**, regardless of specific role assignment, provided the user successfully authenticated against the container realm. In contrast, `<role-name>**</role-name>` specifically requires that the user is authenticated and mapped to at least one declared application role.

---

## Practice

### Q: How does the Synchronizer Token Pattern defend against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks in server-side Java web applications?
<details data-type="solution">
<summary>Reveal Answer</summary>

> **Answer:** CSRF attacks rely on the browser automatically attaching session cookies (`JSESSIONID`) when submitting cross-site requests. The Synchronizer Token Pattern stores an unpredictable random token in user session state and embeds it in HTML forms as a hidden field. Because malicious cross-origin sites cannot read or forge this token under the Same-Origin Policy, the server validates the incoming token against session state and rejects requests where tokens mismatch.
</details>

markdownContent:
## Overview Jakarta Pages (formerly JSP) is a server-side templating technology that combines static markup (HTML/XML) with dynamic Java components. The container's Jasper compiler translates `.jsp` files into standard `HttpServlet` source files (`_jsp.java`) and compiles them to bytecode on first access, exposing 9 implicit runtime objects. --- ## JSP Compilation Lifecycle ``` Browser Request: /index.jsp │ ▼ Container Checks Is _index_jsp.class compiled & up-to-date? ├── NO ──> [Translation Phase]: Jasper converts .jsp -> _index_jsp.java │ [Compilation Phase]: javac compiles .java -> _index_jsp.class └── YES ─> [Execution Phase]: Container invokes _jspService(req, res) ``` --- ## The 9 Implicit Runtime Objects | Object | Underlying Type | Scope | Primary Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **`request`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest` | Request | Parameters, headers, cookies, request attributes | | **`response`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse`| Page | Response headers, status codes, cookies | | **`pageContext`**| `jakarta.servlet.jsp.PageContext` | Page | Context aggregator; provides access to all scopes | | **`session`** | `jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession` | Session | User conversational state across multiple requests | | **`application`**| `jakarta.servlet.ServletContext` | Application | Context parameters, app-wide shared state | | **`out`** | `jakarta.servlet.jsp.JspWriter` | Page | Buffered character output stream to client | | **`config`** | `jakarta.servlet.ServletConfig` | Page | Servlet initialization parameters for the JSP | | **`page`** | `java.lang.Object` (this) | Page | Self-reference to current translated servlet instance | | **`exception`** | `java.lang.Throwable` | Page | Available only if `<%@ page isErrorPage="true" %>` | --- ## JSP Syntax Elements Reference | Syntax Element | Markup Syntax | Translated Equivalent in `_jsp.java` | Production Status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Directive** | `<%@ page import="java.util.List" %>` | Java package imports / page settings | **Standard** | | **Include Directive**| `<%@ include file="nav.jsp" %>` | Static copy-paste of code at translation time | **Standard** | | **Expression** | `<%= user.getName() %>` | `out.print(user.getName());` | Discouraged (use EL `${user.name}`) | | **Scriptlet** | `<% int x = 10; %>` | Placed directly inside `_jspService()` body | **Forbidden Anti-Pattern** | | **Declaration** | `<%! private int counter = 0; %>` | Placed as **instance variable** in servlet class | **Dangerous** (Thread safety bug) | --- ## Production Implementation: JSP View Template ```html <%@ page contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" pageEncoding="UTF-8" session="false" %> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> Order Summary

Order #${order.id}

Customer: ${order.customerName}

ItemPrice
${item.name} $${item.price}
``` --- ## Common Pitfalls & Antipatterns - **Using Scriptlet Declarations (`<%! %>`) for Business State:** Variables declared inside `<%! %>` become instance variables of the generated servlet class. Because Tomcat serves multiple concurrent requests using one servlet instance, state declared here is shared across all concurrent users, causing severe data leakage bugs. - **Unchecked Scriptlet Code in Views:** Embedding raw Java logic inside `<% ... %>` scriptlets violates MVC separation of concerns, makes code untestable via JUnit, and frequently exposes applications to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). Always use Expression Language (EL) and JSTL. - **Default Session Allocation in JSP:** By default, JSPs allocate an `HttpSession` automatically (`session="true"`). For public landing pages or read-only REST views, declare `<%@ page session="false" %>` to prevent memory exhaustion from search engine crawler sessions. --- ## Verification & Practice **Question:** An engineer changes a JSP file on a production server, but users continue seeing the old page content. What causes this in Tomcat's Jasper engine? **Explanation:** In production configurations, Tomcat's Jasper servlet parameter `development` is set to `false`, disabling automatic modification checks on every request for performance. The compiled `_jsp.class` in Tomcat's `work/` directory is cached. To apply changes, either trigger a redeploy, touch the WAR file, or delete the cached `.class` file inside the `work/` folder. --- ## Practice ### Q: Why are Java Scriptlets (`<% ... %>`) considered deprecated legacy practices in modern server-side templating?
Reveal Answer > **Answer:** Scriptlets mix imperative Java code directly with HTML presentation, violating Model-View-Controller separation of concerns, hindering frontend maintainability, making automated unit testing impossible, and introducing critical Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities due to lack of automatic HTML entity escaping.

markdownContent:
## Overview Expression Language (EL) and Jakarta Standard Tag Library (JSTL) eliminate Java scriptlet code from server-side templates. EL provides concise navigation of JavaBeans properties and collections using `${expression}` syntax with automatic null-safe evaluation and scope traversal, while JSTL provides structured conditional branching and iteration tags. --- ## EL Automatic Scope Resolution Hierarchy When evaluating `${user}`, EL searches scopes in order until the first non-null match is encountered: ``` 1. pageScope.get("user") (Current JSP page only) │ (if null) ▼ 2. requestScope.get("user") (Current HTTP request dispatch) │ (if null) ▼ 3. sessionScope.get("user") (Current client HttpSession) │ (if null) ▼ 4. applicationScope.get("user") (Global ServletContext) │ (if null) ▼ Returns null (renders empty string "" without NullPointerException) ``` --- ## JSTL Core Tags Reference | Tag | Primary Attributes | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **``** | `value`, `default`, `escapeXml` | Prints expression with **automatic XML/HTML escaping** (XSS defense) | | **``** | `test`, `var`, `scope` | Evaluates boolean expression; renders body if `true` | | **``** | *(Container)* | Multi-branch conditional parent (similar to Java switch) | | **``** | `test` | Evaluated branch inside `` | | **``**| *(None)* | Default fallback branch inside `` | | **``**| `items`, `var`, `varStatus` | Iterates over arrays, `Collection`, `Iterator`, `Map` | | **``** | `var`, `value`, `scope` | Binds an evaluated value into a designated scope | --- ## Production Implementation: JSTL Core Processing ```html <%@ page contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" %> <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> User Directory

Welcome,

No active users found.
#NameRoleStatus
${status.count} ${u.role} ACTIVE
``` --- ## Common Pitfalls & Security Traps - **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Raw EL Output:** Using bare `${userInput}` outputs unescaped HTML. If `userInput` contains ``, the script executes in the user's browser. Always wrap user-supplied input in `` or configure global EL escaping. - **The Empty Keyword Semantics:** The EL `empty` operator returns `true` for: `null`, empty string `""`, empty `Collection` (`isEmpty() == true`), empty `Map`, and zero-length array. It does **not** evaluate numbers; `${empty 0}` evaluates to `false`. - **Mixing Up URI Namespaces in Jakarta EE:** Using the legacy Java EE URI `<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core" %>` in Jakarta EE 10+ results in `Cannot find the tag library descriptor`. Use the modern Jakarta URI: `uri="jakarta.tags.core"`. --- ## Verification & Practice **Question:** If both `request.setAttribute("tier", "GOLD");` and `session.setAttribute("tier", "PLATINUM");` are set, what value does `${tier}` evaluate to in the JSP? **Explanation:** It evaluates to `"GOLD"`. Following the EL scope resolution order (`page` -> `request` -> `session` -> `application`), the request scope is evaluated before the session scope. To explicitly target the session attribute, use `${sessionScope.tier}`. --- ## Practice ### Q: How does Jakarta Expression Language (EL) handle `null` properties compared to raw Java code?
Reveal Answer > **Answer:** In raw Java, calling a method or property on a null reference throws a `NullPointerException`. In Jakarta EL (`${user.address.street}`), EL gracefully coerces `null` references into empty output (`""`) rather than crashing the page rendering, allowing clean view logic without defensive null-checking boilerplate.
