# Policy Projects & Packaging Decisions

Never hardcode production queue managers, database hosts, or external URLs inside a flow. Put environment settings inside a **Policy Project** so the exact same BAR code works in DEV, UAT, and PROD.

![New menu inside an Application showing Message Flow, Mapping, Subflow, and Policy options](/images/ace/toolkit-app-new-menu.png)

---

## What Goes Where? (Quick Packaging Guide)

| What You Are Creating | Put It In... | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Main business pipeline (`.msgflow`) | **Application** | Isolated deployable runtime unit |
| Shared schemas / subflows / common ESQL | **Shared Library** | Deploy once, update without rebuilding apps |
| App-specific helper files | **Static Library** (or inside the App) | Version-locked with that one App |
| Queue Manager host, port, DB credentials, URLs | **Policy Project** | Change per environment without touching flows |

---

## How a Policy Works at Runtime

1. In the Toolkit: **New -> Policy Project** (`<PolicyProjectName>`), then create a Policy (such as `MQEndpoint` or `HTTPRequest`).
2. Reference it on your flow node using `{PolicyProjectName}:PolicyName` (e.g., `{<PolicyProjectName>}:OrderMQ`).
3. Deploy the Policy Project to the Integration Server. To switch environments later, update only the Policy XML and redeploy the Policy Project.

> [!TIP]
> If you don't set a Policy Project explicitly on a server, ACE looks in the server's **Default Policy Project** set in `server.conf.yaml`.

---

title: What Is a Message Flow (.msgflow)?
shortDescription: Understand what a Message Flow is: an event-driven visual pipeline triggered by incoming messages.
markdownContent:
# What Is a Message Flow (.msgflow)?

A **Message Flow (`.msgflow`)** is a visual assembly line inside an Application. It wakes up when a message arrives, runs each node along the wires you drew, and sends out the result.

![Message Flow Canvas showing wired nodes and the Outline bird's-eye view](/images/ace/toolkit-flow-canvas-outline.png)

---

## The 3 Parts of Every Flow

1. **Input Node (Trigger):** Listens for incoming data (for example `MQInput`, `HTTPInput`, or `FileInput`). Nothing happens until a message arrives here.
2. **Processing Nodes (Middle):** Transform, filter, route, enrich, or log the message (for example `Mapping`, `Compute`, `Route`, `Trace`).
3. **Output Node (Delivery):** Sends the message out to a queue, HTTP client, API, or file (for example `MQOutput`, `HTTPReply`, `FileOutput`).

---

## Simple Mental Model

```text
  [MQInput]  ───(Out)───▶  [Mapping / Compute]  ───(Out)───▶  [MQOutput]
  (Wakes up)                 (Transforms JSON/XML)             (Writes to <OutputQueueName>)
```

- A message flow **does not poll in a loop**; it waits quietly using almost zero CPU until a message lands on its Input node.
- You can inspect big flows easily using the small **Outline** map in the bottom-left corner of the editor.

> [!NOTE]
> Every `.msgflow` runs at least one **Input node** to start. One flow can even have two different input triggers if needed, though keeping one trigger per flow is cleaner and easier to debug.

---

# Create, Add Nodes, Wire & Save a Flow

Building your first flow takes 4 quick actions in the Toolkit.

![New Message Flow dialog inside an Application](/images/ace/toolkit-new-message-flow.png)

---

## Step 1: Create the Flow File

1. Right-click your Application (`<ApplicationName>`) -> **New -> Message Flow**.
2. Type a flow name like `<MessageFlowName>`.
3. Click **Finish**. The blank grid **Flow Canvas** opens in the center.

---

## Step 2: Drag Nodes from the Palette

On the left side of the Flow Canvas is the **Palette**, grouped into drawers:

![ACE Flow Palette showing IBM MQ, Transformation, HTTP, Routing, and File drawers](/images/ace/toolkit-palette-drawers.png)

- Expand **IBM MQ** and drag `MQInput` onto the left side of the canvas.
- Expand **Transformation** and drag `Mapping` (or `Compute`) into the middle.
- Drag `MQOutput` onto the right side.

---

## Step 3: Wire the Nodes Together

Either **click the small `Out` pin** on `MQInput` and click `In` on the next node, **or** right-click `MQInput` -> **Create Connection...** and select the matching source and target terminals:

![Create Connection dialog linking Output terminal to Input terminal](/images/ace/toolkit-add-connection-dialog.png)

---

## Step 4: Fill Required Settings & Save

1. Click `MQInput` -> in **Properties** at the bottom, enter **Queue name** (every field with a red `*` is required).
2. Press **Ctrl + S** to save.
3. Check the **Problems** tab at the bottom — make sure zero red X errors remain.

> [!TIP]
> Notice the **Selection** and **Connection** icons at the very top of the Palette: stay on **Selection** (arrow icon) when moving nodes, and use right-click -> **Create Connection** to avoid missing tiny pins.

---

markdownContent:
# Life of One Message Through a Flow

Understanding what ACE does inside a single flow run explains almost every beginner error around parsers, read-only trees, and lost messages.

![5-step lifecycle diagram: Raw Bytes -> Input Parser -> Logical Tree -> Transform/Route -> Output Serializer](/images/ace/diagram-message-lifecycle.svg)

---

## What Happens Step by Step

1. **Arrival:** Raw bytes land on `MQInput` or `HTTPInput` (for example a JSON string or MQ message).
2. **Parsing (Lazy):** ACE builds the logical **InputRoot** tree using the **Message Domain** you chose on the Input node (such as `JSON` or `XMLNSC`).
3. **Propagation:** Your `OutputRoot` or unchanged `InputRoot` travels node-by-node down each wire as a **Message Assembly** (Data + Properties + Headers + LocalEnvironment + Environment + ExceptionList).
4. **Serialization:** When it reaches `MQOutput` or `HTTPReply`, ACE turns the logical tree back into raw bytes on the wire.
5. **Commit or Rollback:** If the whole flow finishes cleanly, ACE commits the transaction (MQ message disappears from input queue and stays on output queue). If an uncaught error happens, ACE rolls back and restores the input message.

---

## 3 Golden Rules Every Beginner Should Know

- **InputRoot is Read-Only:** You cannot modify `InputRoot` directly in ESQL. You copy or build into `OutputRoot` instead.
- **Synchronous Thread:** A single thread carries one message all the way to the end of its wired path before returning to the input node.
- **No Unhandled Error = Commit:** Wiring `Failure` or `Catch` turns a crash into a handled branch — remember to decide whether that branch logs and commits or rethrows!

---

markdownContent:
# Terminals: In, Out, Failure & Catch

Every node has small colored connection pins called **terminals**. Wiring the right terminal decides what happens on success versus an error.

![Diagram of Input, Processing, and Output node terminals including Out, Failure, Catch, and Alternate](/images/ace/diagram-terminals-wiring.svg)

---

## What Each Terminal Means

| Terminal | Found On | Fires When... |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **In** | Processing & Output nodes | A message arrives from the previous node |
| **Out** | Input & Processing nodes | The node finishes normally (or `MQOutput` succeeds) |
| **Failure** | Almost every node | **This specific node** throws an error inside itself (e.g., bad XML parse or missing queue) |
| **Catch** | **Input nodes** & **TryCatch** | An **unhandled error** happened **downstream** and bubbled back to this node |
| **Out1 / Match / Default** | `Compute`, `Route`, `Filter` | You branch explicitly in ESQL (`PROPAGATE TO TERMINAL 'out1'`) or XPath match |

---

## The #1 Beginner Question: Failure vs. Catch on `MQInput`

- Wire **`MQInput.Catch`** to catch errors thrown anywhere **later in the flow** (like `Compute` or `MQOutput`).
- Wire **`MQInput.Failure`** to catch errors inside **`MQInput` itself** (like corrupt MQ header or parser crash before leaving `MQInput`).

> [!TIP]
> If neither `Catch` nor `Failure` is wired on `MQInput`, ACE automatically **rolls back** the message to the input queue (and eventually moves it to the Backout / Dead-Letter queue after retries).

---

markdownContent:
# Message Domains (JSON, XMLNSC, DFDL, BLOB, MIME)

A **Message Domain** tells ACE *which language* the incoming bytes are written in so it knows how to parse fields into a tree.

---

## Pick the Right Domain on Your Input Node

| Incoming Payload | Choose Domain | Typical Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| JSON (`{"id": 1}`) | **JSON** | REST APIs, mobile/web integrations (`InputRoot.JSON.Data`) |
| XML (`<Order>...</Order>`) | **XMLNSC** | Compact, fast XML parsing for SOAP or enterprise XML (`InputRoot.XMLNSC`) |
| CSV, TXT, COBOL Copybook | **DFDL** | Structured non-XML text or binary records modeled with a DFDL schema |
| PDF, ZIP, Image, Raw Bytes | **BLOB** | Pass-through routing where you don't need to read fields inside |
| Multipart Email / Attachments | **MIME** | Email or HTTP multipart payloads |
| SOAP Web Services (`<soapenv:Envelope>`) | **SOAP** | Standard SOAP 1.1 / 1.2 services |

---

## Where You Set It

1. Select your Input node (`MQInput`, `HTTPInput`, or `FileInput`).
2. Open **Properties -> Input Message Parsing**.
3. Set **Message domain** from the dropdown.

```esql
-- Because Input node domain = JSON:
DECLARE id INTEGER InputRoot.JSON.Data.orderId;

-- Because Input node domain = XMLNSC:
DECLARE id CHARACTER InputRoot.XMLNSC.Order.OrderId;
```

> [!WARNING]
> Setting `XMLNSC` on an `MQInput` node that receives plain JSON causes an immediate **parser exception** (`BIP5025E`). If a single node receives JSON one time and raw text another, use `BLOB` and switch mid-flow with **ResetContentDescriptor**!

---

# Test Your Flow with Flow Exerciser

Before opening external tools like Postman or `amqsput`, use the Toolkit's built-in **Flow Exerciser** to send a test message and inspect what every single node produced.

![Flow Exerciser showing green active wires, blue message envelopes, and the Recorded Message viewer](/images/ace/flow-exerciser-recorded-message.png)

---

## Run Your First Test in 4 Clicks

1. Open your saved `.msgflow` on the canvas.
2. Click the red **Start Flow Exerciser** icon in the canvas toolbar (top-right of the flow editor). *(ACE builds and deploys your app to your selected server automatically.)*
3. Click the **Send Message** icon (envelope with green arrow). Paste your sample JSON/XML or pick a saved file and click **Send**.
4. **Click any blue envelope icon** on a green highlighted wire to see the exact **Recorded Message** at that step!

---

## What Green vs. Blue Tells You

| Visual Cue | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Green highlighted wire** | That path executed during your test |
| **Unlit grey wire** | That branch did not run (for example a Route filter didn't match or no error occurred) |
| **Blue envelope on wire** | Click to inspect `Properties`, `MQMD`, `LocalEnvironment`, and `JSON/XMLNSC` tree right after that node |

> [!TIP]
> Remember to click the red **Stop Recording** button when you are done testing — Flow Exerciser puts the deployed flow into recording mode, which adds overhead in production.

---

# Flow Error Handling (TryCatch vs Terminals)

Every production flow needs a plan when bad JSON arrives or a downstream API fails. You can catch errors either for the **whole flow** or around **one risky section**.

![Error handler subflow recording a message in Flow Exerciser](/images/ace/subflow-error-handler-exerciser.png)

---

## 3 Ways to Handle Errors in ACE

| Strategy | How You Wire It | When to Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Let MQ Roll Back (Default)** | Leave `Catch` / `Failure` unwired | Message goes back to input queue (and Backout Queue after retries) |
| **2. Whole-Flow Catch** | Wire `MQInput.Catch` -> `<ErrorSubflowName>` | One standard place to log `ExceptionList` and send an HTTP 500 or MQ error message |
| **3. Local Section (`TryCatch` node)** | Wire `TryCatch.Try` -> Risky nodes, `TryCatch.Catch` -> Fallback | An optional enrichment API call failed, but the flow should continue with default values |

---

## Reading What Went Wrong in ESQL

When a message enters a **Catch** path, ACE puts the error details in `InputExceptionList`. Always wrap it or call your error subflow to extract the BIP number and message text.

> [!WARNING]
> Once you wire a `Catch` or `Failure` terminal and end that path normally (e.g., at an `MQOutput` to an error queue), ACE considers the transaction **succeeded** and removes the original message from the input queue!

---

markdownContent:
# FlowOrder: Control Which Path Runs First

If you draw **two wires directly** out of one `Out` terminal, ACE decides on its own which wire runs first. Drop in a **FlowOrder** node whenever execution order matters.

---

## How FlowOrder Works

```text
                ┌───(First)───▶ [Audit DB / Log]   (Finishes 100% first)
  [Input] ──▶ [FlowOrder]
                └───(Second)──▶ [Call Partner API] (Runs only if First succeeded)
```

- **First terminal:** Always executes completely from start to finish first.
- **Second terminal:** Runs only **after** the entire `First` branch finishes without an uncaught error.

---

## When to Use vs. Skip It

| Scenario | Use `FlowOrder`? | Reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Write to audit queue, **then** update DB, **then** reply HTTP | **Yes** | Guarantees audit happens before reply (and stops if audit fails) |
| Draw two wires directly from `Compute.Out` | **No** *(if order matters)* | Direct multi-wire order is not guaranteed by design |

> [!TIP]
> Notice that both branches receive the **exact same input message** that arrived at `FlowOrder.In`, unless you mutate `Environment` in Branch 1 — `Environment` changes stay visible in Branch 2!

---

markdownContent:
# 5 Flow Patterns & HTTP vs MQ vs File

Almost every production ACE integration is a variation of one of these **5 simple patterns**.

---

## The 5 Core Patterns

| Pattern | Typical Nodes | Use When... |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Pass-Through / Transform** | `MQInput -> Mapping/Compute -> MQOutput` | Convert XML to JSON or enrich fields between queues |
| **2. Sync REST API** | `HTTPInput -> Mapping/Compute -> HTTPReply` | Mobile/web app needs an immediate JSON response |
| **3. API Gateway / Orchestration** | `HTTPInput -> HTTPRequest -> Mapping -> HTTPReply` | Wrap a legacy backend or combine two REST calls into one |
| **4. Content-Based Router** | `MQInput -> Route -> Out1/Out2 -> MQOutput` | Send high-value orders to VIP queue and normal orders to standard queue |
| **5. Batch File Splitter** | `FileInput -> Compute -> MQOutput` | Drop a CSV/XML batch file in a folder and send 1 queue message per record |

---

## HTTP vs. IBM MQ vs. File: Quick Decision

| Question | Choose **HTTP** | Choose **IBM MQ** | Choose **File** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Caller waits right now for reply? | **Yes** (seconds) | Usually async (fire & forget) | No (batch) |
| Zero message loss if target is down? | Needs caller retry | **Yes** (persistent queues + rollback) | Stored on disk |
| Huge nightly batch dump? | No | Only record-by-record | **Yes** |

> [!TIP]
> Start small: pick **Pattern 1** (`MQInput -> Compute -> MQOutput`) or **Pattern 2** (`HTTPInput -> Mapping -> HTTPReply`) when testing ACE for the first time.

---

# Mapping vs Compute vs JavaCompute: Which Node?

New ACE developers often ask: *"There are three nodes that transform messages — which one should I drag onto my flow?"* Use this simple rule of thumb.

![Decision diagram comparing Mapping, Compute, and JavaCompute nodes](/images/ace/diagram-transform-nodes.svg)

---

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Node | Skill Needed | Best When... | Avoid When... |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mapping** | Visual drag & drop (no code) | You have schemas (XSD, JSON Schema, Swagger, DFDL) and want fast field-to-field mapping + DB enrichment | Incoming JSON has unpredictable dynamic keys |
| **Compute** | ESQL (SQL-like syntax) | You want fast procedural logic, dynamic JSON/XML trees, custom headers (`MQMD`, `HTTP`), or `PROPAGATE` loops | Team prefers pure no-code visual diagrams |
| **JavaCompute** | Java + Maven/JARs | You need Java cryptography, Apache POI/PDF libs, complex regex, or existing Java utilities | Simple XML/JSON copy (slow & verbose compared to ESQL) |

---

## 3-Second Checklist

1. **Have both schemas & want visual docs?** Use **[Mapping Node](#topic-150)**.
2. **Working with schemaless JSON, MQ headers, or fast loops?** Use **[Compute Node](#topic-151)**.
3. **Need an external Java library or AES/RSA crypto?** Use **[JavaCompute Node](#topic-152)**.

> [!TIP]
> Performance tip: `Mapping` maps compile down efficiently at deploy time, and `Compute` (ESQL) runs natively inside ACE with minimal memory overhead. Only drop into `JavaCompute` when you genuinely need Java APIs.

---

# Mapping Node (.map): Drag-and-Drop Mapping

The **Mapping** node transforms messages visually using a **Graphical Data Map (`.map`)** file — drag a wire from an input field to an output field and let ACE generate the runtime transform for you.

![New Message Map wizard Step 1 creating `<MapName>`.map](/images/ace/mapping-wizard-step1.png)

---

## When to Use the Mapping Node

- **Use it** when transforming structured XML (XSD), JSON (JSON Schema / Swagger 2.0 / OpenAPI), or CSV/binary (DFDL) visually.
- **Use it** when business analysts need to review field mappings in pictures instead of code.
- **Skip it** when your payload is completely schemaless JSON with changing keys — use **Compute** instead.

---

## Create a Map in 4 Steps

1. Drag a **Mapping** node onto your flow canvas and double-click it to launch the **New Message Map** wizard.
2. Give the map a clear name (`<MapName>`) and click **Next**.
3. Pick your **Map inputs** (source schema) and **Map outputs** (target schema), then click **Finish**.

![Select map inputs and outputs dialog in the Mapping wizard](/images/ace/mapping-wizard-io-schemas.png)

4. Drag wires between source fields on the left and target fields on the right, choosing transforms like **Move**, **Assign**, **Concat**, **If**, or **For each**:

![Graphical Data Mapping Editor canvas showing Move, Assign, and For each transforms](/images/ace/mapping-editor-canvas.png)

---

## Mapping JSON Fields Too

You don't always need an XSD file — in ACE 12, the **JSON** editor lets you model JSON Schema objects visually or use `Add User-Defined` elements inside `.map`:

![Mapping JSON schema tree inside the Graphical Data Mapping editor](/images/ace/mapping-json-tree.png)

---

## Common Built-in Transforms

| Transform | What It Does | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Move** | Copies value directly | `input.orderId -> output.id` |
| **Assign** | Sets a constant hardcoded value | `output.source = 'ACE'` |
| **Concat** | Joins two+ strings with a separator | `firstName + ' ' + lastName` |
| **If / Else** | Conditional mapping via XPath 2.0 | `$amount > 1000 -> 'VIP'` |
| **For each** | Loops over an array to build output array | `items[*] -> lineItems[*]` |
| **Select / DB Routine** | Queries or calls a database mid-map | Lookup customer tier by ID |

> [!TIP]
> Watch the **Properties -> Transform** panel on the right inside the Map Editor: every green line shows the exact XPath 2.0 condition or custom expression running on that field.

---

# Compute Node: Transform Messages with ESQL

The **Compute** node lets you transform, build, or filter messages using **ESQL** — IBM's fast, SQL-style language built directly into ACE.

![Compute node Properties panel showing Data source, ESQL module, and Compute mode](/images/ace/compute-node-properties.png)

---

## When to Use Compute

- **Fastest coded option** for working with `JSON`, `XMLNSC`, `MQMD`, or `HTTPInputHeader`.
- Ideal when you need loops, conditional branches, database `PASSTHRU` queries, or **`PROPAGATE`** to emit multiple messages from one input.

---

## Key Properties to Know

| Property | Default | What You Set |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ESQL module** | Auto-generated | Links this node to a `CREATE COMPUTE MODULE ...` block in your `.esql` file |
| **Compute mode** | `Message` | Controls whether `LocalEnvironment` and `Exception` trees are copied or freshly rebuilt (`Message`, `LocalEnvironment`, `LocalEnvironment And Message`, etc.) |
| **Data source** | *(empty)* | [ODBC DSN name](#topic-250) if this Compute node queries SQL Server or another DB |

---

## Fast Mini-Example (JSON Enrichment)

Double-click the **Compute** node to open its `.esql` file and edit `Main()`:

```esql
CREATE COMPUTE MODULE <ComputeModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        CALL CopyMessageHeaders();
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.orderId = InputRoot.JSON.Data.id;
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.status  = 'RECEIVED';
        RETURN TRUE;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output</summary>

```json
{
  "orderId": 42,
  "status": "RECEIVED"
}
```

</details>

> [!WARNING]
> Look closely at **Compute mode**: if you change `OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.MQ.DestinationData[1].queueName` in your code, you **must** set Compute mode to **`LocalEnvironment`** or **`LocalEnvironment And Message`** — otherwise ACE ignores your change!

---

# JavaCompute Node: Use Java Libraries & Custom Logic

The **JavaCompute** node runs a Java class (`MbJavaComputeNode`) whenever a message arrives on its `In` terminal.

![New Java Compute Node Class wizard showing package, class name, and superclass](/images/ace/javacompute-new-class-wizard.png)

---

## When to Use JavaCompute

- You need third-party **Java JARs** (Excel/PDF generators, custom JWT/HMAC encryption, Apache Commons).
- You are integrating with existing Java business objects your team already maintains.
- For ordinary JSON/XML field transformations, prefer **[Mapping](#topic-150)** or **[Compute](#topic-151)** — they require less boilerplate.

---

## Generated Java Skeleton

Double-click the node to generate a class extending `MbJavaComputeNode` with an `evaluate()` method:

![JavaCompute node editor showing evaluate(MbMessageAssembly) code](/images/ace/javacompute-code-editor.png)

```java
public void evaluate(MbMessageAssembly inAssembly) throws MbException {
    MbOutputTerminal out = getOutputTerminal("out");
    MbMessage outMsg = new MbMessage(inAssembly.getMessage());
    MbMessageAssembly outAssembly = new MbMessageAssembly(inAssembly, outMsg);
    out.propagate(outAssembly);
}
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>What Happens at Runtime</summary>

```text
Copies the incoming MbMessage into outMsg and propagates outAssembly to the 'out' terminal.
```

</details>

> [!TIP]
> Always wrap temporary `MbElement` / `MbMessage` allocations cleanly or use try/finally `clearMessage()` if you build extra messages inside loops so JVM heap stays flat.

---

markdownContent:
# ResetContentDescriptor: Switch Parser Without Rewriting

Sometimes a flow starts with **BLOB** (raw bytes) so it can inspect a header or check routing rules first, and *later* needs to parse those bytes as **JSON** or **XMLNSC**. Drop in **ResetContentDescriptor** to switch parsers cleanly.

![ResetContentDescriptor Basic properties showing Message domain and Reset check box](/images/ace/reset-content-descriptor-properties.png)

---

## When to Use It

- **One input queue receives multiple formats:** Start `MQInput` as `BLOB`, inspect the first characters or an MQRFH2 header, route JSON messages through `ResetContentDescriptor (JSON)` and XML messages through `ResetContentDescriptor (XMLNSC)`.
- **Save CPU on pass-through audit:** Keep payload as `BLOB` until after logging/archiving, then parse only on the branch that needs fields.

---

## Key Setting: Check `Reset message domain`!

1. Select **ResetContentDescriptor** -> **Properties -> Basic**.
2. Choose your target **Message domain** (e.g., `JSON` or `XMLNSC`).
3. **Check the `Reset message domain` checkbox** — if left unchecked, ACE ignores the dropdown!

> [!TIP]
> `ResetContentDescriptor` does not copy or alter any payload bytes — it simply tells ACE's parser how to interpret the bitstream for all downstream nodes.

---

# MQ Nodes Overview (Input, Output, Get, Reply)

ACE gives you **4 main IBM MQ nodes**. Beginners often mix up `MQInput` vs. `MQGet`, or `MQOutput` vs. `MQReply`. Look at where each node sits in a flow:

![Diagram comparing MQInput (start), MQGet (middle), MQOutput (send to fixed queue), and MQReply (send to ReplyToQ)](/images/ace/diagram-mq-nodes.svg)

---

## Pick the Right MQ Node in 5 Seconds

| Node | Position in Flow | What Queue Does It Use? | Simple Mental Model |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`MQInput`** | **Start** (Trigger) | Fixed queue you configure | *"Wake up whenever a message arrives on `<InputQueueName>`"* |
| **`MQGet`** | **Middle** | Queue you configure (or CorrelId lookup) | *"Pause this flow right now, go fetch one message from `<LookupQueueName>`, and come back"* |
| **`MQOutput`** | **End / Anywhere** | Fixed queue (or `LocalEnvironment` override) | *"Put this message into `<OutputQueueName>`"* |
| **`MQReply`** | **End** | Automatically reads `MQMD.ReplyToQ` & `ReplyToQMgr` | *"Return an answer to whoever sent the request"* |

---

> [!TIP]
> If your flow is triggered by `HTTPInput` and needs to pull an item from MQ in the middle, **you cannot use `MQInput` in the middle** (it has no `In` terminal!) — always use **`MQGet`** instead.

---

# MQInput Node: Start a Flow from a Queue

**`MQInput`** sits at the beginning of a flow and waits for messages on a specified IBM MQ queue.

![Flow Exerciser testing an MQ flow with MQInput and MQOutput connected](/images/ace/mq-flow-exerciser-test.png)

---

## Essential Properties

| Tab | Property | Recommended Setting | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic** | **Queue name \*** | `<InputQueueName>` | Must already exist in MQ (`DEFINE QLOCAL`) |
| **MQ Connection** | **Connection** / **Policy** | Default *(Node QMGR)* or `MQEndpoint` policy | Tells ACE which Queue Manager hosts `<InputQueueName>` |
| **Input Message Parsing** | **Message domain** | `JSON` / `XMLNSC` / `BLOB` | Sets parser for incoming body bytes |
| **Advanced** | **Transaction mode** | `Automatic` *(default)* | Rolls back message to queue if flow throws an unhandled error |

---

## Quick Test Example

1. Put `{"orderId": 101}` onto `<InputQueueName>` (via **Flow Exerciser**, **MQ Explorer**, or `amqsput <InputQueueName> <QueueManagerName>`).
2. `MQInput` picks it up immediately, parses `InputRoot.JSON.Data.orderId`, and passes it out of the `Out` terminal.

> [!WARNING]
> If `MQInput` reports `MQRC 2085 (MQRC_UNKNOWN_OBJECT_NAME)`, the queue name in **Basic -> Queue name** doesn't match any queue defined on that Queue Manager (queue names are case-sensitive on MQ!).

---

# MQOutput Node: Put a Message on a Queue

**`MQOutput`** serializes your message tree and delivers it to an IBM MQ queue.

---

## Essential Properties

| Tab | Property | Common Setting | What It Does |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic** | **Queue name** | `<OutputQueueName>` | Target queue name |
| **Basic** | **Queue manager name** | Empty *(local)* or remote QMGR | Optional remote QMGR name |
| **Request** | **New message ID** / **Reply-to queue** | Optional | Stamps `MQMD.ReplyToQ` when sending a request expecting a reply |
| **Advanced** | **Destination mode** | `Queue Name` *(fixed)* or `Destination List` *(dynamic)* | Pick `Destination List` when ESQL chooses the target queue dynamically |

---

## Dynamic Queue Routing in ESQL

Set **Destination mode** to **Destination List** on `MQOutput`, then set the target queue inside a **Compute** node (with `Compute mode = LocalEnvironment And Message`):

```esql
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.MQ.DestinationData[1].queueName = '<TargetQueueName>';
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Result in IBM MQ Explorer</summary>

```text
Message lands on <TargetQueueName> instead of the static queue name typed on MQOutput.
```

</details>

> [!TIP]
> Wire `MQOutput.Out` to an audit or reply step if your flow isn't finished yet! Note that `MQOutput` is **not** forced to be the last node in a flow.

---

markdownContent:
# MQGet Node: Read a Queue Mid-Flow

**`MQGet`** acts like a synchronous *"read from MQ right now"* step inside an already-running flow (such as an HTTP flow that needs to collect a backend MQ reply).

---

## Why `MQGet` Exists

`MQInput` can **only** sit at the start of a flow. Whenever a message flow is already running (from `HTTPInput` or another `MQInput`) and needs to read a queue in the middle, use **`MQGet`**.

---

## Important Terminals on `MQGet`

| Terminal | Fires When... | What To Wire |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Out** | A matching message was found and read | Continue processing with the retrieved payload |
| **No Message** | Queue was empty (or Correlation ID wait timed out) | Return "Not ready / 202 Accepted" instead of treating it as a crash |
| **Warning** | Message truncated (buffer too small) | Increase buffer or inspect warning |
| **Failure** | Queue doesn't exist / MQ connection down | Error handler |

---

## Tip: Match Request to Reply by `CorrelId`

In **Properties -> Request**, check **Get by correlation ID**. ACE then only pulls the message whose `MQMD.CorrelId` matches your current message's `MsgId` or `CorrelId`, leaving everyone else's messages safely on the queue!

> [!WARNING]
> Keep **Wait interval (ms)** short (e.g., `5000` ms) if calling `MQGet` inside an `HTTPInput -> HTTPReply` flow so HTTP clients don't time out waiting on an empty queue.

---

markdownContent:
# MQReply Node: Reply to ReplyToQ Automatically

**`MQReply`** is a specialized `MQOutput` node that requires **no hardcoded queue name** — it automatically reads `ReplyToQ` and `ReplyToQMgr` straight from the incoming `MQMD` header.

---

## When to Use `MQReply` vs. `MQOutput`

| Situation | Use `MQReply`? | Reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Caller set `MQMD.ReplyToQ = '<ReplyToQueueName>'` and expects dynamic reply | **Yes** | Automatically routes back to whoever called you |
| Flow always pushes to one fixed queue `<OutputQueueName>` | **No** (use `MQOutput`) | Request messages might not have `ReplyToQ` populated |

---

## How Request-Reply Correlation Works

1. Caller sends request on `<RequestQueueName>` with `MQMD.MsgId = 0x1234` and `MQMD.ReplyToQ = '<ReplyToQueueName>'`.
2. Your flow processes the request and reaches **`MQReply`**.
3. Check **`MQMD.CorrelId = MsgId`** (automatic when your `Compute` node copies `MQMD` headers or uses default `MQReply` behavior) so the waiting caller picks up **its exact reply**.

> [!WARNING]
> If the incoming message has an **empty `ReplyToQ`**, `MQReply` throws an error (`BIP2677E`). Make sure calling systems set `ReplyToQ` or validate it first!

---

# HTTPInput & HTTPReply: Expose a REST Endpoint

Pair **`HTTPInput`** and **`HTTPReply`** whenever an external app needs to call your ACE flow over `http://` or `https://` and receive an immediate response.

![Palette HTTP drawer showing HTTPInput, HTTPReply, HTTPRequest, and HTTPHeader nodes](/images/ace/palette-http-drawer.png)

---

## Always Use Them as a Pair

```text
  [HTTPInput]  ──▶  [Mapping / Compute]  ──▶  [HTTPReply]
  (GET /POST)         (Build JSON reply)     (Sends HTTP 200)
```

If an HTTP request enters `HTTPInput` and finishes **without hitting an `HTTPReply`**, the caller hangs until the HTTP timeout expires!

---

## Key `HTTPInput` Properties

![HTTPInput Basic properties showing Path suffix for URL](/images/ace/httpinput-node-properties.png)

| Tab | Property | Example Value | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic** | **Path suffix for URL \*** | `/orders/*` or `/v1/hello` | URL path appended after server host & port (default embedded port `7800`) |
| **Input Message Parsing** | **Message domain** | `JSON` or `BLOB` | Parses incoming `POST` body (GET requests typically have empty body — `JSON` handles GET fine too) |
| **Advanced** | **Use HTTPS** | Unchecked (dev) / Checked (prod) | Toggles TLS listener |

---

## Fast Example: Return HTTP 201 JSON in Compute

```esql
SET OutputRoot.HTTPResponseHeader."Content-Type" = 'application/json';
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.ReplyStatusCode = 201;
SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.message = 'Order created';
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>curl Response from http://localhost:7800/v1/hello</summary>

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"message":"Order created"}
```

</details>

> [!TIP]
> Wire `HTTPInput.Catch` (or a `TryCatch`) to build a JSON error + `ReplyStatusCode = 500` and send it to a second `HTTPReply` node so callers never get ugly stack traces or timeouts!

---

markdownContent:
# HTTPRequest Node: Call an External REST API

**`HTTPRequest`** pauses your flow mid-flight, sends an outbound `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, or `DELETE` request to an external API, and puts the API's response into `InputRoot` (for downstream nodes).

---

## Essential Properties

| Tab | Property | Example | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic** | **Web service URL \*** | `https://<ApiHostName>/<EndpointPath>` | Default endpoint URL |
| **HTTP Settings** | **HTTP method** | `GET` / `POST` | Defaults to `POST` if you forget to switch it for a `GET`! |
| **Response Message Parsing** | **Message domain** | `JSON` | Tells ACE how to parse the API's response body |
| **Request** | **Request timeout (sec)** | `30` (default `120`) | How long ACE waits before failing |

---

## Watch the `Error` Terminal (4xx / 5xx)!

- **`Out` terminal:** API returned HTTP `2xx` (e.g., `200 OK`, `201 Created`).
- **`Error` terminal:** API returned HTTP `4xx` or `5xx` (e.g., `404 Not Found`, `503 Service Unavailable`).
- **`Failure` terminal:** Network error (DNS fail, connection refused, TLS certificate error).

---

## Dynamic URL Override in ESQL

Set the target URL dynamically per request (needs `Compute mode = LocalEnvironment And Message` before `HTTPRequest`):

```esql
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.RequestURL = 'https://<ApiHostName>/<ResourcePath>/' || orderId;
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.RequestLine.Method = 'GET';
```

> [!TIP]
> **Careful with `HTTPRequest` overwriting your message:** By default, `HTTPRequest` replaces your flow's payload with the API response. If you still need your *original* order data afterward, save needed fields in **`Environment.Variables`** first, or configure **Result -> Result data location**!

# FileInput Node: Pick Up Files Automatically

**`FileInput`** watches a local or mounted directory and starts your flow whenever a new file matching your pattern drops into the folder.

---

## Essential Properties

| Tab | Property | Example | Why It Matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic** | **Input directory \*** | `<InputDirectory>` | Folder ACE scans for incoming files |
| **Basic** | **File name or pattern** | `*.csv` or `orders_*.xml` | Picks which files to read |
| **Basic** | **Action on successful processing** | `Move to Archive Subdirectory` | Prevents re-reading the same file forever! |
| **Records and Elements** | **Record detection** | `Whole File` / `Delimited (Line)` / `Parsed Record` | Lets you split a 10,000-line CSV into 10,000 tiny flow runs |

---

## What Happens to Each Processed File

By default, ACE manages subdirectories automatically inside your **Input directory**:

- `mqsitransitin/` — file currently being read (locked while running)
- `mqsiarchive/` — finished files moved here safely (with optional timestamp)
- `mqsibackout/` — files that threw an unhandled error and couldn't finish

> [!WARNING]
> Always set **Action on successful processing** to **Move to Archive** or **Delete** — and avoid pointing two separate servers at the same `Input directory` unless you configure **File -> Locking / FTP** carefully.

# FileOutput & FileRead: Write or Read Files

Just like `MQOutput` and `MQGet` for queues, ACE gives you **`FileOutput`** to write files out and **`FileRead`** to read a lookup file mid-flow.

![FileOutput Basic properties showing Directory and File name or pattern](/images/ace/fileoutput-node-properties.png)

---

## `FileOutput` Basics

| Property | Example | Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Directory \*** | `<OutputDirectory>` | Folder where output file is created |
| **File name or pattern \*** | `report_%u.json` | Output filename (`%u` adds a unique ID if desired) |
| **Mode for writing to file** | `Write directly` or `Stage in mqsitransit and move on Finish File` | Use staging when appending multiple records into one file! |

---

## Important Rule: Staging + `Finish File`

If a `FileInput` splits 500 records and sends all 500 to **`FileOutput`**:
1. Each record enters `FileOutput.In` and appends to a staged file in `mqsitransit/`.
2. Wire **`FileInput.End of Data`** -> **`FileOutput.Finish File`** so ACE finalizes and moves the completed file into `<OutputDirectory>`!

---

## When to Use `FileRead`

Need to read a static JSON config file or customer file **in the middle of an HTTP or MQ flow**? Use **`FileRead`**:
- Wire `In` -> Read configured path -> payload lands at `Out`.
- Wire `No Match` if the requested file might not exist.

> [!TIP]
> You can override the output directory or filename per message using `OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.File.Directory` and `OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.File.Name`.

markdownContent:
# Route vs Filter: Split Messages by Content

Both **`Route`** and **`Filter`** inspect a field inside your message and send it down a matching branch — without modifying the message itself.

![Flow canvas showing a Route node splitting messages into multiple dynamic output terminals](/images/ace/route-node-flow-canvas.png)

---

## Which One Should You Pick?

| Feature | **Route Node** *(Recommended)* | **Filter Node** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **How you write conditions** | Visual XPath 1.0 (no ESQL needed!) | Requires an ESQL module |
| **How many output branches?** | **Unlimited** custom named terminals (`VIP`, `EU`, `Default`) | Fixed 3 outputs: `True`, `False`, `Unknown` |
| **Distribution mode** | `First` (stop at 1st match) or `All` (send to all matching) | Single True/False match |

---

## Setting Up a `Route` Node in 3 Clicks

1. Drag **Route** (Routing drawer) onto your canvas.
2. In **Properties -> Filter table**, click **Add** to create a named rule & output terminal (e.g., terminal `HighValue`).

![Route node Properties showing Distribution mode and Filter table](/images/ace/route-node-properties.png)

3. Use **Edit...** to open the **XPath Expression Builder** and point-and-click at your XML/JSON field:

![XPath Expression Builder dialog for building visual Route conditions](/images/ace/xpath-expression-builder.png)

> [!TIP]
> Remember to always wire the **`Default`** terminal on `Route` (even if only to a `Trace` or error queue) so messages that fail to match any rule never get silently dropped!

---

markdownContent:
# RouteToLabel & Label: Dynamic Branching

When you have **10+ possible message types** (for example SOAP operations or country handlers), wiring 10 spaghetti lines out of one node gets messy. **`RouteToLabel`** jumps by name directly to matching **`Label`** nodes — with **no wires required** between `RouteToLabel` and `Label`.

---

## How It Works

```text
  [MQInput] ──▶ [Compute (sets labelName = 'CREATE')] ──▶ [RouteToLabel]

  [Label: 'CREATE'] ──▶ [<Subflow1Name>] ──▶ [MQOutput]
  [Label: 'CANCEL'] ──▶ [<Subflow2Name>] ──▶ [MQOutput]
```

---

## Step 1: Set the Target Label Name in ESQL

Inside the `Compute` node before `RouteToLabel` (`Compute mode = LocalEnvironment And Message`):

```esql
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.RouterList.DestinationData[1].labelName = InputRoot.JSON.Data.action;
```

## Step 2: Drop Matching `Label` Nodes

- Place **Label** nodes on the same flow canvas and set **Properties -> Basic -> Label name** to exact values like `CREATE` or `CANCEL`.
- `RouteToLabel` jumps straight to whichever `Label` matches `labelName`!

> [!WARNING]
> If `labelName` has no matching `Label` node on the canvas, `RouteToLabel` throws `BIP2670E`. Either validate allowed actions first or handle it on `Failure`.

# TryCatch, Throw & Trace: Handle Errors & Debug

These three nodes (in the **Construction** and **Error Handling** drawers) give you fine-grained error control and easy visibility into message contents.

![Construction palette drawer showing Trace, TryCatch, Throw, and FlowOrder nodes](/images/ace/construction-palette-trace.png)

---

## Quick Role Summary

| Node | Purpose | Key Setting |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`TryCatch`** | Wrap a risky chain (`Try` terminal) and handle errors (`Catch` terminal) | Wire `Try` -> Risky call, `Catch` -> Fallback |
| **`Throw`** | Deliberately raise a custom exception to trigger rollback or `Catch` | Set **Message number** (e.g., `3001`) & **Message text** |
| **`Trace`** | Print message trees or custom debug text to a file or user log | Set **Destination** (`File`) & **Pattern** |

---

## Print Your Whole Message with `Trace`

![Trace node Basic properties showing Destination, File path, and Pattern](/images/ace/trace-node-properties.png)

In **Properties -> Basic**, set:
- **Destination:** `File`
- **File path:** `<TraceFilePath>`
- **Pattern:**

```text
Time: ${CURRENT_TIMESTAMP}
Payload: ${Root.JSON.Data}
Exception: ${ExceptionList}
```

> [!TIP]
> Put a `Trace` node on your **`Catch`** branch during development so you immediately see the exact `ExceptionList` and payload that broke! Turn off or remove verbose file traces in high-traffic production flows.

shortDescription: Call 2 or more backend services in parallel and combine their replies into one message with Aggregation nodes.
markdownContent:
# AggregateControl, Request & Reply: Fan-Out / Fan-In

Suppose one customer order needs price data from **Inventory** AND risk data from **Fraud** — running them in **parallel** cuts total wait time in half. ACE does this across two tiny flows using the **3 Aggregation nodes**.

---

## How Fan-Out / Fan-In Works

### Flow 1 (Fan-Out):
```text
                        ┌──▶ [Compute A] ──▶ [MQOutput (INV.Q)] ──▶ [AggregateRequest ('INV')]
  [Input] ──▶ [AggregateControl ('<AggregateName>', Timeout=10s)]
                        └──▶ [Compute B] ──▶ [MQOutput (FRD.Q)] ──▶ [AggregateRequest ('FRD')]
```

### Flow 2 (Fan-In):
```text
  [MQInput (<ReplyQueueName>)] ──▶ [AggregateReply ('<AggregateName>')] ──▶ [Compute (Combine Results)] ──▶ [Output]
```

---

## Rules to Remember

1. **Matching `Aggregate name`:** `AggregateControl`, both `AggregateRequest` nodes, and `AggregateReply` must share the exact same **Aggregate name** (`<AggregateName>`).
2. **Place `AggregateRequest` *after* `MQOutput` / `HTTPRequest`:** It records each outbound folder name (`INV`, `FRD`) after sending.
3. **Wire `AggregateReply.Timeout`:** Always wire the `Timeout` (or `Unknown`) terminal so partial replies are still handled cleanly if one backend stalls!

> [!NOTE]
> Aggregation nodes store in-flight correlation state inside IBM MQ system queues (`SYSTEM.BROKER.AGGR.*`), so an associated IBM MQ Queue Manager is required when using them.

---

markdownContent:
# What Is IBM MQ vs ACE?

**IBM MQ** and **IBM App Connect Enterprise (ACE)** are two separate products designed to work together like a **post office** and a **processing office**.

![IBM MQ Explorer showing local queues `<InputQueueName>` and `<OutputQueueName>` inside `<QueueManagerName>` with current queue depth](/images/ace/mq-explorer-queues-depth.png)

---

## Simple Analogy

| Product | Analogy | Actual Job | Never Does |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **IBM MQ** | Secure Mailbox / Post Office | Stores messages safely on disk in queues; guarantees **"once-and-only-once"** delivery even if servers reboot | Does **not** transform JSON to XML or call REST APIs |
| **IBM ACE** | Sorting & Processing Worker | Reads messages from queues/HTTP/files, transforms schemas, queries DBs, routes, and delivers results | Does **not** act as a long-term durable message broker itself |

---

## Can You Run ACE Without IBM MQ?

**Yes!** If your ACE flows only handle `HTTPInput -> Mapping -> HTTPReply` or `FileInput -> FileOutput`, IBM MQ does not even need to be installed.

However, as soon as you use **`MQInput`**, **`MQOutput`**, **`MQGet`**, **`MQReply`**, or **Aggregation/Collector** nodes, ACE must connect to an **IBM MQ Queue Manager** (like `<QueueManagerName>`).

---

markdownContent:
# Link an Integration Node to a Queue Manager (-q)

When you create an ACE Integration Node, you can link it to one local IBM MQ Queue Manager with **`-q`**. Then every MQ node without a policy automatically uses that Queue Manager!

---

## Syntax

```bash
mqsicreatebroker <NodeName> -q <QueueManagerName>
```

---

## Fast Example

First ensure `<QueueManagerName>` exists in IBM MQ, then create node `<IntegrationNodeName>` linked to `<QueueManagerName>`:

```bash
mqsicreatebroker <IntegrationNodeName> -q <QueueManagerName>
mqsistart <IntegrationNodeName>
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output</summary>

```text
BIP8071I: Successful command completion.
BIP8096I: Successful command initiation, check the system log to ensure that the component started without problem...
```

</details>

---

## What Happens When You Start `<IntegrationNodeName>`

1. ACE checks that `<QueueManagerName>` is running on the same PC (local bindings).
2. If `<QueueManagerName>` is **stopped**, `mqsistart <IntegrationNodeName>` **auto-starts `<QueueManagerName>`** or fails if `<QueueManagerName>` does not exist (`BIP8018E`).
3. You can verify the link anytime with `mqsilist` — look for `with queue manager '<QueueManagerName>'`.

> [!WARNING]
> **Using an Independent Integration Server?** An Independent Server has **no Integration Node**, so `-q` does not apply — instead use an **`MQEndpoint` policy** or set **`defaultQueueManager`** in `server.conf.yaml`!

---

# Method 1: Connect MQ Nodes by Queue Manager Name

The fastest way to wire an `MQInput` or `MQOutput` node on your local dev machine is directly in its **MQ Connection** tab.

---

## Two Local Options on the Node

1. Click `MQInput` or `MQOutput` -> **Properties -> MQ Connection**.
2. Set **Connection** dropdown to **Local queue manager**:
   - **Leave Queue manager name empty:** Uses the Integration Node's default linked QMGR (`-q <QueueManagerName>`) or `server.conf.yaml`'s `defaultQueueManager`.
   - **Or type `<QueueManagerName>` explicitly:** Connects locally in bindings mode to `<QueueManagerName>` on the same server.

---

## Remote Direct Option (Client Properties)

You can also pick **MQ client connection properties** directly on the node and type:
- **Queue manager host name:** e.g. `<HostName>`
- **Listener port number:** e.g. `1414`
- **Channel name:** e.g. `<ChannelName>`

> [!WARNING]
> Hardcoding host IP, port, and channel directly inside `.msgflow` nodes means **rebuilding the BAR file** for UAT and PROD! For team or multi-environment flows, use **[Method 2: MQEndpoint Policy](#topic-170)** instead.

# Method 2: Connect MQ Nodes by MQEndpoint Policy

An **`MQEndpoint` Policy** stores MQ host, port, queue manager, channel, and security identity in an XML policy file — completely separate from your flow code.

![BAR Editor Manage view configuring or overriding MQ policy settings](/images/ace/bar-editor-manage-mq.png)

---

## Create & Attach an `MQEndpoint` Policy (4 Steps)

1. In Toolkit: **New -> Policy Project** -> name it `<PolicyProjectName>`.
2. Right-click `<PolicyProjectName>` -> **New -> Policy** -> name it `<PolicyName>`.
3. Set **Type = `MQEndpoint`**, **Template = `MQEndpoint`**, and fill in:
   - **Connection:** `CLIENT` (remote) or `LOCAL` (same machine)
   - **Queue manager name:** `<QueueManagerName>`
   - **Queue manager host name:** `<HostName>` *(for `CLIENT`)*
   - **Listener port number:** `1414` *(for `CLIENT`)*
   - **Channel name:** `SYSTEM.DEF.SVRCONN` *(for `CLIENT`)*
4. Back on your **`MQInput` / `MQOutput`** node -> **Properties -> Policy -> Policy**, type:

```text
{<PolicyProjectName>}:<PolicyName>
```

---

## Using the Same Flow in UAT & PROD

Deploy the exact same Application BAR everywhere, and just deploy a different `<PolicyProjectName>` Policy Project per environment (DEV points to `<DevHostName>:<Port>`, PROD points to `<ProdHostName>:<Port>`).

> [!TIP]
> Need a username/password or TLS keystore on that remote MQ channel? Add **`Security identity`** inside the `MQEndpoint` policy and run `mqsisetdbparms <Node> -n mq::<SecurityIdentityName> -u <UserName> -p <Password>`.

---

# Queue Manager Name vs MQEndpoint Policy

Confused whether to type the Queue Manager name directly on the node or set up a Policy Project? Pick using this table.

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Criteria | Direct Queue Manager Name (on Node / `-q`) | **`MQEndpoint` Policy** |

| **Remote MQ server (another IP/container)** | Clunky (hardcoded IP in flow) | **Best** (host/port/channel live in policy) |

markdownContent:
# Local Bindings vs Remote MQ Client Mode

ACE talks to IBM MQ in one of **two transport modes**. Knowing which one you are using solves 90% of connection failures.

---

## How They Differ

| Feature | **Local Bindings Mode (`LOCAL`)** | **Client Mode (`CLIENT`)** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Where MQ runs** | **Same OS machine** as ACE | **Anywhere** (same box or another server/container) |
| **How it connects** | Direct inter-process shared memory (IPC) | Network TCP/IP socket (`host:1414` + `SVRCONN` channel) |
| **Speed** | Fastest | Fast (tiny TCP hop) |
| **Needs MQ Listener & Channel?** | **No** | **Yes** (Listener on port e.g. `1414` + `SVRCONN` channel running) |
| **Needs Local MQ Server Installed?** | Yes (Full MQ server on same PC) | Only client libraries *(already built into ACE!)* |

---

## Common Gotcha on Windows / Docker

If ACE runs inside a **Docker container** and IBM MQ runs in a **separate container** (or on your Windows host), they do **not** share OS memory — you **must** use **`CLIENT`** mode with a hostname, port `1414`, and `SVRCONN` channel!

> [!TIP]
> Notice ACE already bundles IBM MQ client capabilities inside itself, so you **never** have to install a separate MQ Server just to connect remotely in `CLIENT` mode.

---

markdownContent:
# Common MQ Connection Errors (2059, 2058, 2085, 2035)

Whenever ACE cannot talk to IBM MQ, MQ hands back a 4-digit **`MQRC` (Reason Code)**. Here are the 5 you will see 99% of the time — and the exact fix for each.

---

## Quick Fix Lookup Table

| Code | Official Name | Plain-English Cause | Exact Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`2059`** | `MQRC_Q_MGR_NOT_AVAILABLE` | Queue Manager is **stopped**, or wrong host/port in `CLIENT` mode | Start QMGR (`strmqm <QueueManagerName>`) or verify Listener port `1414` is running |
| **`2058`** | `MQRC_Q_MGR_NAME_ERROR` | Typo in Queue Manager name (`<QueueManagerName>` vs `<queueManagerName_lowercase>`) or Node isn't linked | Check exact case via `dspmq`; verify `MQEndpoint` / `-q` spelling |
| **`2085`** | `MQRC_UNKNOWN_OBJECT_NAME` | Queue doesn't exist on that Queue Manager | Run `runmqsc <QueueManagerName>` -> `DISPLAY QLOCAL(*)` and `DEFINE QLOCAL('<InputQueueName>')` |
| **`2035`** | `MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED` | MQ Channel Auth (`CHLAUTH`) or OAM permissions blocked your user | Check `AMQERR01.LOG` for blocked user/rule; update `CHLAUTH` or `CONNAUTH` for dev |
| **`2538`** | `MQRC_HOST_NOT_AVAILABLE` | Firewall blocked port `1414`, wrong IP, or MQ Listener stopped | Start listener in `runmqsc`: `START LISTENER(<ListenerName>)` |

---

## Still Stuck? Check `mqrc` Right in Terminal!

IBM MQ includes a tiny translator command for **any** 4-digit code:

```bash
mqrc 2035
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output</summary>

```text
      2035  0x000007f3  MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED
```

</details>

> [!TIP]
> If you get **`BIP8018E`** during `mqsistart`, it means the Integration Node's linked Queue Manager does not exist or cannot start locally — check `dspmq` first!

# ESQL Introduction: Compute, Filter & Database Nodes

**ESQL** (Extended Structured Query Language) is IBM App Connect Enterprise's built-in language for reading, building, filtering, and transforming the logical message tree that ACE parses from every message. You write ESQL inside **`.esql`** files, and three flow nodes execute it.

---

## The 3 Nodes That Run ESQL

| Node | Module Type | Root Tree Name | Can Change Message? | Return Value Controls |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`Compute`** | `CREATE COMPUTE MODULE` | `InputRoot` (read) & `OutputRoot` (write) | **Yes** (builds a new output message) | `TRUE` sends to `Out`; `FALSE` stops automatic propagation |
| **`Filter`** | `CREATE FILTER MODULE` | `Root` (read-only) | **No** (evaluates condition only) | `TRUE` -> `True` terminal; `FALSE` -> `False`; `UNKNOWN` -> `Unknown` |
| **`Database`** | `CREATE DATABASE MODULE` | `Root` (read-only) | **No** (runs SQL against an ODBC DSN) | `TRUE` forwards message to `Out`; `FALSE` stops flow |

---

## Example 1: `Filter` Node Module (`CREATE FILTER MODULE`)

A `Filter` node routes a message without editing it:

```esql
BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>

CREATE FILTER MODULE <FilterModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        IF Root.JSON.Data.amount > 50000 THEN
            RETURN TRUE;
        ELSE
            RETURN FALSE;
        END IF;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Routing Behavior</summary>

```text
Input {"amount": 75000} -> returns TRUE    -> routed to 'True' terminal
Input {"amount": 1200}  -> returns FALSE   -> routed to 'False' terminal
Input {}                -> returns FALSE   -> (comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN; ELSE runs)
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown (Filter Module)

- **`BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>`**: Declares the logical namespace (matching the folder path inside your ACE Application/Library) that organizes your `.esql` modules and avoids name collisions.
- **`CREATE FILTER MODULE <FilterModuleName>` ... `END MODULE;`**: Defines the module linked to the Filter node's **Filter expression** property.
- **`CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN`**: The mandatory entry-point function ACE calls when a message arrives at the node's `In` terminal.
- **`BEGIN` ... `END;`**: Wraps the statements executed inside `Main()`. Every `BEGIN` requires a matching `END;` with a semicolon.
- **`Root.JSON.Data.amount`**: Inside **`Filter`** and **`Database`** nodes, the incoming message tree is named **`Root`** (NOT `InputRoot`) because these nodes do not build an `OutputRoot`.
- **`IF ... > 50000 THEN ... ELSE ... END IF;`**: Evaluates the numeric comparison. If `amount` is `NULL` (missing), `NULL > 50000` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, which fails `IF` and falls into `ELSE`.
- **`RETURN TRUE;` / `RETURN FALSE;`**: Tells the `Filter` node which output terminal receives the unchanged message (`True`, `False`, or `Unknown` if `Main()` returns `UNKNOWN` directly, e.g., `RETURN Root.JSON.Data.amount > 50000;`).

---

## Example 2: `Database` Node Module (`CREATE DATABASE MODULE`)

A `Database` node executes SQL against a configured ODBC **Data source** (`<DSN_Name>`) without modifying the message payload:

```esql
BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>

CREATE DATABASE MODULE <DatabaseModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        INSERT INTO Database.<DSN_Name>.<TableName> (ORDER_ID, CREATED_AT)
        VALUES (Root.JSON.Data.orderId, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);

        RETURN TRUE;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Runtime Behavior</summary>

```text
Inserts a row into <TableName> using DSN <DSN_Name>, then forwards the original message unchanged to 'Out'.
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown (Database Module)

- **`CREATE DATABASE MODULE <DatabaseModuleName>`**: Links this ESQL block to the Database node's **Statement** property.
- **`INSERT INTO Database.<DSN_Name>.<TableName> (...)`**: ESQL's native SQL `INSERT` syntax targeting an ODBC Data Source configured in the node's **Data source** property (you can also use `PASSTHRU` here).
- **`VALUES (Root.JSON.Data.orderId, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)`**: Pulls `orderId` straight from `Root` (read-only in Database nodes) and passes ACE's built-in `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` value as the second column.
- **`RETURN TRUE;`**: Instructs ACE to pass the original message onward through the `Out` terminal after the SQL executes.

---

## 5 Core ESQL Rules to Know on Day 1

| Rule | Correct ESQL | Common Trap |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Array indexes are 1-based** | `Item[1]` | `Item[0]` throws `BIP2531E` |
| **Text strings use single quotes** | `'PAID'` | `"PAID"` means a field identifier! |
| **Keywords are case-insensitive** | `SET` or `set` | Field names (`orderId` vs `OrderId`) ARE **case-sensitive** |
| **Comments** | `-- single line` or `/* multi-line */` | `//` is NOT valid in ESQL |
| **Statements end with `;`** | `RETURN TRUE;` | Missing `;` causes a syntax error in the Toolkit Problems view |

> [!TIP]
> Most of your integration logic lives in **Compute** nodes (which can transform messages, query databases, and route via `PROPAGATE`). Use **Filter** when you only need a `True`/`False`/`Unknown` branch without altering the message, and **Database** when you only need a pure SQL side effect without building an `OutputRoot`.

---

# ESQL Message Trees: Root, Environment, LocalEnvironment & ExceptionList

When ACE receives a message, it does not hand your ESQL raw bytes — it parses the message into a **logical message assembly** made of **four trees** that travel together from node to node through the flow.

---

## Anatomy of the Four Trees

```text
InputRoot                        -- Read-only message tree
 ├─ Properties                   -- Format, Encoding, CCSID, ContentType
 ├─ MQMD / HTTPInputHeader       -- Transport headers (above the body)
 └─ XMLNSC | JSON | DFDL         -- Parsed body domain
      └─ Data ... your fields    -- (JSON puts fields under .Data)

Environment                      -- Mutable scratchpad (persists flow-wide)
LocalEnvironment                 -- Per-node routing & transport metadata
ExceptionList                    -- Nested chain of error details
```

---

## Comparing the 4 Trees in a `Compute` Node

| Tree | Read-Only Input Name | Writable Output Name | Purpose | Persists Across Nodes? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Message (`Root`)** | `InputRoot` | `OutputRoot` | Transport headers (`Properties`, `MQMD`, `HTTPInputHeader`) plus the body (`XMLNSC`, `JSON`, `DFDL`, `BLOB`) | Replaced by `OutputRoot` at each node |
| **`Environment`** | `Environment` *(same tree)* | `Environment` *(read & write)* | Your own scratch area (for example `Environment.Variables`) shared across all nodes and branches | **Yes** — kept for the entire flow run |
| **`LocalEnvironment`** | `InputLocalEnvironment` | `OutputLocalEnvironment` | Steers ACE nodes (for example `Destination.HTTP.RequestURL`, `Destination.MQ`, or REST parameters) | Passed on only if **Compute mode** includes `LocalEnvironment` |
| **`ExceptionList`** | `InputExceptionList` | `OutputExceptionList` | Chain of `BIP` error numbers, descriptions, and `Insert` details when an exception occurs | Populated on **Catch** and **Failure** paths |

---

## Fast Example: Using All Writable Trees Together

```esql
-- 1. Save a trace value across the whole flow
SET Environment.Variables.orderId = InputRoot.JSON.Data.id;

-- 2. Steer an outgoing HTTP/REST node dynamically
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.RequestURL =
    'https://<ApiHostName>/<ResourcePath>/' || InputRoot.JSON.Data.customerId;
SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.ReplyStatusCode = 200;

-- 3. Build the new output payload in OutputRoot
CALL CopyMessageHeaders();
SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.status = 'ACCEPTED';
SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.id     = Environment.Variables.orderId;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output Payload & Routing</summary>

```json
{
  "status": "ACCEPTED",
  "id": "ORD-101"
}
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown

- **`-- ...`**: Single-line ESQL comment; ignored at runtime.
- **`SET Environment.Variables.orderId = InputRoot.JSON.Data.id;`**: Creates `Variables` and `orderId` inside the single shared **`Environment`** tree and stores the incoming JSON `id` field. Because `Environment` has no separate `Input`/`Output` split, every downstream node (even after `HTTPRequest` overwrites `OutputRoot`, or inside a `Catch` branch) can still read `Environment.Variables.orderId`.
- **`SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.RequestURL = ...;`**: Writes a dynamic target URL into `OutputLocalEnvironment` for a downstream `HTTPRequest` or `RESTRequest` node. Notice **`||`** joins the base URL string literal `'https://<ApiHostName>/<ResourcePath>/'` with `InputRoot.JSON.Data.customerId`.
- **`SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.ReplyStatusCode = 200;`**: Sets the HTTP status code that an `HTTPReply` node will send back to the caller.
- **`CALL CopyMessageHeaders();`**: Copies `Properties` and transport headers (like `MQMD` or `HTTPInputHeader`) from `InputRoot` into `OutputRoot` without copying the old body.
- **`SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.status = 'ACCEPTED';`**: Automatically creates the `JSON` domain and `Data` folder under `OutputRoot` and sets `status` to `'ACCEPTED'`.
- **`SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.id = Environment.Variables.orderId;`**: Reads back the value saved earlier in `Environment` and writes it to the outgoing JSON payload.

---

## What Is `InputBody`?

`InputBody` is a convenient ESQL shortcut that points directly to the **last child of `InputRoot`** (your body domain such as `InputRoot.XMLNSC` or `InputRoot.JSON`), so you can inspect the body without hardcoding the domain name:

```esql
DECLARE rootTag CHARACTER FIELDNAME(InputBody.*[1]);
```

Here `InputBody.*[1]` resolves to the first child inside the message body (for example `Order` in `XMLNSC`, or `Data` in `JSON`), and `FIELDNAME(...)` returns its name as text.

> [!WARNING]
> **`InputRoot`, `InputLocalEnvironment`, and `InputExceptionList` are strictly read-only!** Writing `SET InputRoot.JSON.Data.x = 1;` throws runtime error **`BIP2521E`** (*Cannot alter read-only tree*). Always read from `Input...` and write to `Output...` or `Environment`. Also remember: changes to `OutputLocalEnvironment` are **discarded** unless the Compute node's **Compute mode** includes `LocalEnvironment`!

---

# ESQL Compute Module, `Main()` & Compute Mode

When you double-click a **Compute** node in the ACE Toolkit, ACE generates a `.esql` file containing a **`CREATE COMPUTE MODULE`** block linked to that node's **ESQL module** property.

---

## Standard Shape of a Compute Module

```esql
BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>

CREATE COMPUTE MODULE <ComputeModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        CALL CopyMessageHeaders();
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.greeting = 'Hello from ACE';
        RETURN TRUE; -- send OutputRoot to 'out'
    END;

    CREATE PROCEDURE CopyMessageHeaders() BEGIN
        DECLARE I INTEGER 1;
        DECLARE J INTEGER;
        SET J = CARDINALITY(InputRoot.*[]);
        WHILE I < J DO
            SET OutputRoot.*[I] = InputRoot.*[I];
            SET I = I + 1;
        END WHILE;
    END;

    CREATE PROCEDURE CopyEntireMessage() BEGIN
        SET OutputRoot = InputRoot;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output</summary>

```json
{
  "greeting": "Hello from ACE"
}
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown

- **`BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>`**: Groups modules into a package-like schema matching the folder under your Application or Library. Modules in the default schema omit this line.
- **`CREATE COMPUTE MODULE <ComputeModuleName>` ... `END MODULE;`**: Defines the module body. The name `<ComputeModuleName>` **must match** the Compute node's **ESQL module** property in the Toolkit (`<SchemaName>.<ComputeModuleName>`).
- **`CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN`**: The entry-point function ACE invokes for every incoming message. It must return a `BOOLEAN`.
- **`CALL CopyMessageHeaders();`**: Invokes the helper procedure below to copy `Properties` and transport headers (`MQMD`, `HTTPInputHeader`, etc.) from `InputRoot` into `OutputRoot`, leaving the body empty so you can build a brand-new payload.
- **`SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.greeting = 'Hello from ACE';`**: Creates the `JSON` parser domain and `Data` folder on `OutputRoot` and assigns the string literal `'Hello from ACE'` to `greeting`.
- **`RETURN TRUE;`**: Propagates `OutputRoot` (and `OutputLocalEnvironment` / `OutputExceptionList` depending on **Compute mode**) to the node's `out` terminal. Returning **`RETURN FALSE;`** sends **nothing** automatically — used when you already sent messages manually via `PROPAGATE` or want to drop the message silently.
- **`DECLARE I INTEGER 1;`**: Initializes 1-based loop index `I` to `1` (`InputRoot.*[1]` is always `Properties`).
- **`SET J = CARDINALITY(InputRoot.*[]);`**: Counts all top-level children of `InputRoot` (`Properties`, headers, and the body as the last child).
- **`WHILE I < J DO ... END WHILE;`**: Notice **`<`** (strictly less than `J`, NOT `<=`)! Because the message body is always the **last** top-level child at position `J`, stopping at `J - 1` copies every header and skips the input body.
- **`SET OutputRoot.*[I] = InputRoot.*[I];`**: Copies child `I` (name, type, and subtree) from `InputRoot` into `OutputRoot` using the wildcard `*`.
- **`CopyEntireMessage()`**: Copies the **entire** `InputRoot` tree (`Properties`, headers, **and** body) into `OutputRoot` in one line (`SET OutputRoot = InputRoot;`) — ideal when you only want to add or tweak 1–2 fields without rebuilding the whole body.

---

## Understanding **Compute mode** (Critical Node Property!)

In the Compute node's **Properties -> Basic -> Compute mode**, you choose which output trees the node actually propagates downstream (any tree NOT selected keeps its unchanged `Input...` version, silently throwing away your `Output...` edits!):

| Compute Mode | Message (`OutputRoot`) | `OutputLocalEnvironment` | `OutputExceptionList` | When to Choose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`Message`** *(default)* | Output (`OutputRoot`) | Passed through unchanged | Passed through unchanged | Standard payload transforms that do NOT alter routing/HTTP status |
| **`LocalEnvironment`** | Input unchanged | Output (`OutputLocalEnvironment`) | Passed through unchanged | Dynamic routing only (setting destination URL/queue without touching payload) |
| **`LocalEnvironment And Message`** | Output (`OutputRoot`) | Output (`OutputLocalEnvironment`) | Passed through unchanged | Returning HTTP status codes (`ReplyStatusCode`), dynamic URLs/queues **plus** JSON/XML body |
| **`Exception`** | Input unchanged | Passed through unchanged | Output (`OutputExceptionList`) | Building a custom exception tree |
| **`All`** | Output (`OutputRoot`) | Output (`OutputLocalEnvironment`) | Output (`OutputExceptionList`) | When modifying payload, routing, and exception tree together |

> [!WARNING]
> **Top Beginner Bug:** Writing `SET OutputLocalEnvironment.Destination.HTTP.ReplyStatusCode = 404;` while **Compute mode** is still the default `Message` silently ignores your `404`! Always change **Compute mode** to **`LocalEnvironment And Message`** whenever you edit `OutputLocalEnvironment`.

---

# ESQL Tree Navigation: Paths, Wildcards, Attributes & Namespaces

Every message field in ACE sits at a path starting from **`InputRoot`** (or `Root` in Filter/Database nodes). Mastering index notation, field inspection functions, attributes, and namespaces lets you read any XML, JSON, or DFDL message accurately.

---

## Essential Path Expressions Cheat Table

| Expression | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`InputRoot.XMLNSC.Order.Item[1]`** | **First** `<Item>` element (ESQL indexes start at `1`) |
| **`InputRoot.XMLNSC.Order.Item[<]`** | **Last** `<Item>` element (`[<2]` means second-to-last) |
| **`CARDINALITY(InputRoot.XMLNSC.Order.Item[])`** | **Total count** of `<Item>` elements (`0` if none exist) |
| **`EXISTS(InputRoot.JSON.Data.email[])`** | **`TRUE`** if `email` exists in the tree, **`FALSE`** otherwise |
| **`InputRoot.XMLNSC.Order.(XMLNSC.Attribute)id`** | Value of the XML attribute **`id`** on `<Order id="A1">` |
| **`FIELDNAME(InputBody.*[1])`** | Name of the **root body element** (e.g., `'Order'` or `'Data'`) |
| **`InputRoot.XMLNSC.ns:Order`** | `<Order>` inside an XML namespace (`DECLARE ns NAMESPACE '<NamespaceUri>';`) |

---

## Example: Reading Attributes, Root Name & XML Namespaces

Suppose this namespaced XML arrives on `MQInput`:

```xml
<ord:Order xmlns:ord="https://example.com/orders" id="A1">
  <ord:Item><ord:Sku>X1</ord:Sku></ord:Item>
  <ord:Item><ord:Sku>X2</ord:Sku></ord:Item>
</ord:Order>
```

Read its root tag name, namespace elements, XML attribute, and first/last items in ESQL:

```esql
BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>

DECLARE ns NAMESPACE '<NamespaceUri>';

CREATE COMPUTE MODULE <ComputeModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        CALL CopyMessageHeaders();

        DECLARE orderRef REFERENCE TO InputRoot.XMLNSC.ns:Order;

        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.rootTag  = FIELDNAME(InputBody.*[1]);
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.orderId  = orderRef.(XMLNSC.Attribute)id;
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.count    = CARDINALITY(orderRef.ns:Item[]);
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.firstSku = orderRef.ns:Item[1].ns:Sku;
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.lastSku  = orderRef.ns:Item[<].ns:Sku;
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.hasEmail = EXISTS(orderRef.ns:Email[]);

        RETURN TRUE;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output (When <NamespaceUri> Matches the Incoming XML Namespace)</summary>

```json
{
  "rootTag": "Order",
  "orderId": "A1",
  "count": 2,
  "firstSku": "X1",
  "lastSku": "X2",
  "hasEmail": false
}
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown

- **`DECLARE ns NAMESPACE '<NamespaceUri>';`**: Binds prefix `ns` to the target XML namespace URI (for example `'https://example.com/orders'`). Note that your ESQL prefix (`ns`) does **not** have to match the sender's prefix (`ord`) — ACE matches the underlying namespace URI!
- **`DECLARE orderRef REFERENCE TO InputRoot.XMLNSC.ns:Order;`**: Points `orderRef` directly to the namespaced `<Order>` element inside the `XMLNSC` domain.
- **`FIELDNAME(InputBody.*[1])`**: `InputBody` is shorthand for the last child of `InputRoot` (here `InputRoot.XMLNSC`), `*` matches any element name regardless of tag or namespace, `[1]` picks the first child (`Order`), and `FIELDNAME(...)` returns `'Order'`.
- **`orderRef.(XMLNSC.Attribute)id`**: The field-type qualifier **`(XMLNSC.Attribute)`** tells ESQL to read an XML attribute (`id="A1"`) instead of a child tag `<id>`. (Usually XML attributes themselves have no namespace prefix unless declared `ns:id`.)
- **`CARDINALITY(orderRef.ns:Item[])`**: The trailing **`[]`** turns the path into a list of all matching `ns:Item` siblings so `CARDINALITY(...)` can count them (`2`).
- **`orderRef.ns:Item[1].ns:Sku` / `orderRef.ns:Item[<].ns:Sku`**: `[1]` reads the first item (`'X1'`), and **`[<]`** is ESQL's reverse-index shorthand for the very last element (`'X2'`).
- **`EXISTS(orderRef.ns:Email[])`**: Checks whether any `<Email>` node is present (`FALSE` here). Always pass a list path ending in `[]` inside `EXISTS(...)` and `CARDINALITY(...)`.

> [!WARNING]
> **Field names are strictly case-sensitive!** Writing `orderRef.ns:sku` instead of `orderRef.ns:Sku` does **not** throw a compile or runtime error — ESQL silently returns **`NULL`**. If a field unexpectedly turns up `NULL`, verify exact casing, namespace prefix, and `(XMLNSC.Attribute)` first.

---

# ESQL `NULL` Handling, `COALESCE` & Three-Valued Logic

In ESQL, missing fields and uninitialized variables evaluate to **`NULL`** instead of throwing an exception — and **any string concatenation or arithmetic with `NULL` turns the entire result into `NULL`**!

---

## Why `NULL` Causes Silent Bugs

```esql
-- If middleName is missing from JSON, it evaluates to NULL:
DECLARE fullName CHARACTER 'Mona' || ' ' || InputRoot.JSON.Data.middleName;
-- fullName becomes NULL!
```

Even worse, `IF` conditions follow **three-valued logic** (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, `UNKNOWN`):
- `x = NULL` is **always `UNKNOWN`** (never `TRUE`!).
- `NULL <> 'PAID'` is also **`UNKNOWN`**!
- Whenever an `IF` condition evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, ESQL silently skips the `IF` block and jumps to `ELSE`.

---

## Safe `NULL` Handling Patterns (`COALESCE`, `EXISTS`, `IS NULL`)

```esql
BROKER SCHEMA <SchemaName>

CREATE COMPUTE MODULE <ComputeModuleName>
    CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
    BEGIN
        CALL CopyMessageHeaders();

        -- 1. Supply fallback defaults with COALESCE
        DECLARE custName CHARACTER COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.name, 'Guest');
        DECLARE qty      INTEGER   COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.qty, 1);

        -- 2. Treat BOTH missing (NULL) and empty string ('') as missing
        IF COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.email, '') = '' THEN
            SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.emailWarning = 'No email provided';
        END IF;

        -- 3. Check field presence and non-null value explicitly
        IF EXISTS(InputRoot.JSON.Data.coupon[])
           AND InputRoot.JSON.Data.coupon IS NOT NULL THEN
            SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.couponApplied = TRUE;
        ELSE
            SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.couponApplied = FALSE;
        END IF;

        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.greeting = 'Hello, ' || custName;
        SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.qty      = qty;
        RETURN TRUE;
    END;
END MODULE;
```

<details data-type="output">
<summary>Expected Output (When Input JSON Is {"coupon": null})</summary>

```json
{
  "emailWarning": "No email provided",
  "couponApplied": false,
  "greeting": "Hello, Guest",
  "qty": 1
}
```

</details>

### Line-by-Line Breakdown

- **`COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.name, 'Guest')`**: Scans arguments from left to right and returns the **first non-`NULL` value**. If `name` is missing or JSON `null`, `custName` receives `'Guest'`. You can pass more than two arguments (`COALESCE(a, b, 'default')`).
- **`COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.qty, 1)`**: Ensures `qty` defaults to integer `1` so downstream math never multiplies by `NULL`.
- **`IF COALESCE(InputRoot.JSON.Data.email, '') = '' THEN`**: Classic production validation idiom — converts a `NULL` field into `''` so a single `= ''` check catches **both** missing fields (`NULL`) and blank strings (`""`).
- **`EXISTS(InputRoot.JSON.Data.coupon[])`**: Checks whether a `coupon` node exists in the tree (notice the `[]` list suffix). In JSON, `"coupon": null` **does** create a node whose value is `NULL`, so `EXISTS(...)` alone returns `TRUE`!
- **`AND InputRoot.JSON.Data.coupon IS NOT NULL`**: Always use **`IS NULL`** or **`IS NOT NULL`** (never `= NULL` or `<> NULL`) when testing for `NULL` values. Combining `EXISTS` with `IS NOT NULL` rejects both absent keys and explicit JSON `null` values.
- **`'Hello, ' || custName`**: Safe to concatenate with `||` because `COALESCE` guaranteed `custName` is never `NULL`.

---

## Quick Decision Guide

| What You Want to Check | Correct ESQL Expression |
| :--- | :--- |
| Default value if missing or `NULL` | `COALESCE(field, 'fallback')` |
| Missing **OR** empty string `""` | `COALESCE(TRIM(field), '') = ''` |
| Node is absent **OR** has value `NULL` | `field IS NULL` |
| Node is present even if empty/null | `EXISTS(field[])` |
| Assigning `NULL` to an `OutputRoot` field | **Deletes** that field from the output tree! |

> [!TIP]
> Assigning `SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.temp = NULL;` does **not** write `"temp": null` — in ESQL, setting a tree element to `NULL` **removes** it from the tree! (To output a literal JSON `null`, use `SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.temp TYPE = JSON.Null; SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.temp = NULL;` or `CREATE LASTCHILD OF ... TYPE JSON.Null NAME 'temp' VALUE NULL;`.)

---
